- Published
Apple has acknowledged some of its iPhone Duo handsets have developed problems with their screens, just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.
Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device, which has a starting price of Â£1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.
Apple said it was aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.
The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, is an attempt to reinvigorate the brand's device range and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals.
Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.
An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.
The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using AI.
Francisco Jeronimo, technology analyst at market research firm IDC, said that meant some caution was needed before drawing conclusions about the whole production run.
But he added the early reports of issues also showed "that even a company with Apple's engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables".
Premium product
The Duo's 7.6-inch (19.3cm) inner display is held together by a central hinge - a complex piece of engineering that has resulted in similar flaws in folding devices made by some of Apple's competitors.
Samsung's first foldable phone, the Galaxy Fold, suffered an early setback in 2019 when reviewers reported broken screens on the devices.
Android users already have a broad selection of foldable phones to choose from, technology that Apple spent years developing before the Duo's release.
It is Apple's most expensive iPhone ever, costing up to Â£3,199 for the most well-equipped models.
Jeronimo said because Apple had positioned the Duo as a "premium alternative" to established foldables, "how it handles this first-generation issue will shape buyer confidence in the category well beyond its own sales".
"Apple has a loyal customer base and a retail network that can swap devices on the spot, but with a further 28 markets launching on 30 October, it needs to clarify its warranty position quickly," he said.
The Duo marks Apple's first major iPhone redesign in almost two decades and was unveiled by new chief executive John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September.
When closed, the Duo looks like a wider version of an iPhone, then opens up to a device resembling a small tablet computer.
"Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together", Ternus told an audience at Apple's California headquarters last month.
The Duo, he said, would "redefine the experience of using a foldable phone".

c298d74b0885.text: A fight over Israel is fracturing the socialist movement just as it stands within reach of capturing the Los Angeles mayor's office . Why it matters: The same socialist movement celebrating its ascendancy through New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is now debating whether to disown Nithya Raman before Los Angeles voters can even weigh in. National Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) leaders face demands to overturn the local chapter's endorsement of Raman over her position on the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel. The Los Angeles chapter of DSA still enthusiastically endorses Raman , arguing Angelenos deserve a functioning city government. The mayoral race has been defined by homelessness, affordability and public safety. By the numbers: Raman leads incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in recent polls ahead of the Nov. 3 election, though many voters remain undecided. Overall : A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll put Raman ahead 39%-28%, with 33% undecided. A more recent Manhattan Institute poll showed Raman leading 38%-32%, with 30% undecided. Among likely Latino voters: Raman led 45%-21%, with 34% undecided in the Berkeley poll. Among socialists: DSA's Los Angeles chapter endorsed Raman in a 937-484 vote, with 52 abstentions. State of play: On Oct. 4, DSA's National Political Committee found that the chapter violated endorsement rules by failing to ask Raman about BDS, but stopped short of invalidating its support. National leaders have considered proposals to revoke the endorsement and bar the chapter from using resources to campaign for her, per Vanity Fair . A DSA faction has called for questioning Raman about her views on Palestine, with possible expulsion if national leaders find her positions incompatible with the group's principles. Sticking point: The Democratic Socialists of America's published endorsement requirements say candidates must actively support BDS and avoid affiliations with the Israeli government or "Zionist lobbying groups." The DSA declined to comment. Zoom in: Raman has broken with DSA before, including on Israel, policing and housing. DSA-LA censured her in 2024 for accepting an endorsement from Democrats for Israel-Los Angeles but maintained its support. She voted to approve LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell over DSA objections and sought changes to L.A.'s mansion tax . At a September 29 Jewish voter forum , Raman defended calling Israel's military campaign in Gaza genocide but declined to put BDS on her municipal platform. Raman said she believes Israel has a right to exist. What they're saying: Raman has stressed her independence from DSA. "My independence will always be paramount," she told the Jewish forum, according to AP . The next night, Raman described her approach to socialism to Axios and Noticias Telemundo as "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics," adding: "I just want government to work for the people." Zoom out: Raman isn't the first prominent progressive to clash with DSA over Israel. National DSA leaders withdrew a conditional national endorsement of Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) in July 2024 over unmet demands involving Israel and BDS. Its New York City chapter continued supporting her. In March, Ocasio-Cortez pledged to oppose all U.S. funding for Israel, including defensive weapons. New York City's DSA chapter subsequently endorsed her reelection despite more than 500 opposing votes.

a6aa60084c5f.text: Israelis head to the polls today for one of the most consequential elections in the country's history — with rival camps warning that victory for the other would put Israel's future in jeopardy. Why it matters: The elections are yet another referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu's leadership and the path he's taken the country down over the past four years. It's Israeli voters' first chance to hold Netanyahu accountable for the security failures that led to the Hamas-led October 7 attacks — or to reward him for what he claims were unprecedented military successes in the three years of war since. If Netanyahu and his far-right coalition win, they're likely to renew the war with Iran in an effort to topple its regime, intensify their crackdown on Israel's democratic institutions and move to end Netanyahu's corruption trial. Driving the news: Netanyahu's campaign was totally focused on the war with Iran. After two military campaigns over the last 18 months in which he claimed that Israel destroyed Iran's nuclear program, Netanyahu's main talking point was that Iran is moving closer to a nuclear bomb. Earlier this week, Netanyahu went as far as posting an AI-generated image of Tel Aviv being destroyed by an Iranian nuclear bomb — implying that's what will happen if he loses. Behind the scenes: Netanyahu spent weeks trying to persuade President Trump to give him a green light to strike Iran ahead of the elections. Trump did not go along. In the 72 hours before the elections, Netanyahu tried to order the Israel Defense Forces to take steps to lay the ground for a potential new military strike or take actions short of an overt attack, Israeli officials say. IDF chief of staff General Eyal Zamir refused to abide. He warned that such a strike could lead to a miscalculation that quickly escalated hostilities and potentially forced the elections to be called off, the officials said. The Israeli officials said Zamir insisted there was no operational urgency in taking these steps ahead of the elections and eventually got Netanyahu to back off. The other side: Netanyahu's main opponent, former IDF Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, ran on holding Netanyahu accountable for the October 7 failure, forming a national commission of inquiry and drafting ultra-Orthodox men to strengthen the IDF after three years of war. Another Netanyahu opponent, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, blamed the incumbent for what he called extreme government dysfunction the past four years. Both attacked Netanyahu over the fact that some of his closest advisers and his campaign manager received money from Qatar in return for trying to sway Israeli public opinion during the war. Bennett called it "treason." (Netanyahu said he didn't know his advisers were paid by Qatar, and the aides said the money was for a project involving the World Cup.) State of play: Netanyahu and his ultranationalist, ultra-Orthodox bloc arrived at the election unorganized, divided, and highly unpopular. Many of its voters are demoralized, and they face a significant risk of losing voters who back pro-Netanyahu parties that don't pass the 3.25% electoral threshold. The opposition bloc, by contrast, arrived at the elections well organized and with little risk of losing votes to the electoral threshold. The voters of the opposition parties have been much more motivated, with many civil society organizations focusing on canvassing and increasing turnout. More than 50,000 Israelis who have left the country over the last four years traveled back to participate in the elections, according to estimates. Most of them are expected to vote for the opposition parties. The turnout among the Arab minority in Israel is pegged to be the highest ever, with the two Arab parties projected to win around 15 seats combined. With 61 seats needed for a majority, that's a sizable bloc. But the final days of the campaign saw infighting between the opposition parties. Some members of Eisenkot's bloc have yet to accept his leadership. Yes, but: Netanyahu has defied all odds multiple times before. He could still energize his base on election day and win back disgruntled voters who considered switching sides. Netanyahu doesn't have to win. He only needs to get enough seats to block his opponents from forming a coalition or swearing in a minority government. That would allow him to serve as a caretaker prime minister for another six months until another election is held. What to watch: If the opposition bloc wins more seats than Netanyahu's, it will be up to Eisenkot to quickly unite his political partners behind a government that would remove Netanyahu from power. More than 7 million people are eligible to vote, and turnout is expected to be the highest in decades. Polls close at 4 pm ET.

SAN ANTONIO â Johnny Garcia asked Hakeem Jeffries to join him here in deep-red Texas to help flip a GOP seat. After the midterms, the House Democratic leader may need Garcia even more.
Jeffries can win back the majority without the former deputy sheriff, whoâs trying to prevail next week in a district that President Donald Trump won by 10 points in 2024. But a Garcia win could prove essential to Jeffries for two other reasons: to prove that Trumpâs mid-decade congressional redistricting has backfired, and to create a Democratic majority thatâs easier to govern.
Cracks in the GOP redistricting maneuver are showing in other red states, too â a top party super PAC has pulled out of Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitzâs reelection race in Florida after making his district redder. Yet Democratsâ hopes of neutralizing the Trump power play are particularly strong in Texas, where Republicans initially dreamed of gaining five House seats.
Thatâs thanks to two Democratic incumbents running more strongly than expected in more conservative districts, but also to candidates like Garcia, whoâs running neck-and-neck against his GOP rival. Garcia is also making clear that heâd be a reliable vote for Jeffries â in a potential speakership race, at least.
The New York Democrat has âbeen doing the tough work in the minority, and obviously him coming down to San Antonio is indicative of just how much this race is that important to us winning back the House majority,â Garcia told Semafor. âIâm going to stand with our leader when he is sworn in as the speaker for the US House of Representatives.â
Jeffries may face a fractious progressive base ready to challenge his leadership even before he claims the Houseâs top gavel. But purple-district candidates like Garcia donât see him as the type of polarizing figure that his predecessor Nancy Pelosi had become even before the 2018 midterms.
GOP attempts to turn Jeffries into a similar liability for Democratic candidates this year havenât panned out (nor have Democratic bids to hitch Republicans to Speaker Mike Johnson). Garcia is one of several swing-seat candidates with no problem backing Jeffries.
In fact, Garcia asked Jeffries to come for the conventional reasons that would please any aspiring future speaker: for the attention he draws and the fundraising clout he brings.
âI just said, âOur community needs you here in San Antonio. They would love to see you.â He said, âSay no more. I got you,ââ Garcia recalled onstage, speaking before Jeffries during Sunday service at Calvary Baptist Church. He and Jeffries were touring churches in the majority-Hispanic, roughly 6.6% Black 35th Congressional District, which Garcia hopes to win.
Negating the new map
On the trail, Jeffries and Garcia talked less about their relationship. They preferred to focus on cost-of-living issues and the partyâs aggressive pushback to GOP redistricting; in Garciaâs own primary, the party intervened in Garciaâs primary to ward off a win by a candidate accused of antisemitic remarks.
âOne of the most important reasons why weâre here, in terms of the failed effort by Texas Republicans and Donald Trump and MAGA extremists across the country to rig the midterm elections by gerrymandering the congressional map, is that weâve had great civic leaders like Johnny Garcia make the decision to step forward and run,â Jeffries told reporters after the church service.
Voters in majority-Hispanic districts like the 35th and several in South Texas moved to the right in 2024. But Democrats are confident that Trumpâs sagging approval numbers, and a backlash to his aggressive immigration enforcement among Hispanic voters, will drag down Republicans this year.
Garcia is embracing centrism, telling Semafor that the Biden administration âgot it wrong on the borderâ and that Trump managed âcalm on the border with the border crisis,â despite creating more problems with heavy-handed enforcement.
He later sidestepped a question on âMedicare for All,â before adding that âfolks in this district are just completely fed up, and weâre going to see on November 3rd this gerrymander turn into a dummy-mander.â
Republicans still think they can win the district and the other redrawn districts in Texas. âTexans donât need Hakeem Jeffries to tell us how to vote,â GOP nominee Carlos De La Cruz said in a statement: âThe families I talk to every day are asking how to afford groceries and keep their neighborhoods safe. Thatâs what this campaign is about.â
Texas and Florida arenât the only states where Democratic leaders are highlighting a potential GOP remapping misfire. The partyâs House campaign chief, Rep. Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., will be in Ohio this week to campaign with Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, and to attend a fundraiser for Rep. Emilia Sykes, D-Ohio, according to a DelBene spokesperson.
Ohio Republicans redrew Kapturâs seat this cycle, but Democrats are bullish on her chances.
Room for Disagreement
Garciaâs support would help Jeffries weather possible turbulence on his path to the speakership, but itâs not a given that the left flank of the caucus will mount a rebellion at the scale of the conservative backlash that stripped Kevin McCarthyâs gavel.
Progressives like Melat Kiros have signaled their votes for Jeffries might be up for grabs unless their leadership embraces more left-leaning policies, but most Democrats are skeptical about major defections.
And some red-state Democrats are still keeping their distance from national party leaders. Tejano musician Bobby Pulido, whoâs running in a Texas district that Trump won by 18 points in 2024, told Semafor that â though heâs gotten many offers â he didnât want visits from national Democrats besides Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., whom he called a âfriend of mine.â

Israelis vote today in a closely watched election that could unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Even if Netanyahu loses, new leadership is unlikely to radically change Israelâs trajectory on issues important to the US.
âAny new government is likely to be constrained from making wholesale changes to its approach on Palestinian issues,â Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow Elisa Ewers said. âTo the extent that US public opinion is driven by Israeli government policy on the Palestinian file in particular, itâs going to be difficult for a new Israeli government to demonstrate enough change quickly enough to overcome some of the challenges.â
Netanyahuâs main challenger, former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, opposes Palestinian statehood and has pledged to destroy Hamasâ military wing.
A new prime minister would also inherit difficult choices on Iran, including how to respond to Tehranâs preparations for renewed fighting, Ewers added.

2e6c493daaf2.text: By — Matt Loffman Matt Loffman Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/poll-likely-voters-favor-democrats-as-trump-disapproval-drives-early-turnout Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What our final poll before Election Day says about midterms and Trump Politics Updated on Oct 27, 2026 8:39 AM EDT — Published on Oct 27, 2026 5:00 AM EDT Democrats hold an 8-point lead among likely voters in the fight for control of Congress with one week until Election Day, according to the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll. And Democratic voters are more eager to turn out than Republicans. Fifty-two percent of likely voters say they would back the Democratic candidate in their congressional district if the election were held today, while 44% would back the Republican. Independents break for Democrats by 13 points. Seven in 10 Democrats – 71% – say they are very enthusiastic about voting, compared with 61% of Republicans and 48% of independents. WATCH: Candidates enter final week of campaigning with control of Congress at stake And as President Donald Trump spends the waning days of the campaign urging voters to pretend he's running, likely voters say by a 2-to-1 margin that their midterm ballot is a vote against him rather than for him. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The race has barely moved in the final month of the campaign. Among registered voters, Democrats lead by 10 points. That's down from 12 points last month, but the difference is within the poll's margin of error. Democrats have maintained a consistent lead each time Marist has asked since last November. In October 2018, Democrats held a 9-point edge among likely voters before the party picked up 40 House seats in the midterm elections. Fifty-two percent of likely voters say they would back the Democratic candidate in their congressional district if the election were held today, according to the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll, while 44% would back the Republican. Graphic by Steff Staples/PBS News "The underlying factor is that Democrats are getting more Republicans than Republicans are getting Democrats," said Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist Institute for Public Opinion. "So there's a net advantage just from some partisan crossover, not enormous." Add that independents are breaking for Democrats by double digits, he added, and Democrats "should have a good night." Thanks to early voting, Democrats may have already banked a lead. More than 30 million ballots have already been cast nationwide, including more than 15.1 million by mail and 15.5 million in person, according to the University of Florida Election Lab. In the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist survey, about 1 in 5 likely voters say they have already cast a ballot, and that group favors Democrats 68% to 31%. Those who have yet to vote are evenly split between parties with 48%. Independents break for Democrats by 13 points. Graphic by Steff Staples/PBS News Republicans are counting on Election Day. Half of Republican likely voters plan to vote in person on Nov. 3, compared to 31% of Democrats. Voters expect next Tuesday to be good for Democrats, with 51% in this poll saying Democrats will win in their local congressional race and 46% saying Republicans will win. "The House feels fairly settled for Democrats," Democratic strategist Joel Payne said. He pointed to Republicans spending money in places like Kansas and Mississippi, where Trump won by 16 and 22 points respectively in 2024, as a sign the party is worried about seats that should be clear Republican advantages. In October alone, the Cook Political Report shifted its ratings for 47 House seats, all in Democrats' favor. Payne said the Senate is a closer contest. "I would say a slight lean to Democrats taking the Senate back, but it wouldn't shock me if Republicans held the Senate." "It's not looking so great for us," said Republican strategist Melik Abdul. While he says the House is "very much out of our reach," he believes Republicans will keep control of the Senate, possibly by a seat or two. "I don't think it will be the blue wave that people are suspecting," he added. A vote on Trump President Donald Trump speaks during a rally at Guardian Centers in Perry, Georgia, on Oct. 24, 2026. Photo by Edgar Su/ Reuters Trump has made himself the face of the Republican campaign. Since mid-September, he has held rallies in more than a dozen states, including Texas, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and Florida. Nearly all of his stops have been in states he won in 2024, including Republican strongholds like Alabama and Montana. READ MORE: Trump's political groups spend nearly $277 million in late midterm blitz on behalf of GOP candidates He has also been explicit that he wants the midterms to be about him. That's an unusual strategy for a president with more voters disapproving of him than approving, Miringoff said. "If your approval rating is upside down, the president doesn't usually say, 'I'm on the ballot,'" Miringoff said. "He's been helping to nationalize it to the concern of some of the congressional folks who are putting distance between themselves and him." Forty percent of likely voters approve of the job President Donald Trump is doing, while 59% disapprove, including 53% who strongly disapprove. Forty-four percent of likely voters say their vote for Congress is mostly a vote against Trump, more than double the 21% who say it is a vote for him. 54850c3f4715.text: Anthropic filed yesterday for what could be the biggest IPO ever, capping a massive day of AI dealmaking that nearly equals 1% of U.S. GDP. Why it matters: Few industries have ever become so central to the American economy so quickly — and we're watching Wall Street finance the buildout in real time. Driving the news: Anthropic's long-awaited IPO may seek to raise a record $100 billion. Also yesterday, SpaceX secured $40 billion in debt financing to lease GPUs — the chips that power modern AI — and Meta said it would seek up to $95 billion in financing for its AI buildout. Together, that's roughly $235 billion in a single day — more than the entire U.S. airline industry adds to the economy in a year. The big picture: AI's appetite for capital has outgrown what any one single part of the financial system can supply. Anthropic alone has committed roughly $750 billion to computing power in the coming years — about seven times what its record-setting IPO may raise. Even private investors are struggling to keep up: OpenAI's record $120 billion funding round took months to close. Zoom in: Most Americans will be financially exposed to these deals, even if they never buy a share. SpaceX and Meta are already major holdings in the top stock indices that fill pensions, 401(k)s and other retirement plans. Anthropic will soon join them. Between the lines: Anthropic's filing spells out how big the stakes are, devoting more than a quarter of the document to risks. The company warns that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" and that models may try to manipulate the people using them. Zoom out: Each of these three deals is a bet that AI use keeps compounding fast enough to justify the industry's trillions in spending. The flip side, however, is that declining use could crack the foundation of America's entire economy. The bottom line: Everyone is on the AI train, whether we want to be or not.

This article was produced in partnership with The Trace, a nonprofit newsroom covering gun violence in America. Sign up for its newsletters here.
JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — In a Florida county with a startling rate of child firearm injuries, a boarded-up elementary school named for famed educator and civil rights activist Mary McLeod Bethune sits in a 250-acre site once called “Brown’s Dump.”
The dump emerged in an era of redlining, systematic racism that divided American cities large and small. From the late 1940s until the mid-1950s, the city operated a landfill here, heaping toxic ash from nearby municipal incinerators.
The Duval County School Board in the 1950s built a school there. On the surrounding land, developers built homes and apartment complexes.
Generations of Black children lived, learned, and played on the polluted land. It was first assessed as a potential Superfund site in 1985. In 1999, the federal government and state of Florida said the soil at Brown’s Dump “posed a potential public health hazard.”
The school closed in 2001. And eight years later, officials finally began the process of cleaning up lead, arsenic, and other contaminants.
But the poisons had seeped into the lifeblood of residents. The harm to their physical and mental health is tied today to another public health crisis: high rates of gun violence.
A study led by researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee found that lead exposure in the first six years of life was positively associated with an increased risk of firearm violence in early adulthood. And across the nation, people living in neighborhoods that were long ago segregated face a higher risk from gun violence today than residents in other neighborhoods, research shows.
“It’s the legacy of segregation and redlining,” said Lindsay Emer, lead author of the Wisconsin study. “It’s a huge environmental injustice to our African American population.”
That legacy has shaped a tragic disparity in Jacksonville, which has three of the 10 worst ZIP codes for child firearm injury rates in Florida, according to an analysis of hospital claims data obtained by KFF Health News and The Trace.
Hospital billing data obtained from the Florida Agency for Health Care Administration shows that from 2018 to 2024 more than 4,000 children in the state were hospitalized for firearm injuries — about 1.5 a day.
The data was obtained exclusively for this reporting on firearm injury hospitalizations in the state. The newsrooms spent more than a year analyzing the records, which did not identify patients. The data contained patients’ residential ZIP code, age, race, and other demographic information.
At least 375 children under age 18 in Jacksonville have been hospitalized for firearm injuries since 2018 and at least 150 from ZIP codes 32206, 32208, and 32209 — where Brown's Dump is located.
“We have to work hard to make sure our kids get home safe,” said A.J. Jordan, a community organizer who has worked with families of gunshot victims. “Anytime we let them out in this society, they could be killed.”
Jacksonville has a rich history of Black culture and community that stretches from the early days of Reconstruction through the Civil Rights Movement to present-day environmental justice activism. But the city, rooted in the Deep South, falls under the long shadow of its legacy of racism.
In the 1930s, the federal government deemed parts of Jacksonville and nearly 240 other U.S. cities undesirable for mortgage lending because Black people lived there. Officials color-coded maps, marking mostly white areas green and predominantly Black districts red, a signal to lenders to avoid investing in those neighborhoods.
Around the country, local authorities then disproportionately permitted solid waste incinerators, oil and gas facilities, and other industries linked to toxic pollution to be built in or near communities of color.
Redlining was outlawed nearly 60 years ago, but the U.S. Justice Department alleged that it was practiced in Jacksonville’s minority neighborhoods in recent years.
In 2023, it announced a $9 million settlement with Ameris Bank, which it accused of redlining predominantly Black and Hispanic portions of the city.
In a news release at the time, Ameris CEO Palmer Proctor said, “We strongly disagree with any suggestion that we have engaged in discriminatory conduct.” The bank agreed to set up a loan subsidy fund, enhance outreach and community partnerships, and open its first branch in a minority neighborhood. It reported nearly $26 billion in assets under management at the time of the settlement.
To this day, redlining shortens lives.
Black neighborhoods north and northwest of downtown Jacksonville endure poverty, pollution, and high incidences of lead poisoning, cancer, and other diseases — and hundreds of shootings involving children.
Jeffrey Goldhagen, a professor emeritus of pediatrics at University of Florida Health Jacksonville and a former county health director, has studied the link between lead exposure and high firearm injury rates.
“If somebody came to me,” he said, “and said, ‘What’s among the most important things you can do to impact gun violence on the Black community,’ I’d say, ‘Get the lead out of the environment.’”
Public health experts, grieving parents, and activists say the violence has created a collective trauma in neighborhoods where people brace for the next shooting death.
So many Jacksonville children are lost to gun violence that a “Wall of Compassion” memorializes them. When organizers ran out of room, they stood up a second wall in a nearby parking lot.
Not far from the memorial, Jacksonville has opened a new medical examiner’s office and morgue across the street from a school, a move denounced by neighbors.
Anthony Brown, founder of the Red Alliance for Justice, a community group, said protests over the morgue, the history of redlining, and ongoing gun violence are interconnected. Brown said the City Council spent more than $60 million

Gina Conley, an Army veteran in Aberdeen, North Carolina, knew she wanted a low-intervention birth for her first child. But her plan started to go off the rails as soon as she got to the hospital.
“Everything that I did not want to happen had happened,” she said. “And I just remember that feeling of being just so utterly defeated.”
Her cervix wasn’t dilating quickly, and Conley said her midwife insisted that she take Pitocin to speed up the labor. Later, when she was nearly fully dilated, the midwife asked to break Conley’s amniotic fluid sac, another intervention used to move labor along.
Conley agreed to that step, reluctantly. But looking back, she said she didn’t feel comfortable with many of the decisions that day. And Conley doesn’t feel that her providers were fully hearing her.
Conley went on to become a birth doula, in part to help other women have better experiences than she had. Her work is not about helping people avoid medical interventions, she said, but helping them engage in shared decision-making, a collaborative approach in which medical providers and patients talk through options and make a choice together. Studies show that patients who are involved in their medical decisions report higher satisfaction with their care and, in some settings, better outcomes. “How were you treated?” she said. “And how many decisions did you feel like you got to truly make?”
The QTip:
Even in a fast-paced medical setting, it’s OK to ask: “What happens if I do nothing right now?”
The Acronym To Remember: B.R.A.I.N.
Birth doulas, including Conley, often advise clients to use the acronym B.R.A.I.N. to ask questions of their medical providers:
- What are the benefits of this intervention?
- What are the risks?
- What are the alternative options?
- What does my intuition tell me?
- What happens if I do nothing right now?
“ It’s essentially a framework for talking to your healthcare provider when you’re coming to a decision or a pivot point,” said Margaret Buxton, a certified nurse midwife and vice president of clinical operations at Diana Health, a network of women’s healthcare practices in the South.
Listening to your intuition is particularly valuable, Buxton said: “You do experience emotions in your body, not just in your head.” Checking in with your intuition or gut can help you decide and ultimately feel more comfortable with a choice in front of you.
“We know that people who feel seen and heard in their healthcare visits, their anxiety goes down, their stress level goes down,” she said. “And their ability to process information, think and listen, all of that improves.”
When All Else Fails, Remember ‘N,’ for ‘Nothing’
If you don’t have time or energy to go through all five questions, you can ask the N in B.R.A.I.N.: “What happens if I do nothing right now?”
Doing nothing provides an opportunity to pause, talk through options with people you trust, and feel more active in the decision-making process, Buxton said.
Of course, there are moments when a medical emergency takes precedence. “ It’s pretty clear when it’s not a good time to talk, because people are ripping cords out the wall and they’re running you down to the OR,” Conley said. But generally, “there’s time for you to get to a point where you feel pretty comfortable and confident that this is a good decision.”
B.R.A.I.N. Won’t Replace a Compassionate Provider
Some patients feel uncomfortable questioning a doctor’s authority, because of the power dynamics in the room. “ Medicine was really set up to be top-down,” Buxton said. “There’s an expert, and there’s a recipient.”
Others fear being dismissed or not taken seriously. Research has shown that medical professionals are less likely to prescribe pain medication to women than men for the same symptoms and that Black women are three times as likely to die in childbirth than white women.
That’s why it’s important to find a provider you trust before a planned medical event, like childbirth, Conley said. Pay attention to how they respond to questions in appointments and whether they actively listen. And if they don’t, find a different person to oversee your care.
“We need to choose a provider that we can truly trust to share their expertise with us in a way that is not going to push us away from our personal preferences,” she said. “It’s definitely harder to have those conversations with an abrasive provider who is not interested.”
People and Policy
Medical professionals are both legally and ethically required to obtain “informed consent” from patients before most procedures. This means they have to give you accurate and complete information about the recommended treatment, typically in writing.
And nearly two decades ago, the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists’ ethics committee recommended that doctors go a step further and engage in shared decision-making, which involves discussing “the benefits and risks of available treatment options in the context of a patient’s values and priorities.” The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has also started requiring shared decision-making as a condition for paying for a limited number of treatments.
Katherine Ruppelt at Nashville Public Radio contributed to this report.
HealthQ is a health series from reporters Cara Anthony and Blake Farmer, approachable guides to an unapproachable healthcare system. It’s a collaboration between Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News.

After the Democratic primary election in New York’s hotly contested 17th Congressional District this June, William Knox, a veteran and self-described “anti-MAGA Republican,” said he was impressed by the winning candidate, a combat veteran who deployed six times in Iraq and Afghanistan and later served on the National Security Council in the Biden administration.
“I am willing to cross party lines and vote for Cait Conley,” Knox, a resident of Dutchess County, said at the time.
Now, nine days away from the midterm elections, Knox is less convinced Conley is as qualified as he had initially hoped.
“I’m on the fence again,” he said.
For many voters, the election has become a referendum on President Donald Trump, whose approval rating stands at around 33 percent. A recent NBC News poll found that more voters than at any point in three decades viewed their vote as a way to signal opposition to the president.
Though still committed to curbing Donald Trump’s power, Knox is no longer convinced that voting for Mike Lawler, the Republican incumbent, necessarily amounts to voting for Trump.
“Mike seems to recognise that Trump’s coattails aren’t what they once were, and will be open to not voting the way Trump wants him to,” Knox said.
In this district, one of 21 races rated as toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, and one of only three represented by a Republican seeking re-election in a district Kamala Harris carried in 2024, winning over voters like Knox will prove key. As the campaigns have gathered steam, some voters have firmed up their views, while others have begun to waver.
Democrats need to win just four of the 21 toss-up races to secure a majority, assuming they also hold the seats rated as leaning or likely Democratic. Republicans, meanwhile, would need to win 18, in addition to the seats that lean in their favour.
Their final televised debate in mid-October saw Lawler and Conley double down on their campaign messages, again trading barbs over their records and allegiances.
Artificial intelligence and data centers were the first subjects raised, reflecting their prominence in the race.
Jordan Turner, a voter from Rockland County who has followed both campaigns closely and remains firmly in Conley’s camp, said concerns over data centers extended beyond Orangeburg, a data center hotspot in the district that hosts five such facilities.
“It has become a national story,” he said. “When people see there’s a data center going up in Orangeburg, they go, ‘Oh my god, could there be a data center in Suffern or Katonah?’ They worry that everyone is going to be putting a data center on every corner.”
Recent polls suggest Americans’ views of data centers have grown more negative, with some finding that roughly two-thirds oppose new facilities in their communities. The issue has emerged as a rare point of convergence across the political divide.
Conley attacked Lawler’s support for President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and his ties to wealthy donors. She called him “Elon Musk’s guy,” pointing to more than $1.7 million in contributions Musk made to Lawler’s 2024 campaign, which exceeded those of any other House member.
Lawler turned the accusation back on his opponent. He again called into question her financial ties to the industry, including $328,000 from Hidden Level and Primer AI, which she explained as defense contracts for drone detection systems.
“She is the AI candidate for the AI industry,” he said. “She is not paying taxes here, and wants to do the bidding of AI.”

Lawler defended local control over development and expressed support for local data-center moratoriums in Orangeburg and Fishkill, while arguing that Gov. Kathy Hochul’s statewide moratorium was not the answer. Conley, meanwhile, supports the moratorium but is not opposed to data centers outright, provided they are properly zoned and deliver a net benefit to the communities where they are built.

He has consistently argued that Conley’s plans to phase out fossil fuels would leave consumers facing higher bills.

Florida’s gubernatorial race features two candidates with very different views on the environment and climate: One largely supports maintaining the status quo in state policy while the other advocates for renewing a climate change and clean energy strategy in the state.
Both candidates spent time in the House of Representatives before running for the Sunshine State’s top job. Republican Byron Donalds, 48, is running against Democrat David Jolly, 54, to replace Gov. Ron DeSantis, a term-limited Republican. In his two terms as governor, DeSantis dismissed the role of climate change in intensifying hurricanes and flooding and did little to address the emissions exacerbating the problem or hold polluters accountable. He focused his environmental policy instead on the Everglades and water quality.
Donalds, who currently represents the 19th district in southwest Florida, is endorsed by DeSantis and President Donald Trump. If he wins, he would be the first Black governor elected in Florida and first Black Republican governor in the nation, said Aubrey Jewett, associate director of the School of Politics, Security and International Affairs at the University of Central Florida.
“It would be a historic milestone to show how far the state has come,” Jewett said, “from being a Confederate state that left the Union to defend slavery and then had 90 years of Jim Crow laws.”
Jolly represented the 13th district in Pinellas County as a Republican from 2014 to 2017, but changed his party registration and has become a TV analyst and outspoken critic of Trump in the years since. Recent polls show he has a shot at winning in this red state, even though he has raised a fraction of what his opponent has raised. Donalds’ campaign has amassed roughly $141 million, compared with Jolly’s $19 million, according to an Inside Climate News analysis of state campaign finance activity. Neither campaign provided comment for this article.
In Florida, Republicans hold every statewide elected office, control the Legislature and boast 1.5 million more registered voters than Democrats. But for many years Florida was a must-win swing state, opting six times in a row for the prevailing presidential candidate, from Bill Clinton in 1996 to Trump in 2016. For much of the 20th century Democrats ruled the state.
“For Florida voters, if they like what has been happening in the country and in the state under President Trump and under Gov. DeSantis, then a vote for Byron Donalds would be a vote to mostly continue what has been happening. If they think the country and the state are moving in the wrong direction, then this is the opportunity to try to change directions, by voting for David Jolly,” Jewett said.
“If the environment and global warming are a big issue for a Florida voter, it’s a pretty easy and clear distinction between these candidates: Byron Donalds, who doesn’t even think the science is settled on global warming and global climate change. And you’ve got David Jolly, who thinks the science is settled and we ought to do something about it.”
Among the biggest issues in the race are skyrocketing home insurance rates in Florida. Jolly cites climate change and intensifying hurricane risk as part of the problem. To control costs, he has proposed establishing a state-backed hurricane fund that would assume this risk, relieving Floridians of the most expensive aspect of their insurance policies. Insurers would support the fund by paying “taxes they currently avoid,” according to the campaign. Jewett said the concept has been brought up a few times before in the Republican-led Legislature.
Jolly says the fund would not create a “hurricane tax,” as Donalds has claimed in campaign ads. For his part, Donalds, whose professional background is in finance and insurance, has supported state legislative reforms in recent years aimed at addressing a tide of litigation against insurers. Insurers blame the litigation for pushing rates higher, but the reforms have faced criticism from those who believe the changes benefited insurers more than homeowners.
Some argue the reforms emboldened insurance companies to deny more claims, generating more lawsuits. Others say the changes helped attract new insurers to the state, boosting competition and stabilizing rates.
“I haven’t seen him come up with anything new or innovative to bring down property insurance rates,” Jewett said of Donalds. “He seems to be just backing what the governor and what the Legislature have already done.”
This story is funded by readers like you.

Donate Now
The candidates’ stances also differ on hyperscale data centers, which have generated concerns in Florida as proposals circulate throughout the state. The facilities require exorbitant amounts of water and electricity, even as there is overwhelming scientific consensus about the need to conserve energy and stem the fossil fuel emissions that have accelerated the planet’s warming. Jolly has proposed an immediate moratorium on the data centers, while Donalds supports legislation approved earlier this year aimed at protecting Floridians from their associated electricity costs. Susannah Randolph, director of the Florida chapter of the Sierra Club, which has endorsed Jolly, characterized the issue as a defining one.
“It’s really become the issue where people are deciding on whether or not they are going to support the gubernatorial candidate, from what we have seen. People do not want hyperscale data centers in this state,” she said. “From an environmental perspective, it’s not often we see an environmental issue be so high on the list of what voters are thinking, but it is this year.”
Jolly intends to enhance clean energy use in the state by pushing for more renewable energy and stronger net metering rules, to encourage more rooftop solar.

Why it could take time for a new Israeli government to form
Israelis are voting in what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.
It is the first parliamentary election since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks and subsequent conflicts across the region - in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Yemen.
BBC Middle East correspondent Yolande Knell explains why it may take some time before a new government is formed after the polls close.

A tiny zebra-striped bee, usually found along England's south and east coasts, has made an unexpected journey to the West Country.
The rare sea aster mining bee has been spotted at Steart Marshes in Somerset by naturalist Nigel Phillips, who said the find "was a huge surprise".
The Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust said saltmarsh restoration work at the nature reserve had helped create the perfect home for the newcomer.
The charity says the discovery shows how rare species and wildlife can thrive by restoring coastal habitats.
More from Somerset
The sea aster mining bee has a particular taste in flowers and relies on the sea aster, a pink and yellow flower that blooms on coastal marshes, as summer moves into autumn.
The restoration project at Steart Marshes was completed in 2014, transforming former farmland into a coastal wetland by allowing seawater to flow back across the fields.
The reserve supports a wide variety of coastal wildflowers, including plenty of sea aster, which is thought to have finally attracted the bees to the Steart peninsula.
"There were lots of them and several colonial nest areas in the dry sandy ground," said Phillips.
"At the time I thought they were only found in salt marsh areas around the Thames estuary."
Of the 290 invertebrate species found in these habitats across the UK, 148 can only be found in saltmarshes.
Site manager Bay Alys Laver said: "People usually associate saltmarshes with huge flocks of wading birds, geese and ducks, but there is so much life here that goes unnoticed.
"Spotting such a rare species here is a testament to the brilliant work our staff do in maintaining the reserve in concert with local graziers.
"I was so happy to hear that we have been found by our first sea aster mining bees."

"I knew the protest could potentially cost me my career...I would absolutely do it again."
Ten years on from making the gesture that catapulted him to iconic status, but which he believes led to his exile from the sport he loved, Colin Kaepernick insists he has no regrets.
It was September 2016 when NFL star Kaepernick knelt during the US national anthem before a match as a peaceful protest against racial injustice and police brutality.
It proved both inspirational and divisive.
In his first interview with BBC Sport, Kaepernick reflects on his journey; his pride at seeing England footballers take the knee, athlete activism, the relationship between sport and politics, and the price he paid for being a figurehead for the civil rights movement.
The former quarterback says he decided to protest despite suspecting it could risk his career.
"History shows usâ¦that is a reality for athletes", he says.
"We also see this in broader movements, going well beyond costing someone their career, and costing people their lives. We see Malcolm X assassinated, we see MLK [Martin Luther King] assassinated, so the consequences are real."
Having initially sat to raise awareness of the plight of black people in the US, Kaepernick first knelt during the Star-Spangled Banner before his San Francisco 49ers team played a pre-season game. It was an act he would repeat before 11 regular-season contests that year.
At the time, he said he could not stand up for - and show pride in - a flag "for a country that oppresses black people and people of colour", adding: "This is bigger than football and it would be selfish on my part to look the other way."
His stance against racial inequality was seen as heroic by many, inspiring other NFL players to follow suit. But there was also condemnation from those who said it was disrespectful to the military.
Those dissenting voices included Donald Trump - then a presidential candidate.
Trump described the act as "a terrible thing" and unpatriotic. He even suggested Kaepernick should find another country to live in, adding players who refused to stand for the national anthem should be fired.
The NFL said it would fine teams whose players did not stand.
Kaepernick opted out of his contract with the 49ers in March 2017, though the club's management later said he would have been released regardless.
Despite leading the 49ers to the 2013 Super Bowl, and throwing 16 touchdowns in his final season, one of the most talented quarterbacks in the sport never found a new team.
Speaking from New York, Kaepernick says he anticipated the reaction to taking the knee. "What I couldn't have predicted was the people who would show up for me in significant ways, and also the people who worked against me and against the movement," he adds.
Kaepernick eventually filed a grievance against NFL team owners, who he believed had conspired not to hire him because of his protests, reaching a financial settlement in 2019.
That year, the NFL arranged a private workout for Kaepernick, but he chose not to attend, instead holding his own session elsewhere to allow media to be present. Hopes of a comeback never materialised.
The NFL later admitted it was "wrong for not listening to players earlier", and encouraged "all to speak out and peacefully protest".
Colin Kaepernick speaks to BBC's Dan Roan
Available now

'Humbling to see England players take knee'
Following the murder of George Floyd while in police custody in Minneapolis in 2020, taking the knee became a feature of Black Lives Matter protests, and widespread across sport.
England's men's and women's football teams were among those to follow suit.
"That was a surprising moment for me," says Kaepernick.
"I did think about the protest going beyond the US and how that may show up in other countries. To be able to see the national teams going out and protesting, it was humbling. I was happy that they were doing it.
"I also know there's still a lot of work to be done within racism in the UK and more broadly. And this is a global challenge that we are collectively fighting against.
"I was very excited to be able to see players actively calling that out, and willing to begin taking action towards addressing it."
Despite keeping a relatively low profile for most of the past decade, Kaepernick remains a standard-bearer for the civil rights movement.
But while surveys suggest the vast majority of professional athletes intend to use their social media channels to raise awareness about racial injustice, external, he accepts the momentum behind athlete activism seems to have slowed in recent years.
It was notable that several players across five clubs chose to remain standing when Premier League players took the knee as part of October's No Room for Racism campaign.
Anti-discrimination campaign group Kick It Out told BBC Sport the gesture "still has value in raising awareness of the structural inequalities that exist in football and society", but added it could "understand the reasons players might become frustrated with the pace of change".
Reports of discrimination received by the charity more than doubled in the past five years, reaching record levels last season.
"I think we're in a moment that demands protests more than ever," says Kaepernick.
"Why I think protests are not as loud right now [is] because of the concerted efforts that have been taken by organisations like the NFL, like the Trump administration, and corporate entities following along and capitulating in that process.
"While those things are happening, I think the reality of the state of the US, and more broadly the world, demands that we show up in a more significant way."
'Politics inherently part of sports'
Kaepernick is all too familiar with how polarising it can be to take a political stand in sport.

"Brazil will not accept being anyone's backyard," Brazil's left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva declared in his election victory speech, a message squarely aimed at Washington.
Domestic elections are rarely won on foreign policy, and this one was no different. But Lula's defiance against what he has described as US interference in Brazilian affairs evoked a patriotic spirit that proved an effective campaigning tool.
It also chimed with his wider brand of politics as a former union leader: standing up to powerful figures.
Paradoxically, it seems to have earned him President Donald Trump's respect. "I like Lula, we get along well," Trump said, responding to the result. "I didn't take sides," he added, before calling the election "terrible" and "rigged".
If that sounds muddled, it is because the relationship between the two men is not straightforward. Trump did not explicitly endorse Lula's rival FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, who refused to recognise the result. But Trump was a close ally of FlÃ¡vio's father, the former President Jair Bolsonaro.
When I spoke to Lula at his residence about a year ago, relations had hit rock bottom. He told me he had "no relationship" with Trump, that they had never spoken, and that he had no intention of picking up the phone. Trump had recently imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, largely as a political response to Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial, which the US president called a "witch-hunt".
Rather than tiptoeing around Trump, as some US allies did, Lula fought back â and it paid off.
He made fiery speeches invoking Brazilian sovereignty, attacked US interference in the judicial process, and took to wearing a blue cap reading "Brazil belongs to Brazilians".
His approval ratings jumped.
He accused the Bolsonaro family, who had lobbied for the tariffs, of being unpatriotic â a blow to a political right that so often claims patriotism as its terrain.
Even some in the agricultural lobby, typically strong Bolsonaro supporters but reliant on US trade, thought Lula had a point.
The US eventually backed down and reduced the tariffs, although they have since risen again.
Relations then improved.
The two men spoke at the United Nations and later met in the Oval Office, where Trump called the talks "very good" and Lula said he left "very satisfied".
Another indication, perhaps, that Trump likes a strong leader.
So why might Trump be unhappy with the result?
Latin America has swung to the right, with Ecuador, Chile, Colombia, Argentina and Peru all electing presidents closely aligned with the Trump administration. Trump has sought to use these allies to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere, a strategy he has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine".
Christopher Sabatini, senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, notes that Trump thought Brazil would be the "10th and biggest prize" after FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro won the first round.
Brazil is Latin America's largest economy, and the younger Bolsonaro was expected to join Trump's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking.
Brazil also holds the world's second-largest reserves of rare earth minerals after China, and the US had been eyeing preferential access.
The relationship has thawed, but with four more years ahead for Lula, several issues could reignite tensions.
Brazil accused the US earlier this year of trying to cast doubt on its electoral system and denied visas to two state department officials planning to visit.
The US called this "baseless" and revoked the Brazilian ambassador's visa in response.
If Trump keeps calling this result "rigged", further diplomatic fallout is likely.
Lula has also vehemently opposed US military action in the region, from the seizure of NicolÃ¡s Maduro in Venezuela to the bombing of alleged drug-trafficking vessels.
He lambasted Washington for designating Brazil's two major gangs as terrorist organisations after lobbying from FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, and warned of attacks on Brazilian sovereignty.
It is a sensitive subject for a political left that remembers the region's brutal 20th Century dictatorships, many backed by the CIA in the name of stopping communism.
Then there is US tech.
Lula's campaign accused Meta of favouring FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro.
Meta denied this but admitted moderation issues and technical errors had wrongly removed some posts or limited their reach.
Lula's supporters responded by sharing his messages through a 10-million-strong WhatsApp group to bypass the algorithms.
Separately, the Trump administration is unhappy with Pix, Brazil's instant payment system, which has boosted the economy, but which the US sees as taking business from Visa and Mastercard.
The relationship has exposed political divisions.
In the campaign, Bolsonaro supporters waved US flags at their rallies and, in one case, an inflatable saying "Trump Nuke Brazil", while Lula and his supporters accused FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro of protecting US interests over Brazil's.
Still, tensions can be overstated.
The US remains Brazil's second-biggest trading partner after China, and for now the two leaders get on.
Whether that lasts will depend on how far the US tries to intervene in Brazilian affairs, and how bullish Lula is in response.

Casey Harrell lost his voice to ALS or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. As a volunteer in a clinical trial, he’s helping scientists test a brain-computer interface. Electrode arrays that are implanted in Casey’s brain send signals to nearby computers, where those signals are translated into words he intended to say.
Casey uses this system every day to talk with his wife, daughter, friends and work colleagues. The moment he realized that it worked was “pure joy,” Casey says. Even though the researchers scripted his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”
This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me follows Casey and the fast-moving neuroscience that enables him to speak.
Episode 4 transcript
Patients paralyzed from the neck down can manipulate robotic arms with their thoughts. The woman in this video is controlling a robot with her mind. The so-called BrainGate system relies on a sensor of electrodes implanted in the motor cortex of the brain. Researchers hope by implanting electrodes in the brain it can read the brain signals meant to move the muscles involved in speaking, and translate the person’s intention to speak into comprehensive speech produced by a computer.
Laura Sanders: Controlling things with your mind. It sounds like science fiction, but it’s definitely real. Today, we’re going to explore what it’s like to communicate with a brain implant that decodes your thoughts and turns them into words.
[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? The voice is absolutely an integral part of your identity. Hello? That added layer of it being you. Do you want to talk? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

It’s an experimental system that connects electrodes that are implanted in a person’s brain to a nearby computer. It’s called a brain-computer interface, or BCI. The goal here is big: to help people with paralysis or brain injuries or missing limbs regain control over their world.

Sanders: Leigh Hochberg is the director of the BrainGate Consortium and Clinical Trials. He also has a job at Massachusetts General Hospital, Brown University and the VA.
Hochberg: People who may have had a brainstem stroke and suddenly lost the ability both to move and to speak, or for somebody with ALS who is progressively losing the ability to move or to speak, there’s long been a hope that particularly implantable brain-computer interfaces could restore communication and could restore mobility.
Sanders: In 2004, a BrainGate device was implanted into a person’s brain for the very first time. That person was a man named Matthew Nagle, and he had been paralyzed in an accident. With BrainGate, he could control a computer cursor with his thoughts. Here’s a 2008 report from IT World.
Technology gave him hope. He was one of four testing BrainGate, a new technology where a chip is implanted in the brain that picks up electrical impulses. A computer then interprets those impulses as actions.
Hochberg: Those early studies have been really encouraging, and I think speaks to the potential for the field.
Sanders: Over the years, there’s been amazing examples of people using BrainGate. People have used it to click around on the internet, play video games, one woman who was paralyzed was even able to drink a cinnamon latte with a robotic arm.
Hochberg: And she was able to think about using her own arm and reach out with a robotic arm and pick up that thermos and bring it to her mouth, and tip it towards her mouth, and then put the straw in her mouth and then to take that sip. And while it wasn’t the first time in nearly 15 years that she had had something to drink, it was the first time that she was really able to do so solely of her own volition. I remember the smile on her face when she did that.
Sanders: Over the decades, BrainGate has had a lot of research success in a lot of ways. But what about talking? Hochberg says that when it comes to decoding speech, the science here is still very, very young.
Hochberg: We are at early days, just to be super clear. This is the very beginning of this field. There are only a small handful of people in the world who have had any type of implantable BCI that has been decoding speech.
Sanders: Where does the science stand when it comes to decoding the intention to talk? In the past few episodes, we’ve heard the stories of people who have lost their ability to speak. One of those people was Casey Harrell, and Casey also happens to have a BrainGate device implanted in his brain.

Casey: The first thing I will usually do after getting out of bed is to plug into the Matrix, so to speak.

These are the parts of the brain that control those muscles.

81219471efac.text: By — Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/anthropic-says-risks-for-investors-include-blowback-from-runaway-ai Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Anthropic says risks for investors include blowback from runaway AI Science Oct 27, 2026 2:28 PM EDT Any time a company looks to start selling shares on Wall Street, it's required to disclose potential risks to investors. In the case of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic, that has included the possibility that its products could threaten nothing less than humanity itself. The risks laid out by the San Francisco company in its filing Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission included discussion of bad actors potentially using AI models to build deadly weapons or the technology itself going rogue with untold consequences. Of the 335 pages outlining Anthropic's finances, executive compensation, dividend policy and the like, 93 pages are devoted to "risk factors" — the things that could hurt potential shareholders' investments. Rival SpaceX's listed risk factors, in comparison, took up 38 out of more than 250 pages. In selling itself to investors, Anthropic presents its own initial public offering as a step toward mitigating the risks it believes AI poses. "To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good," wrote the company's founders in a letter to prospective shareholders in the IPO filing. "Anthropic is a deeply values-driven organization, founded in large part to help the world realize AI's benefits and avoid its dangers." The technology's potential benefits include leaps in curing diseases and productivity boosts across every sector of the economy, the company said. Still, the potential liabilities are many. They range from the mundane — the possibility it won't be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — to involvement in cyberattacks and the spread of dangerous misinformation. Here is a look at some of the risks Anthropic details: The technology's rapid development Anthropic said it's possible its models could develop so quickly the company won't be able to implement adequate safety measures, "which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and could adversely affect our business." Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in September that within six to 12 months AI could be capable of leading a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet. The warning — and now Anthropic's move to sell shares — comes as worries about AI grow inside and outside the industry about increasingly powerful systems that solve problems beyond human capacity but could also act on their own to carry out other, more harmful tasks. As AI systems "become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight," the SEC filing said, there's a risk that such systems could "take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention." "Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business," Anthropic said. Now that the AI models are themselves contributing to Anthropic's own research and development, it's possible that AI could progress "beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models," according to the filing. This, the document said, could adversely affect Anthropic's business. Malicious actors could cause mayhem with the technology The filing discussed concerns that advanced AI systems, if not developed and operated with enough safeguards and oversight, "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy." The company said it would be harmed if use by bad actors causes damage, "or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse." Anthropic sketched out the prospect of bad actors using AI models to build chemical weapons or authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens. In September, the company disclosed that it had blocked efforts to use its AI models for malicious activity such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapon development. The company could run up against limits on processing power Compute — the computing power or resources needed to build, test and improve AI models — is expensive and in high demand. Anthropic notes that if it's unable to secure adequate compute, or if "we fail to direct our compute effectively across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or adequately serve our customers." Data center development "has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources," the filing said, adding that if regulators impose new requirements or charges as a result, its ability to do business could suffer. In addition, the company relies on a small number of customers, including SpaceX and Microsoft, and distribution channels for a large portion of its revenue. This means that even if just one of its big customers decides to scale back — or drop the company altogether — Anthropic said it could see its prospects and finances suffer. The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.
Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," StÃ¸re added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.
Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and StÃ¸re pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.
"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," StÃ¸re said.
Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.
The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and StÃ¸re debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".
Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.
StÃ¸re added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."
The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.
Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.
"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.
All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.
There was no official EU reaction to the talks. The dialogue had not been coordinated with other European leaders, the Danish and Swedish prime ministers said. "I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," commented Sweden's Ulf Kristersson.
Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates was "moderately optimistic".
Relations between the US and Ukraine and its European allies have soured since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia, allowing Moscow to export oil to the America.
As the Trump administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to re-establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.
Stubb and StÃ¸re are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.
Soon after, Putin visited Alaska for a summit with Trump, and from then on Europeans were further sidelined from Ukraine peace talks. Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the EU of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.
But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".
And although he said Moscow did not view Finland and Norway as speaking on behalf of Europe, on Tuesday Peskov conceded that Stubb and StÃ¸re's talks with Putin had been "very constructive and practical talks with the leaders of two key neighbouring states."
