For a read into which jobs in tech are mission-critical, take a look at Microsoftâs buyout offer, extended this week to a quarter of its employees.
Excluded from the 60,000 workers eligible for severance are people who work in roles tied to data centers, cybersecurity, quantum computing, sales, and marketing, Bloomberg reported. Employees eligible for the buyouts include those in its Xbox, Windows, Copilot, and finance divisions.
Some of the cuts may reflect overstaffing: AI was already responsible for 30% of code at Microsoft as of a year and a half ago â and Meta, Google, and Amazon have also made big staffing cuts. But the teams companies choose to protect during layoffs can often help serve as a guide to the future, something investors will be asking about when Microsoft releases earnings Wednesday.

b4ad179f9b44.text:
Lizâs view
Anthropicâs IPO prospectus is a perfect ink-blot test.
Believers will see a fast-growing company with blue-chip backers, $131 billion of cash, and founders with a seriousness of purpose. Anthropic has burned less than 7% of the capital it has raised, good enough for respected industry trade SemiAnalysis to declare it âthe most efficient scaling of a business in the history of capitalism.â
Skeptics will see a loss-making company whose marketing expenses are rising twice as fast as revenue. Anthropic is carrying huge future liabilities â at least $542 billion in payments due for data-center leases and chips, a figure that appears only in footnotes and one it canât hope to meet without continuous fundraising.
While the believers will see narrowing operating losses as a sign Anthropic is getting costs under control, skeptics see the number just underneath it, $81 billion in net losses, as proof that a lot of Anthropicâs expenses were shifted to investors and lenders whose bill is coming due.
Even the dystopian risk factors, which are dazzling even cloaked in legalese, are a Rorschach test; AI that is powerful enough to kill us all is powerful enough to capture huge economics.
I donât give financial advice, as Iâm constantly reminding my colleagues. AI will transform the economy, more than we can imagine in the long term and less than we assume in the short term. Among the frontier labs, Anthropic probably is in a better position to win than OpenAI, with its trust issues and consumer-first approach, and a worse one than a credible and wired-in Google. But like all of them, it needs enough investors in the believer camp to bridge it to that promised land.
Notable
- âMuch of Anthropicâs pitch is that a company with a single product â one it admits is dangerously uncontrollable and unpopular â can justify a $1.5 trillion price tag,â Semaforâs Business team wrote after the prospectus was released.

19bab704aa48.text: By — Tia Goldenberg, Associated Press Tia Goldenberg, Associated Press By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israelis-are-voting-on-whether-to-oust-netanyahu-in-first-election-since-oct-7-attack Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israelis are voting on whether to oust Netanyahu in first election since Oct. 7 attack World Oct 27, 2026 9:40 AM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Israelis are voting in a pivotal election Tuesday as their country wrestles with unresolved wars, continues to reel from Hamas' 2023 attack and is deeply divided over the character of the state and the right person to lead it. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who voted just after midday, faces an array of parties seeking to oust Israel's longest-serving premier from power. Opinion polls have suggested a tight race with his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Over 7 million people are eligible to vote, and tens of thousands have reportedly arrived from overseas. WATCH: Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in first election since Oct. 7 and Gaza war "This is a very moving and fateful moment," Netanyahu said. He told journalists after voting that he believes the Arab parties that could make or break the election "are receiving massive, truly massive, support. They are heading to the polls in unprecedented numbers." He urged supporters to forget about the beach or the barbecue and vote. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. More than 31% of Israelis voted by noon, the highest voter turnout by midday since 1977, according to figures by the Central Elections Committee. Inside Israel, the race is largely about security and who should serve to defend the country. Outside Israel, it's mainly about the country's reputation — and the security of Jewish people worldwide — after growing criticism over the war in Gaza and Jewish settler violence in the occupied West Bank. READ MORE: Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are expected to fly in for pivotal vote In Israel's fragmented parliamentary politics, no single party has ever won an outright parliamentary majority. There is a chance that neither Netanyahu's religious and ultranationalist coalition nor the group of parties hoping to remove him has enough support for a majority. That could set off weeks of negotiations before a leader is declared. Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers — if other parties agree to join forces with them. "Our vote will change the government," Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party, said while voting, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities. Arabs in Israel make up about 20% of the population. READ MORE: Whatever the outcome of Israel's election, Netanyahu's policies toward Palestinians will likely endure Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for taunting Palestinian detainees and saying some Palestinians in Gaza are "not even people," warned that "it will be Mansour Abbas' government" if Netanyahu and his allies don't win. Emotions run high among some voters Some emotions were high. In Kiryat Shmona, a Netanyahu stronghold near the border with Lebanon, one man kicked and tore down a poster of Eisenkot. The election is Israel's first national vote since the Oct. 7, 2023, attack that sparked the war in Gaza and related conflicts. In Tel Aviv, families of some killed on Oct. 7 or former hostages held a moment of silence. "Remember all those whose voices are no more," said Yona Adam, whose daughter Mapal Adam was killed. Around 330,000 young Israelis, many facing compulsory military service under the shadow of war, are eligible to vote for the first time. READ MORE: Netanyahu denies allegations he's escalating tensions with Iran before Israel's election Eisenkot started the day by visiting communities attacked on Oct. 7. "If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here" in the communities near Gaza, he said. After voting, standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of "the worst government Israel has known." He noted that victory wasn't certain, adding that "we are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state." Eisenkot's Yashar party said it filed an urgent complaint over nine incidents in which its ballot slips were missing, damaged or turned over inside voting booths, and suggested a "systematic and deliberate" sabotage attempt. Overall, the acting director-general of the elections committee, Dean Livne, said the number of reports about irregularities or issues at polling stations was much lower than in previous elections. Security, military conscription and integrity are top issues The vote serves not only as a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership but also on what kind of country Israel should be — heavily influenced by religious and nationalist forces, or more firmly anchored in liberal and secular values. Israel has found itself increasingly isolated over its conduct in Gaza and the West Bank. Public support among Americans has plummeted, and partners in Europe and elsewhere have slapped sanctions on Israel. Also hanging over the election are lingering tensions with Iran. Netanyahu ramped up threats ahead of the vote, warning Tehran it would face "a devastating blow" if it attacked Israel. Netanyahu's supporters see him as a steady hand and a consummate statesman who they believe has triumphantly guided Israel through multiple wars. They think he is protecting Israel's Jewish identity while keeping in check what they see as an interventionist judiciary. Anthropic warned potential investors in its landmark public offering that it expects its already-high energy costs to get higher, and that delays in securing access could slow down the AI buildout.
In its IPO prospectus filed on Monday, the tech giant revealed it is on the hook for about $400 billion in chip purchases and data center leases, and lost $81 billion in the first half of this year. Energy in particular is raised repeatedly in the document as a risk: Negotiations with third parties, delays, cost overruns, and growing requirements for AI companies to pay for grid upgrades even if they donât use them directly are all liable to increase the firmâs operating costs, the filing said, adding that because of how the companyâs contracts are structured, âwe may bear these costs even if the underlying [power] capacity is delayed or never realized.â Rising temperatures and heightened risk from wildfires due to climate change also pose physical threats to the companyâs infrastructure, it warned.

7e9b1fcd1358.text:
Timâs view
The balance of power in Ukraineâs energy war is shifting.
In Washington, bipartisan blowback is mounting against the Trump administrationâs dangling of lucrative energy prizes for the Kremlin. Senate Democrats issued a stern warning on Monday that they plan to investigate any US entity that imports Russian diesel if they regain their majority after next weekâs elections. Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell piled on, charging in a Wall Street Journal column that Trumpâs handling of Russian President Vladimir Putin is âfactually wrong, strategically naive, and morally bankrupt.â The EU is sticking to its guns on plans to end Russian gas imports next year. The days in which Moscow will be able to leverage its oil and gas to squeeze concessions from the West are rapidly shrinking.
Scrutiny is also mounting of Russiaâs bombardment of Ukraineâs energy infrastructure, which continued last night; a UN commission concluded on Monday that these attacks constitute war crimes and crimes against humanity. As temperatures dwindle, Ukraineâs surprising ability to keep its grid from total collapse, plus its ongoing deep-strike drone campaign against Russian oil infrastructure, has allowed Kyiv to effectively achieve an âenergy stalemate,â if not a ceasefire, scholars at Columbia University and the Carnegie Endowment wrote in Foreign Affairs.
Still, with more attacks ahead, Kyiv has failed to take some basic steps that would leave it better prepared this winter, a report from the research and advocacy group Ukraine Facility Platform concluded, mainly by putting off regulatory reforms that could entice more private investment into decentralized, grid-connected power generation. âThe government is still preparing for last yearâs heating season,â UFP analyst Mariia Tsaturian, a former official at the state grid operator, told me. Nearly a gigawatt of replacement energy hardware from Western donors has also not yet been set up, she said.
Escalation from both sides is forthcoming, which means more costs and suffering for civilians. So far, this cycle of energy destruction and adaptation has served more to prolong the war than to push either side to the negotiating table. The US still has the power to tip the balance; the next few weeks after the midterm elections should give a clearer sense of where that leverage is headed.
Notable
- European officials expect only modest gains in the USâs position towards the Russia-Ukraine war, such as a restoration of satellite services and an acceleration of the delivery of air defense missiles, if the Democrats win the midterms.

Conservation groups aiming to raise Â£30m to buy a vast upland estate are within touching distance of their target following a Â£1.9m government pledge.
The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust are looking to acquire the 9,500-acre Rothbury Estate in its entirety as part of plans boost wildlife, restore bogs and promote nature-friendly farming.
Their fundraising efforts - now standing at Â£29m thanks to the latest donation - have attracted backing from the likes of Sir David Attenborough with the window for public donations running until the end of this week.
However, some members of the Northumberland farming community said they viewed the project as "a folly".
The wildlife groups previously purchased part of the estate, including the Simonside Hills, from the Duke of Northumberland's son, Lord Max Percy, in 2024.
If successful in buying the remainder, the organisations claim there is the potential to develop a "40-mile nature recovery corridor stretching from the North East coast to Kielder on the central Scottish border".
'Stamp of approval'
It could also see a reduction in the number of sheep from 1,500 to 500 with the number of cattle quadrupled to 200.
The government grant was announced on Monday at the UN Global Biodiversity Conference, COP17, taking place in Armenia.
Craig Bennett OBE, chief executive of the Wildlife Trusts, said the funding would "take us another step closer to realising our vision for one of the largest nature recovery projects England has ever seen".
He added it was a "stamp of approval" for the project on the back of "millions generously donated by philanthropists, charitable funds and thousands of members of the public".
Earlier this year, though, tenant farmer Chris Armstrong, who oversees 1,000 acres (405 hectares) close to the site, warned local opinion was split.
He told the BBC: "I would put it very much akin to the Brexit vote. I would think it would be that finely split.
"I think the majority of the farming community see this as a folly."

Harry Kane has taken the scenic route to the Ballon d'Or - a road littered with doubts and diversions, but one that eventually led to the ultimate destination: being crowned as the world's best player.
The 33-year-old's glory at the London Palladium on Monday is fitting reward for an exemplary career that has seen records fall at his feet for England, Tottenham Hotspur and Bayern Munich.
Kane is England's top goalscorer with 91 goals. He has 125 England caps, joint-highest with Peter Shilton. He is Spurs' record scorer with 280 goals in 435 appearances. He scored a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for Bayern Munich and England during the 2025â26 season.
This is the Kane of recent vintage, the world-class striker and complete footballer who beat Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe, as well as Spain's teenage Barcelona forward Lamine Yamal, to the sport's biggest personal honour.
Kane's humility has seen him described as an 'anti-superstar' and his achievement has been commended both inside and outside the football world.
One post on social media from Kane as he celebrated the greatest moment of his career said it all: "Work hard in silence. Let success be your noise."
And yet, Kane's journey was not always smooth.
It was one that started with loan moves around the lower divisions with Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City before he developed into a great for club and country.
The same Kane sat on the bench on loan at Leicester City â alongside future England team-mate Jamie Vardy â when the Foxes lost a dramatic Championship play-off at Watford in May 2013.
Kane went through hard schools and hard times away from his more familiar environment at Spurs, joining Orient on loan as a 17-year-old in January 2011, playing 18 games with nine starts and scoring five goals.
He joined Millwall in similar circumstances a year later, with some behind the scenes at Spurs fearing the traditionally hostile atmosphere at the New Den might intimidate the teenager, but he acquitted himself well, scoring nine goals in 24 starts.
Former Spurs manager Tim Sherwood said: "I used to watch Harry a lot at Millwall and it was an intimidating atmosphere. I remember overhearing one of our scouts come and talk to Harry Redknapp - who was Spurs manager at the time - and say: 'We need to get Harry Kane out of Millwall, it's no good for him there'.
"I went straight in and said: 'This is the perfect atmosphere for him'."
Kane made his Spurs debut in August 2012 before a spell at Norwich City, where he failed to score in three starts and suffered a serious foot injury.
It was an unhappy time but Chris Hughton, the former Spurs defender who was manager at Carrow Road, said: "What I saw in him was a desire to do well. Did I see him having the mobility and flexibility he has in his game now? Probably not. He was a very good finisher. He would stay out after training for half an hour every day, left foot, right foot."
Next stop was Leicester City between February and May 2013, when he made five starts and scored two goals, a stint best remembered for that dramatic Championship play-off game when Troy Deeney scored for Watford to send them to Wembley seconds after Anthony Knockaert's penalty was saved by Manuel Almunia.
Kane was not even selected in Leicester's starting line-up, only being sent on after 61 minutes. And who was alongside him on the bench? Vardy, who later won the Premier league with the Foxes and played alongside Kane for England.
He later admitted this was a time of self-doubt, saying: "That was probably the time in my career where it was the hardest - I was 19 and I was thinking, 'If I can't play for Norwich or for Leicester, even in the Championship, then how I am going to get back and play for Tottenham?'"
It is testimony to Kane's strength of character, even as a youngster, that he not only returned to Spurs but left for Bayern Munich in August 2023 as one of their greatest ever players.
Even at Spurs, Kane's superb record always carried the qualification that he never won a trophy, a stick used to unfairly beat a player whose remarkable consistency and approach marked him down as the consummate professional.
Kane has put that right spectacularly at Bayern, winning the Bundesliga twice, the move propelling him to the level of global superstar, giving him the profile and platform to win the Ballon d'Or - the first English player to win the trophy since Michael Owen in 2001 and the fifth overall.
Former England midfielder Danny Murphy told BBC Sport recently: "He's a born goalscorer. He's a super professional. He's technically brilliant. He's been an absolute credit to himself and his family in the way he's conducted himself and the longevity he's had in his career."
There is still that one space on his roll of honour, namely success with England after losses in two Euros finals and two World Cup semi-final defeats, but who would bet against Kane being fit and motivated enough to have one last crack at Euro 2028 in the UK and Ireland.
Kane is now at the peak of his powers and fitness, not just a goalscoring machine but the complete player capable of dropping deep into midfield to play the sort of breathtaking defence splitting pass exemplified by Alphonso Davies' goal against Arsenal in the recent Champions League game.
One of Kane's illustrious predecessors in England's number nine shirt, Alan Shearer, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "It was so well deserved because he hasn't had things all his own way. He's had to go round it the hard way. He had to start off the hard way by someone telling him, 'You're not quite good enough, you're going to have to work a lot harder to get to where you want to'.
"He did that. He went out on loan and worked harder than anyone else. He's got to the very, very top and now he's the best player in the world and that's what dedication does for you. It's a message to everyone.
"Harry said it in his speech - that if you're told you're not good enough,

de15d49f8dcc.text: By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/grand-jury-refuses-to-indict-former-white-house-aide-cassidy-hutchinson-ap-sources-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Grand jury refuses to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson, AP sources say Politics Oct 27, 2026 6:40 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department on Tuesday failed to secure a grand jury indictment against a former White House staffer who provided dramatic but disputed testimony against President Donald Trump before a House committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, U.S. Capitol insurrection, according to two people familiar with the matter. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. A grand jury in Washington rejected prosecutors' request to return an indictment charging Cassidy Hutchinson, said the people, who spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the case. It's the latest setback in the Justice Department's efforts to charge perceived adversaries of the Republican president. Details of prosecutors' allegations against Hutchinson were not immediately clear, but Republican lawmakers had accused her of lying under oath in her explosive testimony in 2022 about Trump's behavior on Jan. 6, when a mob of his supporters stormed the Capitol to halt the congressional certification of his election loss to Democrat Joe Biden. WATCH: Cassidy Hutchinson discusses what she saw and experienced in the Trump White House The account, at a surprise hearing announced just 24 hours earlier, was seen at the time as particularly powerful given Hutchinson's proximity to power as special assistant to Mark Meadows, Trump's chief of staff. Hutchinson described an angry, defiant president who was trying to let armed protesters avoid security screenings at a rally that morning to protest his 2020 election defeat and who later grabbed at the steering wheel of the presidential SUV when the Secret Service refused to let him go to the Capitol. And when the events at the Capitol spiraled toward violence, with the crowd chanting "Hang Mike Pence," she testified that Trump declined to intervene. Trump at the time denied much of what Hutchinson said on his social media platform, Truth Social. He called her a "total phony" and "bad news." Hutchinson's description of the altercation inside the presidential SUV was regarded as particularly explosive, even as she acknowledged during her testimony that she was relaying what she had heard from a White House security official and did not have firsthand knowledge of the episode because she was not there. Her account was quickly disputed. In March 2024, House Republicans released a previously undisclosed transcript of the Select Committee's interview with a Secret Service officer who drove the presidential SUV. That transcript of the presidential limo driver contradicted some of Hutchinson's testimony but corroborated other aspects of her account, including Trump's attempt to join the mob scene at the Capitol. READ MORE: Read the transcripts of Cassidy Hutchinson's closed-door Jan. 6 testimony The driver said he did not see the altercation that Hutchinson described. But the driver said Trump "never grabbed the steering wheel." "I didn't see him, you know, lunge to try to get into the front seat at all," the driver said. Hutchinson has alleged that members of Trump's inner circle dangled job opportunities and financial assistance while she was cooperating with the committee. She also testified that her own lawyer — a former ethics counsel in the Trump White House — told her "the less you remember, the better." "It feels ridiculous, because in my heart I knew where my loyalties lied, and my loyalties lied with the truth," she told the committee. "And I never wanted to diverge from that." The U.S. House of Representatives impeached Trump in 2021 on allegations that he incited the mob that attacked the Capitol, but he was later acquitted by the Senate. The Justice Department under Biden charged Trump with felony offenses, accusing him of illegally working to overturn his 2020 election loss in the run-up to the Capitol attack, but then-special counsel Jack Smith abandoned the case after Trump's 2024 presidential victory. Longstanding Justice Department policy says sitting presidents cannot face criminal prosecution. Hutchinson, a native of Pennington, New Jersey, previously worked in the White House Office of Legislative Affairs and interned for Republicans, including Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 0f2f0b6a081b.text: The Justice Department failed to secure an indictment against Cassidy Hutchinson , a former White House aide who testified about President Trump's actions on Jan. 6, multiple media outlets reported Tuesday. Why it matters: The grand jury's refusal to indict Hutchinson is another blow to the DOJ in its ongoing effort to prosecute President Trump's perceived political enemies . The latest: A Justice Department lawyer told a magistrate judge Tuesday that a grand jury could not agree on an indictment, according to the Washington Post. The lawyer, whom the Post identified as Neville S. Hedley, the division's acting senior litigation counsel, did not say who the indictment referenced, but multiple sources told the Post and other outlets that it relates to Hutchinson. Catch up quick: Hutchinson's 2022 testimony before Congress revealed several bombshells about the Trump administration's actions leading up to and on Jan. 6, 2021. She testified that she had been told Trump lunged at a Secret Service agent who refused to drive him to the Capitol, that Trump knew some of his supporters were armed, and that Meadows had been warned of potential violence on Capitol Hill. She also described Trump's reluctance to call on his supporters to back down as violence unfolded at the Capitol. Zoom out: Republicans have long disputed Hutchinson's testimony, and Secret Service agents she identified as familiar with the events of that day have also said they do not recall some of the incidents she described. Earlier this year, Rep. Barry Loudermilk (R-Ga.) sent a criminal referral of Hutchinson to the Justice Department for investigation. House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) co-signed it. Criminal referrals are recommendations to the Justice Department and do not necessarily indicate criminal wrongdoing or result in charges. The intrigue: In a break from precedent, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, led by Trump loyalist Harmeet Dhillon, conducted Hutchinson's investigation, according to the New York Times. The U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C., currently led by Jeanine Pirro, typically handles investigations into allegations of lying to Congress. The Times noted that Pirro has struggled to secure indictments against Trump's perceived enemies, with several high-profile cases faltering after evidence proved thinner than initially believed. The right governor can put a state on a dramatically different energy and environmental path—and next week’s election could set the stage for major policy shifts across the country.
Democrats are favored to retain governorships in Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, according to Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia.
The party is also poised to take control from Republicans in Alaska, Iowa and Ohio, with opportunities to win Georgia and Nevada, and less likely paths to victory in Florida and Texas. Kansas is the only state where Republicans have a strong chance of winning a seat currently held by a Democrat.
Going into the election, Republicans hold governorships in 26 states and Democrats do in 24 states; 36 states have governor races on the ballot.
Recent experiences suggest Democratic governors advocate for more ambitious climate and energy policies—especially when their party also controls both chambers of the state legislature. Those unified governments can be better positioned to expand renewable energy, curb greenhouse gas emissions and promote energy efficiency.
Gubernatorial races carry added significance this year as voters grapple with high energy prices and scrutinize how state policies affect utility bills.
“The number one office that can control the action and direction of energy policy in states and over their utility bill is the governor,” said Dylan Reed, managing director of Advanced Energy United, a trade association for renewable and low-carbon energy businesses.
Governors can act as a counterweight to a likely divided federal government. Republicans are on track to lose control of the U.S. House and maybe the U.S. Senate, which would reduce the likelihood that President Donald Trump and Congress can agree on major policies.
“If Congress is at a place of not being able to get things done, then so much can wind up falling to a state to try and really govern,” said Bill Ritter, a Democrat who was governor of Colorado from 2007 to 2011 and is now a consultant for clean energy and transmission companies.
Advocates point to the governors elected in 2018 as evidence of how much state leadership can matter. In Illinois, JB Pritzker’s victory gave Democrats control of the governor’s office and both chambers of the legislature, paving the way for a series of climate and energy laws.
Jennifer Walling, longtime leader of the Illinois Environmental Council, said the combination of the political environment and the right candidate made the difference. She sees a similar mix of opportunity in many states this year.
States Where Democrats Are on Track to Retain Control
In interviews with trade groups, advocates and analysts monitoring governor races, Wisconsin was the state most often cited as well-positioned for significant changes on energy and environmental policy.
Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, is running against Republican U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany. The winner will replace Democrat Tony Evers, who chose not to run after two terms.
The race “leans Democrat,” according to Sabato’s Crystal Ball and it’s a toss-up according to the Cook Political Report.
Democrats also have a chance to gain majorities in the state House and Senate, which, if Crowley also wins, would give the party its first “trifecta” in more than a decade. Democrats are optimistic about legislative races thanks to a Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling that threw out gerrymandered district maps that favored Republicans.
Joshua Basseches, a public policy and environmental studies professor at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, said “arguably the most important” governor races this year are those that are closely contested and give the winner the power to appoint utility commission members. Wisconsin is one such race.
The stakes are especially high there with the Wisconsin Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities. Republicans in the legislature have stalled voting on Evers’ nominees for two of the panel’s three seats, hoping Tiffany will become governor. The nominees are serving on the commission while they await a confirmation vote, so all three seats are filled for now. But if elected, Tiffany could choose his own nominees.
Crowley and Tiffany have sharply different positions on energy policy.
“The Republican candidate is doubling down on fossil fuels and nuclear and calls solar a green energy boondoggle, and the Democrat, Crowley, is more focused on a clean energy future,” said Tom Content, executive director of Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin, a consumer advocacy organization.
Both candidates favor developing more nuclear power, which is concerning to Content because it could raise costs for ratepayers.
Wisconsin could build much more renewable energy and batteries, but state policies that keep old power plants open hold it back, said Reed of Advanced Energy United. He expects substantial investment in the state if lawmakers can remove some of the current obstacles.
Other notable races in which Democrats are on track to retain control of governor’s offices:
Arizona: Democrat Gov. Katie Hobbs is running for re-election against Republican U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs. As in Wisconsin, Arizona’s opportunity depends on Democrats gaining majorities in one or both chambers of the legislature, which would give Hobbs more leeway to advance her agenda. Arizona is one of the sunniest states in the country and has long been viewed by the solar power industry as having high potential for developing cleaner, cheaper power.
One factor limiting Hobbs’ authority on energy issues is that the Arizona Corporation Commission, the utility regulator, is elected, not appointed. The panel has a 5-0 Republican majority, with two seats on the ballot next week.

A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.
Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.
That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.
Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".
A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".
Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.
Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.
One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.
Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".
The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.
Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".
Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.
Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.
Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.
It is hard to make contact with people there as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians.
Those residents or relatives who have spoken to the BBC have expressed fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or might examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could put them in danger.
Ukraine's military general staff urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".
He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.
One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".
However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.
Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.

de3141d19eed.text: By — Lauran Neergaard, Associated Press Lauran Neergaard, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/daylight-saving-time-is-coming-to-an-end-again-heres-how-the-time-change-may-impact-you Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Daylight saving time is coming to an end again. Here's how the time change may impact you Nation Oct 27, 2026 5:58 PM EDT An extra hour of sleep is on the way for most Americans, though the "fall back" to standard time will bring darker afternoons, too. One tip: Try to get outside for some morning sun — it'll help your body clock reset faster. READ MORE: America already tried permanent daylight saving time. Could it work now? Daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday, which means you should set your clock back an hour before you go to bed. Standard time will last until March 14, when we will again "spring forward" with the return of daylight saving time. There's a lot of grumbling about the twice-a-year time changes. An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of it, while almost half opposed it. Lawmakers in Washington took up the issue yet again over the summer. People often find the spring switch harder, losing that hour of sleep we allegedly recover in the fall. But many people also mourn fall's end of daylight saving time, when days already are getting shorter and moving the clocks can mean less daylight after school or work for exercise or outdoor fun. The poll found that, if forced to choose, most Americans would prefer to keep that extra hour of daylight in the evening. But health groups, including the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine, have long urged adopting standard time year-round. That's because it aligns more with the sun, which rises later in the winter, and with human biology, what's called the circadian rhythm. Brighter mornings and less light at night are key to keeping that rhythm on track, making it easier to wake up on time and stick with healthy sleep patterns. Most countries do not observe daylight saving time. For those that do — mostly in North America and Europe — the date that clocks are changed varies. In the U.S., Hawaii and most of Arizona don't change and stay on standard time. Here's what to know about the twice-yearly ritual. How the body reacts to light The brain has a master clock that is set by exposure to sunlight and darkness. This circadian rhythm is a roughly 24-hour cycle that determines when we become sleepy and when we're more alert. The patterns change with age, one reason that early-to-rise youngsters evolve into hard-to-wake teens. Morning light is key to synchronizing that internal clock. By evening, levels of a hormone called melatonin begin to surge, triggering drowsiness. Too much light in the evening — whether from later time outdoors during daylight saving time or from artificial light like computer screens — delays that surge and the cycle gets out of sync. And that circadian clock affects more than sleep, also influencing things like heart rate, blood pressure, stress hormones and metabolism. How do time changes affect sleep? Even an hour's change on the clock can throw off sleep schedules because even though the clocks change, work and school start times stay the same. Right after the spring change, darker mornings and lighter evenings make it harder to fall asleep on time. Those first few days have been linked to increases in car crashes and even an uptick in heart attacks. READ MORE: Trump urges calls to Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton in push for permanent daylight saving time During the fall and winter, some people with seasonal affective disorder, a type of depression usually linked to the shorter days and less sunlight, often struggle. Many people easily adjust to the clock switch, like how they recover from jet lag after traveling. But a time change can add pressure on shift workers whose schedules already are out of sync with the sun, or those regularly sleep-deprived for other reasons. About 1 in 3 U.S. adults sleep less than the recommended seven-plus hours nightly, and more than half of U.S. teens don't get the recommended eight-plus hours on weeknights. Chronic sleep deprivation is linked to heart disease, cognitive decline, obesity and numerous other problems. How to prepare for the time change In both fall and spring, changing bedtimes by as little as 15 minutes a night in the days before the change can help ease into it. But sunshine in the morning is critical to helping reset your circadian rhythm for healthful sleep. If you can't get outdoors, sit by windows. Will the U.S. ever get rid of the time change? Every year, there's talk about ending the time change. The nation even tried it in the 1970s, but it lasted less than a year after a public outcry. The latest attempt came in July, when the U.S. House of Representatives overwhelmingly passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent. President Donald Trump backs the idea and is pressuring reluctant senators to support it, even posting the cellphone number of Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, an opponent, on social media. President Donald Trump has offered a $1m (Â£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud in the US which lead to a conviction.
Ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, Trump has been casting doubt on the security of the vote - alleging "rampant" cheating in postal voting and non-citizens voting.
However, studies suggest actual cases of these are extremely rare.
BBC Verify has taken a look at the evidence and Trump's proposed changes to the voting system.
How has Trump tried to change postal voting?
For years, Trump has made repeated unsubstantiated claims that postal voting leads to widespread fraud.
He has also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail in the midterms and has said he has cast his ballot by post in the past.
The president has been unsuccessful in his push for Congress to pass an act which would only allow people to vote by mail if they are disabled, ill, serving in the military, or travelling.
The majority of states allow, external people to vote by mail without having to provide a reason, and in the 2024 presidential election about 48 million people cast postal ballots.
Trump signed an executive order last year which directed the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on lists of citizens compiled by government agencies. It also sought to require states to use the same envelope style for postal votes.
However, the order was rejected by the US Supreme Court which called such changes so close to the midterm elections "arbitrary and capricious" - but said it could revisit the issue afterwards.
US states have different rules for verifying postal ballots, but every state matches certain voter information on the ballots against what they have on file to check they are eligible and most also conduct signature checks, external.
What does the evidence show on postal voting fraud?
Studies of multiple US elections suggest postal vote fraud has been extremely rare.
The Brookings Institute policy research think tank, external looked at the 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections and found an average of about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million postal votes.
The report used a database kept by the Heritage Foundation - a think tank which has been aligned with Trump in the past - which records cases of electoral fraud that have ended in a conviction.
We looked back in the database, external over the last 20 years and found it has tallied 325 convictions as a result of the fraudulent use of postal ballots.
A 2020 study by the American Statistical Association, external looked at cases of voter fraud in eight states which send postal ballots to all eligible voters and found no evidence that voting by mail increased the risk of voter fraud overall.
For example, according to the study, Oregon recorded 40 fraud cases between 2000 and 2020 having sent out more than 100 million postal ballots over that period.
How has Trump tried to change voter ID rules?
Trump has claimed non-citizen voting is widespread, and prior to the 2024 election he said Democrats were allowing millions of migrants into the US "so they can vote, vote, vote".
It is illegal for non-citizens to vote in US federal elections - punishments can include a prison sentence, a fine, and deportation.
The voting act the president has pushed Congress to pass would require voters to show a government-issued photo identification before they cast their ballots, as well as proof of citizenship when registering to vote and ongoing citizenship verification.
Critics have raised concerns that stricter voter ID requirements could harm voter turnout as people may not have a passport or the required government-issued photo ID.
"We don't have a national ID card that the government gives out, unlike a lot of countries. Drivers licence is most common but it doesn't identify your immigration status so the ID that most Americans carry around wouldn't be enough for you to vote," says Jonathan Diaz, a voting rights expert at the Campaign Legal Center.
A 2023 survey by the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external suggested that about 21.3 million voting-age American citizens, or about 9%, do not have documents proving citizenship readily available.
However, others argue that there has been no noticeable impact from existing voter ID laws.
"When scholars look at the effect of voter ID laws - either what the conservatives say on fraud or what progressive groups warn against about voter suppression - there doesn't seem to be a lot of proof that either has happened," says Walter Olson, an election expert at the conservative Cato Institute.
A number of largely Republican-run states have tightened voter ID requirements in the last couple of years. There have been 21 restrictive voting laws enacted since the 2024 election to establish stricter ID requirements, according to a study by the Brennan Center for Justice, external.
What does the evidence show on non-citizens voting?
Multiple studies show proven instances of non-citizens voting in past US elections have been very small.
The Heritage Foundation's database identified 24 cases of non-citizens being convicted for voting between 2005 and 2025.
A 2026 analysis by Reuters, external of non-citizen voting cases brought in federal courts found that over the last 30 years 129 people have been criminally charged and 73 of those cases resulted in a conviction.
"The fact that it's illegal for non-citizens to vote is a pretty strong deterrent in the first place as many worry about their immigration status and it would be an extremely risky move to vote," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institute.
"There's never been any evidence that there are many people who have done that, certainly not enough to influence an election."

6957dce29aa6.text: By — Ben Finley, Associated Press Ben Finley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-military-says-5-were-killed-by-a-strike-on-an-alleged-drug-smuggling-boat-in-the-eastern-pacific Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. military says 5 were killed by a strike on an alleged drug smuggling boat in the eastern Pacific World Oct 27, 2026 5:37 PM EDT UWASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military said it attacked a boat it accused of smuggling drugs in the eastern Pacific Ocean on Tuesday, killing five people, as the Trump administration continues its campaign against alleged traffickers in Latin America. READ MORE: Fact-checking U.S. military boat strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific as death toll passes 200 The latest attack brings the number of people who have been killed by the U.S. military's boat strikes to at least 240 in more than 70 strikes. The Trump administration began targeting those it calls "narcoterrorists" in September 2025. As with most of the military's statements on strikes in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea, U.S. Southern Command said it targeted the alleged drug traffickers along known smuggling routes and that "intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narcotrafficking." The military did not provide evidence that the vessel was ferrying drugs. A video posted on X showed a small boat in the water before it was enveloped by an explosion. President Donald Trump has said the U.S. is in "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and he has sought to justify the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the United States and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing "narcoterrorists." Critics have questioned the overall legality of the boat strikes as well as their effectiveness, in part because the fentanyl behind many fatal overdoses is typically trafficked to the U.S. over land from Mexico, where it is produced with chemicals imported from China and India. The attacks have drawn intense scrutiny from some Democratic lawmakers and military legal scholars. The Pentagon's watchdog said in May that it plans to look into whether the U.S. military followed an established targeting framework when carrying out the lethal operations, which include a military commander's intent, target development and execution. But the evaluation will not probe the legality of the strikes. Tuesday's strike is among a few that have followed Secretary of State Marco Rubio's pledge in September to seek the approval of U.S. allies in the region for carrying out such attacks. Rubio told reporters that while the U.S. has "the capacity to act unilaterally," it would rather work with its allies because that is "the most effective way to do it." Rubio's statements in Peru last month appeared to signal a shift in strategy. However, Rubio also said the U.S. military would "still blow up ships if need be" and the approach would be "a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination." Financial aid for Ukraine is getting harder to find
Helping a European neighbor remains politically popular, but rearming amid economic stress leaves less money to give.
European leaders meet next month to discuss ways to help Ukraine fill a projected €70 billion budget deficit. But their capacity for direct aid is constrained by efforts to rearm their own militaries amid a challenging economic environment, while Belgium continues to oppose the conversion of frozen Russian assets into a loan.
Western financial aid—€170 billion ($189.5 billion) since 2022—has been key to helping Kyiv stay financially afloat since Russia's wider invasion, according to the Kiel Institute. But the U.S. has drastically cut aid under the second Trump administration, leaving the European Union, Canada, Japan, Norway, and the United Kingdom to shoulder most of the burden.
Earlier this year, the EU approved a plan to lend Ukraine €90 billion to Ukraine through 2027, two-thirds of which will go to buy weapons and the rest to budgetary support. Around €14 billion has been disbursed to date, and by year's end that figure should grow to €45 billion.
But Russian attacks on critical infrastructure and other stresses mean that Kyiv is still looking at a budget deficit of around €70 billion for 2027.
European governments are spending more on their own defenses. In 2021, the defense budgets of NATO's European members averaged around 1.6 percent of GDP, below NATO’s then-target of 2 percent. The alliance has since boosted its goal to 2.5 percent of GDP, and at last year's summit, committed to raising ‘core’ defense expenditure to 3.5 percent over the next decade.
At the same time, they are facing rising debt and slowing economies. Eurozone countries have an average debt-to-GDP ratio of nearly 89 percent, and nearly 83 percent in EU nations generally. Buffeted by the trade wars and energy shocks of the Trump administration, eurozone economies will grow only 1.1 percent in 2026, according to a recent projection by the International Monetary Fund. Some northern EU members are in much better fiscal shape than their southern and western counterparts.
The budget picture is getting cloudier. Annual inflation in the eurozone rose to 3.8 percent in September, according to Eurostat, well above the European Central Bank (ECB) target of 2 percent. The ECB raised interest rates at its June and September meetings, and is expected to deliver another hike at one of the year's two remaining meetings. Rising prices may force the ECB to continue tightening policy, raising debt-service payments from government budgets.
Supporting Ukraine remains broadly popular in the EU, but the challenging economic environment makes it a tough sell for governments to increase aid to Ukraine along with their own defense spending. European governments are already facing domestic criticism over rearmament. Italy, for example, was approved for an allocation of up to €14.9 billion from the E.U.’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) loan facility, meant to aid rearmament. Yet Rome requested only about €8 billion from SAFE, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government sparred with critics within her own coalition and in the opposition on financing more defense spending with debt.
Frozen Russian assets
EU countries are thus once again looking at alternative methods of backstopping Ukraine’s budget. One of the most obvious options is the conversion of frozen Russian financial assets into a loan to Kyiv.
After Russia's February 2022 invasion, the G7 froze Russian government securities held abroad. As much as $300 billion was impounded as a result and remains in limbo to this day, including about €210 billion held in the European financial system.
While the principal has remained untouched, the EU has begun to use the interest income on those securities to help Ukraine, on the grounds that Russia, as aggressor, should pay for the damage caused to Ukraine. That has generated about €8 billion, of which €3.8 billion has been delivered to Ukraine, and €4.2 billion has been reserved to repay E.U. or G7 loans to Ukraine.
In September, Germany and other E.U. members revived the topic of converting the Russian assets into a loan for Kyiv, POLITICO reported. Berlin views the step as a ‘win-win’ for the E.U., enabling the bloc to help Kyiv address its financial needs, while replacing some of the funds that would be reserved for Ukraine in the E.U.’s upcoming multi-year budget.
But the politics around seizing the Russian assets have barely budged.
Belgium is the custodian of much of those Russian funds, which are housed in the Brussels-based Euroclear. The Belgian government blocked a 2025 proposal to seize the funds, fearing that it alone would bear the legal and financial risk of seizing the funds. Earlier this year, the Bank of Russia sued Euroclear in a Russian court for the funds, arguing that they were illegally seized. The court backed the Russian central bank’s challenge in a ruling two months later, though it lacks jurisdiction to enforce the judgment.
Concern over the legal risks means Brussels will likely stymie the proposal again.
“I am certain that the European Commission will not make proposals to meet Ukraine’s financing needs through a new operation linked to Russian assets,” Belgian Prime Minister Bart de Wever told reporters on Oct. 21. “I am certain of that, because that is what was said.”
As European leaders prepare for a November meeting to iron out next year's assistance to Ukraine, the EU is already pushing other partners to increase their contributions to Kyiv.
The situation is becoming more urgent. Ukraine has largely exhausted its stockpile of interceptors, leaving its cities and energy grid vulnerable to Russian attack. The Ukrainian military intelligence agency HUR recently estimated that Russia can produce 10,000 long-range strike drones and decoys each month. Three brothers - two of them wealthy real-estate moguls - were sentenced to 30 years each in prison for drugging and raping dozens of women over decades.
Tal Alexander, 40, and twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, were found guilty in March of using their wealth and social status to lure women to parties and luxury homes, where they sexually assaulted them.
"Your conduct was monstrous," said Judge Valerie Caproni before sentencing them. "Your crimes wreaked havoc on their lives."
On Tuesday morning, the court in New York heard from 12 victims, including one who did not testify during the trial.
One by one, they spoke of the psychological trauma they endured after the Alexander brothers raped them, and their desire for the shame they had felt to instead fall on the defendants.
Many asked the judge to impose the maximum sentence of life in prison for each brother.
Maya Miller told the court that after Tal Alexander raped her in 2014, she lost all sense of safety. "I carry a quiet funeral within me for the person I might've become if this never happened to me," she said.
Another victim, using the pseudoym Isa Brooks, said after being raped by Tal and Alon Alexander when she was 16, she lost the ability to trust herself.
"I had no idea the danger I was in till it was too late," she said.
Another woman said when she planned to come forward about being raped, Tal Alexander threatened her, saying he knew where her sister worked.
Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said the brothers deserved the maximum punishment for their crimes, saying facts "paint a truly devastating picture".
"For years, they honed their methods of luring women with the promise of luxury," she said, adding that they were "completely unmoved by the path of suffering they left behind them."
During the women's speeches, the three Alexander brothers showed little emotion. They stared ahead or conferred with their lawyers, who said they advised their clients not to look at the victims so it couldn't be misconstrued.
Attorneys for the brothers pushed for sentences of 15 years, arguing that they had become devoted fathers whose families would suffer in their absence.
The three men all addressed the court, continuing to profess their innocence.
"We had a work-hard, play-hard mentality," Tal Alexander said, adding he saw how his behavior "hurt people's feelings".
But their statements did not assuage Caproni, who chastised them for refusing to admit their crimes.
"How can someone who never acknowledged the wrongs they did be rehabilitated?" she asked.
At the end of the hearing, she sentenced them each to 30 years in prison for certain crimes. She also sentenced each to 20 years in prison for additional crimes, but said the men would serve the sentences concurrently.
During the five-week trial, 11 women - several said they were minors at the time of the assaults - testified that the brothers gave them gifts and flew them places including Aspen and the Bahamas where they fed them drugs before raping them.
Prosecutors said the brothers' pattern of abusive behaviour began in high school, though the trial involved crimes starting in 2008.
They said the three slipped drugs into women's drinks, and "physically restrained and held down their victims during the rapes and sexual assaults and ignored screams and explicit requests to stop".
Lawyers for the brothers argued the sex was consensual and that they were womanisers, but not abusers.
Two of the brothers, Tal and Oren, became wealthy selling luxury properties in New York and Miami.
They worked for American real estate giant Douglas Elliman, with clients including Lindsay Lohan, Kim Kardashian and Kanye West. In 2022, they founded their own New York-based firm called Official. Alon worked at the family's private security firm, Kent Security.
As they heard their sentences, the brothers stared straight ahead.

bce18870ada9.text: By — Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Thomas Beaumont, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/libertarians-could-siphon-republican-support-in-the-fight-for-control-of-the-u-s-senate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Libertarians could siphon Republican support in the fight for control of the U.S. Senate Politics Oct 27, 2026 5:10 PM EDT DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Republicans are worried that Libertarian candidates could siphon away votes in some of this year's most consequential U.S. Senate elections, potentially costing them control of the chamber. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. It's a particular concern in Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa, which are bracing for razor-thin contests in which even a few percentage points for a third party can be enough to swing the outcome. Although all of those states lean Republican, a number of party strategists say unhappiness with President Donald Trump could lead some conservatives to cast protest ballots. An unpopular war with Iran and Trump's expansion of executive power — two issues that grate on an anti-establishment slice of the American right — could fuel the Libertarian Party's message of nonintervention and limited centralized authority. "Libertarians, we believe, could draw enough votes to affect the outcome in a number of these races," said Republican former Ohio state lawmaker Gene Krebs, who is working on a project to diminish the impact of spoiler candidates. Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Texas on Tuesday, Ohio on Wednesday and Iowa on Sunday. Republican Senate campaign officials said they were less concerned about Iowa, where Libertarians are not a regular presence on the ballot, than they are about Ohio, Kansas and Texas. The officials spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy. In Ohio, former Libertarian Party national chairman Bill Redpath is running against Republican Sen. Jon Husted and Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown. "The Libertarian can easily pull enough votes away from the Republican so that the Democrat wins," Krebs said. Third parties could work against Democrats, too. An organization with Republican ties has distributed fliers promoting a socialist candidate, an apparent effort to pull support away from Brown. Enough Promises Ohio PAC, which sent out the fliers, received $2.5 million from Conservative Americans PAC, according to federal disclosure reports. Libertarian David Graham is running in Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is locked in a close race with Democrat Adam Hamilton. WATCH: How the Kansas Senate race became surprisingly competitive This is Graham's second campaign. He received 3% of the vote in a race Republican Sen. Jerry Moran won by 23 percentage points. In Texas, Libertarian Ted Brown received only 2.3% of the vote in 2024, when Republican Sen. Ted Cruz easily glided to another term. However, the race is tighter this year, with Democratic nominee James Talarico facing off with Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Wayne Hamilton, a former executive director of the Texas Republican Party, said Paxton's history of legal and ethical problems could have some conservatives looking for another choice. "Nobody's voting for the Libertarian. It's a protest vote," Hamilton said. "They are going to be voting that way because they don't want to vote for Paxton, and this is an option." Brown is a former insurance adjuster from California who has been a longtime activist in the Libertarian Party going back to supporting Ron Paul's presidential campaign in 1988. He said some conservative voters have turned on Trump. "Some libertarians supported him thinking he was an anti-war candidate. And that's where he's lost them," Brown said. "But my view and a lot of libertarians' view is that separation of powers is very important. This president has seized way too much power in this imperial presidency." Brown is under no illusions that he can compete with Paxton and Talarico for the seat. His campaign has a budget of about $30,000 and has spent $7,000 on advertising, running a spot on streaming services in four Texas counties where Libertarians have fared better in recent elections. That's compared with the combined advertising total of roughly $390 million that Talarico, Paxton and aligned groups have spent since the May 26 primary, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. Brown got 267,039 votes in 2024, a record for his party in a Texas Senate race. A great day for him on Nov. 3, he said, would be if he matched that, certain to net a higher percentage in the lower-turnout midterm. Brown dismissed the criticism he says he gets regularly from Republicans that he is merely spoiling Paxton's chances. "They could avoid that problem by nominating a better candidate," he said. Brown said he tells Democrats the same thing. "You can't spoil a system that's already rotten," he said. "There are a lot of people making a protest vote, and there's good reason to." The former wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president has been freed from remand after seven years while on trial for his attempted murder.
Marry Mubaiwa was charged in 2019, after her then husband Gen Constantino Chiwenga accused her of trying to impede his medical treatment in South Africa.
Ordering her release, a magistrate said Mubaiwa had suffered mental, physical and financial prejudice during the trial, state-owned daily the Herald said.
The ruling was made after the state asked for the trial to be postponed by a month in order to engage witnesses.
Her lawyer described the ruling as a victory that had come too late, because her client's rights had been violated by the delay in the trial.
Speaking outside court in the capital Harare on Tuesday, the lawyer added that if the state moved for a new trial, they would deal with it when it happened.
Mubaiwa was accused of attempting to kill Chiwenga, while he was in hospital in Pretoria. The vice-president then went to China for four months of treatment.
Mubaiwa was remanded in custody and denied bail.
According to the New Zimbabwe news website, Mubaiwa celebrated her release outside court, and said justice had been achieved and that she was proud of her lawyer.
In 2017, Chiwenga played a key role in overthrowing then President Robert Mugabe.

938b64a45dad.text: President Trump has increasingly singled out Muslim politicians and communities in a bid to rally his base in the final push before election day. Why it matters: Trump's comments could energize some Republican voters in close races, but the strategy could alienate those who see the rhetoric as fearmongering or discriminatory . Driving the news: Trump's Monday appearance at a Michigan rally for GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers included several barbs at Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed's Muslim faith. Trump suggested that El-Sayed posed a security threat, saying, "He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." He also called El-Sayed a "jihadist," baselessly claimed the Senate candidate wants to impose sharia law in Michigan, and again accused him of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied ties to extremist groups, and no evidence has emerged linking him to the Muslim Brotherhood. His campaign did not respond to a request for comment. Between the lines: Republican political consultant Dennis Darnoi told Axios that Trump's rhetoric "doesn't really move the needle one way or the other" in Michigan, where voters have heard similar language before. Darnoi says the strategy could "energize and mobilize" Trump's base. But it could also discourage Jewish and Black Democrats who backed El-Sayed's primary opponent, Haley Stevens, from supporting him in November. "It's not always about winning, but if you can minimize the size of your loss and then go into more Republican areas and gin up your turnout and gin up your margin of victory, then you can win a very close statewide race." By the numbers: About 38% of Michigan likely voters said they would be less likely to support a Muslim candidate, according to a Michigan State University poll released Monday. But 58% said a candidate's being Muslim would make no difference, while 52% said a Trump endorsement would make them less likely to support a politician. What they're saying: Trump and some in the GOP "have chosen to use bigotry and racism" as their election strategy "because there's no other message they're able to run on," Haris Tarin, vice president of policy and programming at the Muslim Public Affairs Council, tells Axios. He added that it doesn't matter if voters or politicians agree with El-Sayed's policies, "all of that is up for debate. But they've chosen not to debate the issues. They've chosen to instill fear in people, promote lies, pure lies." Tarin predicted the attacks would have "an opposite effect for both American Muslims and Americans in general." The other side: A White House spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement that "President Trump is calling out the radical extremists stoking division, defrauding their communities, and perpetuating violence." "The President will continue to unapologetically fight for American greatness and call out extremists like Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed without apology." Zoom out: Trump isn't alone. Several Republican lawmakers have made anti-Muslim comments this year. Trump has also repeatedly targeted Somali Americans and Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), and previously called Somali immigrants "garbage." Somalis predominantly practice Islam. What we're watching: Whether moderates and independents take the bait, or whether the attacks backfire with Muslim Americans and other voters. The Army’s only remaining SFAB helped broker a ceasefire in southeast Asia
The service’s last train-advise-assist unit is working to counter Chinese influence in the Indo-Pacific theater.
A year ago, after months of fighting spurred by a century-old border dispute, Thailand and Cambodia struck a peace deal in Malaysia, with help from a small U.S. Army unit that had long been training both Thai and Malaysian troops.
The peace talks were led by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Malaysian Land Forces, which sought the advice of the 5th Security Force Assistance Brigade, the unit’s commander told Defense One.
“They asked our advisors, who were in the space of the land force headquarters, ‘Hey, what should we be thinking about? How can we effectively do this?,” said Col. Daniel Hodermarsky. “And we were reporting back to [U.S. Army Pacific] and leveraging experts from the higher headquarters to provide that advice to more rapidly enable them to to take the lead.”
At the same time, 5th SFAB had a team on the ground in Thailand.
“We didn't have anyone near the front or in the conflict, but we were able to say, "Hey, here's what we're seeing with the country team in Thailand,” Hodermarsky said.
But 5th SFAB—the Army’s only remaining train-advise-assist unit—didn’t just happen to be in the right place at the right time. The specialized unit, made up of experienced conventional troops who have already led a squad or platoon, and so on, has been regularly deploying to INDOPACOM to work with partner militaries since 2020.
“So we're able to give a bit more granular, real-time reporting back to the theater, and we're tied in directly with each country team, security cooperation office and defense attaché wherever we have adviser teams,” Hodermarsky said. “So we can get those liaise cells, those assessment cells, and say, ‘Hey, here's what we're granularly seeing, hearing. Here's what the partner is asking, or here's what they're talking about.”
The Army developed the SFAB concept in 2017, when training and advising the Afghan army had no end in sight and the service was anticipating expanding that mission beyond U.S. Central Command. The idea was that rather than rotating conventional infantry and other units as advisers, the service would cultivate specialized units for the mission. The 1st SFAB deployed in Afghanistan in 2018.
By May 2020, six SFABs had been established, each aligned to a different part of the world. They were staffed by volunteers coming off operational assignments, now experienced and theoretically qualified to train a partner unit.
Last year, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered most of the SFABs to be dissolved. The units assigned to European and Africa Commands have been shuttered, and their CENTCOM and National Guard counterparts will be gone by year’s end. 1st SFAB was reorganized as Army Security Cooperation Group-South in January.
That leaves only Hodermarsky’s 5th, doing its part to keep the United States in the good graces of INDOPACOM countries that might otherwise align themselves with China’s growing military power.
Some have argued that the moves are shortsighted.
“If the U.S. military continues marginalizing the advising mission or ignoring it altogether, then it means going back to the failed train-and-pray model,” argued a 2025 piece published by West Point’s Modern War Institute. “Fully staffed SFABs are not a luxury; they’re a necessity. Without them, the United States risks being flat-footed in the next war.”
ASCG-S and 5th SFAB’s continued existence are an acknowledgement that the train-advise-assist mission is still important for the DOD’s top two priority regions.
5th’s farflung efforts
In INDOPACOM, 5th SFAB has been shaping militaries from Mongolia to the Philippines, embedding in their professional military academies as well as advising their senior leadership.
“We were in the Philippine Army headquarters and their [Training and Doctrine Command] equivalent for years, as they transitioned from a counterinsurgency focus across the Philippines, to a national-defense focus for their land forces” Hodermarsky said.
His unit’s relationships have also laid the groundwork for major exercises the Army now does in INDOPACOM, including Balikatan and Cobra Gold.
“A persistent advisor team can stay in between the planning conferences and come up with the training plan, if we identify the partner unit that's going to exercise with the 25th Infantry Division or the the 7th Infantry Division,” Hodermarsky said. “And say, what are the training objectives for that Royal Thai Army unit or Philippine Army unit or Malaysian Land Force element? And then help them through that training progression.”
He said some division leaders call the SFAB the WD-40 of U.S. Army Pacific, because their teams ease friction between partner nations and conventional units visiting for exercises.
“We see sort of a reverse slope of advisor presence, as we hopefully work our way out of jobs in certain countries, so that you go from a partner force requesting more hands-on training and capability development through security force assistance, to where they're now really exercising as a flank unit or an integrated part of a U.S. division or brigade that is more capable, more trusted to be on our flank, or integrated into one of our major formations,” Hodermarsky said.
