4e82121518b2.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition is projected to lose its parliamentary majority, but his opponent Gadi Eisenkot's bloc is short of 61 seats, according to Israeli exit polls. The exit polls show Eisenkot's bloc with 52 to 53 seats, Netanyahu's with 50, and Arab parties with 17 to 18. Why it matters: If the election results match that poll, Eisenkot would have to try to swear in a minority government supported by the two Arab parties. It's unclear whether all of his political partners would agree to do that. It would also mean that Netanyahu's coalition shed 14 seats from the 64 seats it won in the 2022 elections . What they're saying: Eisenkot said that the exit poll results "point to an unequivocal lack of confidence in Netanyahu and the government responsible for Oct. 7, on the part of the Zionist majority and the majority of Israeli citizens. If these results hold, it will be a victory for Israel's Zionist, pro-state majority." He added, "I will act immediately to implement the people's verdict, replace Netanyahu's government, and establish a Zionist government committed to military service, as soon as possible." Driving the news: The exit poll results came after voters flocked to polling stations throughout the day, with turnout reaching a three-decade high . It was the culmination of a campaign that each side warned would lead to catastrophe if the other side won. An Eisenkot-bloc victory would offer Israel a chance to reset its strained relationships abroad and chart a new course domestically. The former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff, however, vowed to maintain a hawkish approach on security matters. Yes, but: Though Eisenkot's bloc outpaced Netanyahu's, the incumbent prime minister's Likud Party received one to two more seats than Eisenkot's Yashar Party, per the exit polls. But because Israel has a parliamentary system, the bloc totals are what ultimately matter. Go deeper: Israeli turnout hits four-decade high

b509154e4426.text: By — Tia Goldenberg, Associated Press Tia Goldenberg, Associated Press By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/no-clear-winner-in-israeli-election-exit-polls-indicate-as-netanyahus-fate-hangs-in-the-balance Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter No clear winner in Israeli election, exit polls indicate, as Netanyahu's fate hangs in the balance World Updated on Oct 27, 2026 4:21 PM EDT — Published on Oct 27, 2026 4:11 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Israel's election ended Tuesday with no clear winner, exit polls indicate, likely setting off weeks of jockeying before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is scheduled. An inconclusive result would leave Israel in political limbo after the country's first national election since Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack. The vote served as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's wartime leadership. WATCH: Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in first election since Oct. 7 and Gaza war Exit polls released by major Israeli TV stations suggest that neither Netanyahu's political bloc nor that of his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. Those polls indicated that Netanyahu's bloc won 50 seats, the opposition won 52-53 and Arab parties won 17-18. The strong showing by Arab-led parties could allow them to decide the next prime minister, but both blocs have until now refused to partner with them. Like all surveys, exit polls are subject to potential error. Preliminary results are expected in the coming hours. Final results are expected in the coming days and may vary from the exit polls. The pivotal election comes as Israel wrestles with unresolved wars, lingering grief and anger over Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack, and deep divisions over its longest-serving leader, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Netanyahu, who voted just after midday, faces an array of parties seeking to drive him from power, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. More than 74% of eligible voters had cast ballots by 8 p.m., the highest turnout at that time in decades, and 8 percentage points higher than in the last elections in 2022, according to the Central Elections Committee. The race is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's nearly unbroken 17-year rule, which had left Israelis bitterly divided on a host of issues even before the deadliest attack in its history. The resulting wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, along with settler violence in the occupied West Bank, have stoked worldwide outrage, straining ties with Israel's closest allies and fueling a rise in antisemitism. Among Israelis, the election is widely seen as a struggle over the character of the state, pitting Netanyahu and his ultranationalist and religious allies against those seeking to preserve its liberal and secular foundations. Over 7 million people are eligible to vote, and tens of thousands have reportedly arrived from overseas. Arab turnout could be crucial In Israel's fragmented parliamentary politics, no single party has ever won an outright parliamentary majority. There is a chance that neither Netanyahu's coalition nor the group of parties hoping to remove him has enough support for a majority. That could set off weeks of negotiations before a leader is declared. "This is a very moving and fateful moment," Netanyahu said before the exit polls. He told journalists after voting that he believes the Arab parties that could make or break the election "are receiving massive, truly massive, support. They are heading to the polls in unprecedented numbers." Netanyahu in past elections has warned of high Arab turnout to energize his own right-wing voters. While he did not provide evidence for his latest claim, turnout appeared to have increased significantly in Arab communities and liberal bastions, according to data from the Central Elections Committee. In another sign of concern, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party petitioned to extend voting hours past 10 p.m., but the election commission ruled against it, saying there was no justification. Eisenkot had rejected the proposed extension and called on voters to ignore Netanyahu's "scare tactics." Israel's Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers — if other parties agree to join forces with them. "Our vote will change the government," said Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party, while voting was still underway. Arabs in Israel make up about 20% of the population. Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for taunting Palestinian detainees and saying some Palestinians in Gaza are "not even people," warned that "it will be Mansour Abbas' government" if Netanyahu and his allies don't win. Emotions run high among some voters Some voters' emotions ran high. In Kiryat Shmona, a Netanyahu stronghold near the border with Lebanon, one man kicked and tore down a poster of Eisenkot. The election is Israel's first national vote since the Oct. 7 attack that sparked the war in Gaza and related conflicts. In Tel Aviv, families of some killed on Oct. 7 or former hostages held a moment of silence. "Remember all those whose voices are no more," said Yona Adam, whose daughter Mapal Adam was killed. READ MORE: Whatever the outcome of Israel's election, Netanyahu's policies toward Palestinians will likely endure Around 330,000 young Israelis, many facing compulsory military service under the shadow of war, are eligible to vote for the first time. Eisenkot started the day by visiting communities attacked on Oct. 7. "If someone in the government had a shred of responsibility, they would start the morning here" in the communities near Gaza, he said. Standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of "the worst government Israel has known." d02358e9edc2.text: By — Ed White, Associated Press Ed White, Associated Press By — Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/authorities-say-serial-killer-ted-bundy-is-responsible-for-the-1974-murder-of-another-utah-teenage-girl Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Authorities say serial killer Ted Bundy is responsible for the 1974 murder of another Utah teenage girl Nation Oct 27, 2026 4:01 PM EDT DNA connects serial killer Ted Bundy to the death of a Utah teenager, authorities announced Tuesday, exactly 52 years after her body was discovered in the woods by a hunter. WATCH: Rapid DNA testing helps police solve old crimes, but raises privacy concerns Bundy has been dead since 1989, but the tally of his confirmed victims continues to grow due to advances in DNA testing. He killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries. Investigators are satisfied that Bundy was responsible for killing 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith in 1974, a death that had long been listed as a cold case, Summit County Attorney Margaret Olson said at a news conference. Besides DNA evidence, Smith's death had the hallmarks of Bundy's "pattern, motive, means and opportunity," Olson said. Investigators were able to close the cold case by making crucial DNA connections between Smith and Laura Aime, another Bundy victim whose case was resolved last April in Utah County. A highly similar DNA profile linked to Bundy was found in evidence obtained from Smith's autopsy, Utah County Sgt. Mike Reynolds said. "This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence," said Salt Lake County Sheriff Rosie Rivera. Officials have been in touch with Smith's next of kin, none of whom still live in the area. "With every case closure, may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out," Reynolds said. Bundy was executed in 1989 by electric chair in Florida for the 1978 murders of two women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University. He gave a series of confessions in his final days, including to some crimes that were previously unknown to police. Not all of those cases have been confirmed. Besides Florida and Utah, authorities said Bundy had victims in Colorado, Idaho and Washington state. They said they're working to solve the death of 16-year-old Nancy Wilcox, another likely victim in Utah. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Authorities in Utah have used advanced DNA technology to link notorious serial killer Ted Bundy to the murder of a 17-year-old girl whose body was discovered by hunters 52 years ago.
Melissa Ann Smith, the daughter of a local police chief, was found on 27 October 1974 with signs of rape and torture.
In April, Utah officials identified teenager Laura Ann Aime as another of Bundy's victims. Evidence gathered from that case was subsequently used to help solve Smith's case.
Before his death by execution in 1989, Bundy had confessed to killing two other teenage girls in Utah. He has been linked to at least 30 murders across the US.
At a press conference on Tuesday, Utah County Sgt Mike Reynolds said there were more Bundy cases still being examined in the state. "With every case closure may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out," he said.
Salt Lake County Sheriff Rosie Rivera added that the case should be a sign to other cold case victims "that there is hope out there".
"Every single day forensics is changing and we have the ability to take a look at these cases again and again," she said.
She also praised detectives for preserving evidence from the case for so long, saying it "demonstrates the need to preserve evidence even when decades pass".
In April, the director of the Utah Bureau of Forensic Services told the Salt Lake Tribune, there were 444 unsolved death investigations in the state, including 258 homicides.
Bundy is among America's most infamous serial killers, and began his spree by attacking victims throughout the US Pacific north-west.
Known to often approach women in public places, he would gain their trust with his charm or a fake injury, and then lure them to secluded areas and kill them.
He was first arrested in 1975 for kidnapping a woman and sentenced to 15 years in jail. But in 1977 he escaped by jumping out of a prison library window.
He was recaptured for eight days and then escaped again, continuing to kill until he was finally caught in 1978.

dfe23806c9d2.text: By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/brazils-flavio-bolsonaro-leaves-brazil-for-the-united-states-after-presidential-loss-according-to-multiple-media-reports Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil for the United States after presidential loss, according to multiple media reports World Oct 27, 2026 3:44 PM EDT SAO PAULO (AP) — Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has left Brazil for the United States following a stunning loss to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election, according to multiple media reports. A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election. WATCH: Lula prevails in Brazil but Flávio Bolsonaro refuses to concede Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: His brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest. While Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America, he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged." Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied. Bolsonaro, 45, was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud. Bolsonaro initially asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that prompted authorities to extend voting by two hours. On Monday, he urged the electoral court to investigate alleged election fraud and nullify Lula's and Vice President Geraldo Alckmin's candidacies, which the electoral court has never done before. To overturn the result, Bolsonaro would have to present evidence of fraud affecting Lula's 4.4 million-vote margin and convince the eight-member electoral court before the results are certified on Dec. 18. Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%. Bolsonaro said in a video posted Monday on his social media channels that he had no plans to leave Brazil and instead was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court. Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. In one, he's accused of using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In the other, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker. He has denied any wrongdoing in both cases. Prosecutors suspect the funds from the banker were used to pay his brother Eduardo Bolsonaro's expenses and to promote Flávio Bolsonaro's political agenda with the Trump administration, documents show. Brazilians had earlier taken to social media to ask where Bolsonaro was. Reporters gathered outside his home in the capital, Brasilia, but he did not appear. A spokesperson for the Ministry of Security of Argentina denied reports the Brazilian senator had entered the country. Brazilian media outlets reported that many Bolsonaro allies had been unable to reach him. Paulo Figueiredo, a close ally of Bolsonaro's who lives in the United States, was asked about the senator's whereabouts and did not answer directly. "At this moment — following months of intense work that were unfairly thwarted — I have no desire to speak with the press. I kindly ask that you do not persist. Should I have a statement to make on any matter, I will reach out," Figueiredo said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.
The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.
She sustained injuries to her head and neck and had emergency surgery, but the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.
An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.
Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.
"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.
The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.
It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.
Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injuries she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition.
A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.
"They are, and remain, predators."
Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.

ce5aa207de50.text: President Trump applauded Quebec's new separatist premier Tuesday, continuing to jab at Ottawa despite fragile trade talks that seemed to be gaining momentum. The big picture: Even as Trump's top economic adviser suggested a deal to ease the ongoing trade war is possible, the president has continue to antagonize Canada. The U.S. recently accused Canada of trying to influence American elections through retaliatory tariffs, which Canadian officials have denied. Meanwhile, Trump's continued to antagonize Canada from the campaign trail, saying at a Mississippi stop Monday that it was "charging us massive tariffs" and has "treated us badly." Driving the news: In a brief shoutout Tuesday, the president congratulated Paul St-Pierre Plamondon for his win some three weeks ago. While a recent vote stymied an Albertan separatist push , St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to hold Quebec's third referendum on independence, though he's said it wouldn't happen until after Trump leaves office. St-Pierre Plamondon's center-left Parti Québécois won 60 of 127 seats, leaving it four short of a majority. It would likely need support from a fellow separatist party to advance a referendum. Prime Minister Mark Carney has emphasized the importance of Canadian unity as the nation faces unprecedented hostility from the American president. Trump shared an Irish Times article that framed the Quebec vote as a "blow to Mark Carney" that could "hamper" his "efforts to maintain national unity against Trump." Zoom out: Trump on Tuesday also congratulated British Columbia's premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, after his Conservatives swung the province rightward. "Conservatives are moving strong in Canada!" the president wrote . Doerkson, however, has rejected suggestions that he's aligned with the president, similar to St-Pierre Plamondon. Friction point: The U.S. Embassy in Canada last week accused Canadian leaders of trying to influence American politics with reciprocal tariffs on politically important products and states in the U.S. The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The intrigue: White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett said in a Fox interview Sunday that negotiations with Canada have "picked up" and are "gathering steam." Carney told reporters Monday trade talks had intensified slightly since the talks last fell apart in August . Midterm politics are complicating Trump's tariff agenda, Axios' Courtenay Brown reports. Last week, the the White House exempted certain Canadian imports from 50% tariffs following pressure from Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) . Collins pledged to seek to seek further tariff relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada. The bottom line: Trump relationship with Canada has been tumultuous — rattled by trade tensions and the president's persistent "51st state" threats. Go deeper: Trump's Canada feud collides with Alberta's separatist vote

1733ec212dc3.text:
When asked to choose, Florida’s likely voters have picked protecting the environment over economic growth by more than 2 to 1, a margin that surprised even the pollster who asked the question.
In a University of North Florida poll released last week, 61 percent of respondents said state and local officials should prioritize the environment “even at the risk of curbing economic growth.” Twenty-six percent chose growth. Registered Republicans sided with the environment 48 percent to 35 percent, and so did a plurality of 2024 voters who backed Donald Trump.
“I expected probably [the] environment to win narrowly, but this was a blowout,” said Sean Freeder, who directs UNF’s Public Opinion Research Lab.
Less than two weeks before Election Day, that sentiment has echoed through Florida’s U.S. Senate race between Republican Ashley Moody, the incumbent, and Democrat Angie Nixon, a state representative. Instead of a broad climate debate, it shows up in specific fights over data centers, power bills, hurricane recovery and the fixes either candidate can offer.
The race is closer than many expected in a state Trump won by 13 points in 2024. The UNF poll showed Moody, whom Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed in 2025 to serve the rest of Marco Rubio’s term, ahead 49 percent to 45 percent, down 8 points from July. Nixon outraised Moody by nearly $2 million in the third quarter, but Moody and her affiliated committees had about $7.1 million on hand on Oct.1, compared with about $4.5 million for Nixon. The two will not debate.
Nixon’s sharpest environmental position is on data centers. “There needs to be a moratorium,” she told Inside Climate News. “You cannot build any more data centers.” Her campaign platform calls for no new construction “before there are real federal guardrails.”
The Sierra Club, whose political arm has endorsed Nixon, also wants federal rules. “Absent those, yes, we support a statewide moratorium,” said Susannah Randolph, director of Sierra Club Florida.
In June, Walton County commissioners voted unanimously to prohibit large data centers. In Polk County, residents are fighting a proposed $2.6 billion project on a former phosphate mine in Fort Meade, where Nixon held a town hall last month.
Moody, whose campaign did not respond to requests for comment, has said data center decisions belong to communities and states. “It needs to be up to the people of a community or a state to decide what works best for them,” she said in a Fox News interview last month. In September, she cosponsored the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would push utility regulators to make large data centers cover the grid costs of serving them.
“If billion-dollar tech companies want to build a massive data center, Floridians should not be left to foot the bill,” she said at the time.
The Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the House 417-3 but has not cleared the Senate, would direct state utility regulators to consider standards requiring large data centers that draw more than 100 megawatts—roughly the electricity used by 65,000 Florida homes—to pay the full cost of new power plants, transmission lines and grid upgrades built to serve them. It would also have regulators consider requiring those customers to post financial guarantees before construction begins and to cover costs if they walk away from a contract early.
Florida’s new data center law, Senate Bill 484, signed in May, goes further. It already requires utilities to make large data center customers pay their full cost of service so those expenses don’t shift to other ratepayers, and it applies to more facilities than the federal bill.
“Anybody that would be covered by the Ratepayer Protection Act is already covered by Senate Bill 484,” said Ted Kury, director of energy studies at the University of Florida’s Public Utility Research Center. “When it comes to electricity, essentially all they’re saying is, ‘Hey, the state PSC has to do their job.’”
A national moratorium, he added, would likely be challenged by states that want data centers, “and the federal government would probably lose.” (The research center’s sponsors include Florida Power & Light and the Florida Public Service Commission.)

Randolph was blunter about Moody’s sponsorship weeks before the election: “The timing is really suspicious and doesn’t smell good.”
Both candidates also pitch themselves as capable of offering relief from rising power bills. Nixon said she would “call for investigations” when rate increases follow large utility campaign contributions. Moody has built her affordability message around the federal tax cuts she voted for.
Florida Power & Light customers are absorbing the biggest rate hike in the utility’s history, approved last November: $945 million in 2026 and $705 million in 2027, with more on the horizon. An inquiry into the deaths of 33 detainees in Nigeria's Minna state has found they died as a result of severe overcrowding, poor ventilation and failure by officers to respond to distress calls.
Forensic and medical evidence showed the "entirely preventable" deaths had resulted from acute respiratory failure linked to prolonged confinement, aggravated by heat stress and dehydration.
The evidence did not support initial claims of a disease outbreak.
The detainees were found dead on 17 September while being held by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps on suspicion of illegal mining. The investigation found that the mining sites had been licensed.
Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said those found responsible for the deaths would face the full force of the law.
He added that the detention hall had been cleaned before investigators arrived, raising concerns about possible attempts to compromise evidence.
Implicated officers will face suspension and the report would be forwarded to the attorney general of the federation for further legal action, Tunji-Ojo said.
The investigating committee found that the raid on the miners had been conducted without an approved operational order, proper planning or consultation with the Mining Marshals Unit.
It said that 50 detainees had been held in a cell measuring about 20 sq m, with no running water or functioning toilet, and inadequate food, drinking water and airflow.
Adults and minors were detained together, and some detainees were held beyond lawful detention periods.
Officers reportedly ignored repeated calls for help, despite a medical worker having raised concerns about the conditions.
"Detainees repeatedly banged on cell doors and walls, shouted for assistance and pleaded for water," said the head of the investigating team, Jonathan Kure.
"These distress calls were heard by officers assigned to nearby duties... but were not acted upon."
Kure said the detention conditions amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.
"The tragedy demonstrates the consequences of systemic disregard for detention standards, supervisory responsibilities and the welfare of persons in custody," he added.
The investigating committee also recommended compensation of 30m naira (Â£16,683; $22,285) for each of the bereaved families and 10m naira for each survivor.

Twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman have pleaded guilty to being part of an international criminal network that defrauded people on dating sites and social media.
The group targeted elderly people in the US and Europe, using fake identities to lure their victims into believing they were in a romantic relationship, before persuading them to transfer large sums of money into bank accounts in Ghana.
The 22-year-old twins, Jamal and Kamal Abubakari, and 53-year-old Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie from Hawaii face up to 20 years in jail and will be sentenced next year.
Between July 2024 - April 2026, the victims collectively lost $9m (Â£6.7m).
While many of them were from Ohio - where the charges were brought - other victims were located in 24 other US states, as well as Germany and Austria.
As part of the plea, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit pieces of jewellery which investigators seized during their arrest, including luxury watches, rings, chains and earrings.
The three accused go by several names:
- Jamal Abubakari, also known as Jamal Abubakar and Arrangement
- Kamal Abubakari, also known as Kamal Abubakar and Lancaster
- Joy Opoku-Boachie, also known as Amanda Joy Glum and Amanda Joy Kessei Bierman
In recent months, US authorities have stepped up their crackdown on criminal networks operating in the US and West Africa which seek to defraud elderly Americans.
Earlier this month, FBI Director Kash Patel said it had made hundreds of arrests after dismantling a scam centre in Ghana.
In June, a Ghanaian social media influencer known as Abu Trica, whose real name is Frederick Kumi, was extradited to the US to face trial for allegedly running a romance scam that defrauded elderly Americans of more than $8m (Â£5.9m).
He targeted victims through social media and online dating platforms, and is accused of requesting money or valuables under false pretences such as urgent medical needs.
The case against Kumi is being prosecuted under the US Elder Abuse Prevention and Prosecution law. He denies all the charges against him.

A controversial Islamic cleric in Nigeria has been murdered outside his home in the northern state of Katsina.
Two assailants arrived on a motorcycle and shot Yahaya Masussuka in the town of Dutsin-Ma as he was saying goodbye to visitors on Monday evening, sources told the BBC.
The 47-year-old preacher and one of his guests, who was also shot, were rushed to hospital but both were pronounced dead by the attending doctor, police said.
It is not clear why Masussuka was targeted, but the cleric had received death threats on social media where he posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam, including what happens to people after their death.
It is widely believed in Islam that a person's soul will be questioned in the grave by two angels. If they answer correctly, their soul sleeps peacefully until the day of judgement - if not it will be tormented.
This understanding comes from what is known as the Hadith, a collection of texts believed to be the spoken words and actions of the Prophet Muhammad.
This serves as a key source of Islamic knowledge to help interpret the Quran, the central religious text of Islam.
But Masussuka based his teachings mainly on what was in Islam's holy book, questioned some of the hadiths - and did not believe that the dead were reawakened and questioned.
He was once jailed for nine months because he teased some respected scholars over their belief in this hadith and other teachings.
Masussuka, who had two wives and seven children, began preaching at the age of 13 in Quranic schools.
He later attended Al-Azhar University in Egypt and later went to Oman for further studies.
At his home, he had a studio where he would record videos of his teachings for broadcast on social media for his followers.
The cleric was also outspoken about violent extremism, radicalisation and openly advocated for interfaith dialogue and peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians, who make up nearly equal parts of Nigeria's population.
Thousands of Christians and Muslims have been killed in ethnic and religious violence here over the past 25 years.
For Masussuka's efforts, Nigeria's Network for Good Governance and Transparency honoured him with a Peace Ambassador Award last year.
Six other prominent Muslim preachers have been murdered over the last two decades in northern Nigeria - several targeted by Boko Haram for criticising the jihadist group that began its insurgency in 2009.
Founded in north-eastern Nigeria, it opposes Western culture, education, the secular government - and its political goal is the creation of an Islamic state.
Additional reporting by BBC Pidgin

A bank of white freezers hums away at a former watch factory in central London. Inside: dozens of small boxes with barcoded glass tubes, collectively containing one hundred billion genes. Just two boxes may hold 10 times more information than all the text on the internet, says Dr Oliver Vince, the facility's co-founder.
His firm, Basecamp Research, plans to collect as much DNA as possible to create an artificial intelligence that can speak the language of biology, in the same way that US and Chinese tech firms have hoovered up written material online to create Large Language Models (LLMs), the basis of current AI systems.
Vince, like many in business and academic research, believes AI will supercharge scientific research. But increasingly, it also comes with controversy.
Last month, OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, said it had solved one of maths' great unsolved problems, relating to the famous NavierâStokes equations. The company said its AI agents had cracked it in 88 hours. The body that runs a prize for whoever can solve the problem said it had "apparently been settled", but that its review would take time.
But hours before the announcement, Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at New York University, went public with concerns. He formed an independent team with Levent AlpÃ¶ge, a mathematician employed by day by the rival company Anthropic.
They had been working towards the same goal, and kept their drafts in OpenAI's coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster said that his co-researcher was tipped off that news of their progress had "reached" OpenAI, though he did not specify how. He asked whether his research, stored in Codex, could have fed into OpenAI's own work, though he stressed he was "not accusing anyone of anything".
OpenAI said that nobody at the company, human or AI, saw the other teams' work before it was published. Initially it said that while unlikely, it could not "rule out" that anonymised data from use of its products may have helped improve its models. Days later, it said Buckmaster's Codex prompts from the two months before the announcement "could not have influenced the system in any way".
It's a complicated story; we still don't fully know what happened. But it highlights a growing issue about the use of AI in science. Usually, those words make us conjure up images of robots building terrible genetically-engineered viruses, or chemical weapons, to wipe out humanity. But there's a more subtle problem that hasn't attracted the same headline-grabbing attention: that AI could undermine faith in the scientific process, raising questions about the novelty and accuracy of research.
And there's another concern. It's well known that AI chatbots like Claude or Gemini can sometimes hallucinate things that simply aren't true. They will tell you about a film that never existed, or a quote that was never said. Now there is evidence that this is increasingly happening in science. Eventually, it's feared, it will become difficult to separate true scientific discovery from AI-generated fiction.
And all of this could threaten to erode - if not explode - the rock on which scientific research rests: trust.
A 'watershed moment'
One threat is to scientific journals, the guardians of scientific integrity, which are seen to be failing to deal with a tsunami of AI-generated distortions.
"Generative AI has basically disrupted the whole scientific process," says Dalmeet Singh Chawla, a science journalist who has spent a decade reporting on research misconduct.
He tells the BBC that publishers' integrity staff - the people who screen submissions for accuracy and reliability - will need to "drastically increase [in number and effort] if they're anywhere near the fight". He says: "Right now, it seems like they're not."
On the face of it, AI seems just the right tool to power scientific research. Scientists deal with huge amounts of information. Telescopes and particle accelerators, for example, collect billions of data points â too large for the brain to comprehend. AI can pick the scientific highlights from the surrounding humdrum.
The poster child of scientific AI is the UK-based firm Google DeepMind, which in 2020 solved one of biology's biggest problems: how proteins in living things fold into their precise shapes.
It may sound dull, but proteins are the tiny machines that make life work, and the shapes they fold into determine what they can do; from building cells and fighting infection to helping form the tissues and organs of the body.
Before AI, scientists had to conduct time-consuming experiments in the lab. Then, Google DeepMind developed an AI model called AlphaFold that accurately predicted 200 million protein folds in just one year.
The equivalent experimental work would have taken hundreds of millions of years in laboratories. The firm gave the results away for free to researchers. The head of DeepMind and the project's lead scientist were both awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry.
It was big hugs all round.
Dr Pushmeet Kohli, who leads DeepMind's science work, told me that AlphaFold could be seen as a "watershed moment".
Questions over AI's work
But elsewhere, the use of AI in science has come with accusations of hype. Some computer models are accused of exaggerating the significance of their findings, with the human researchers that oversee them then believing some of the claims without enough scepticism.
Basking in its success over AlphaFold, for example, DeepMind turned its attention to predicting the structure of new materials. The work could lead to the development of better batteries, cheaper solar cells and electronic components that are not dependent on rare earth elements. (In theory, no-one would need to argue about mining rights ever again, and Greenland would be safe from invasion.)

A decade after world leaders signed the legally binding Paris Agreement to combat climate change, the crisis’ health harms are getting worse and progress is lagging, according to a new report from leading international scientists.
The 10th annual Lancet Countdown report, published Tuesday, is authored by 146 researchers from more than 30 countries, led by University College London and produced in collaboration with the World Health Organization. Following a slew of record-breaking findings in last year’s report, the authors found that heat, famine, disaster and disease are costing millions of lives around the world. Health harms from climate change, they say, have accelerated faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement than they did in the decade prior.
These harms are global, but they fall disproportionately on lower-income nations that have contributed relatively little to the climate crisis.
Meanwhile, rising energy demand, continued fossil fuel reliance and a slow transition to clean energy mean the world is failing to respond to the speed and scale of the hazards.
“Climate change is not only getting worse, but it’s getting worse a lot faster than it used to, and that has to do with the fact that year on year we’re reaching record levels of greenhouse gas emissions,” said Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown. “It’s a stark call to action.”
Recent months saw catastrophic floods, wildfires and heat waves, and news that the world is on course to overshoot the key 1.5 degree Celsius warming threshold set in the Paris Agreement within the next few years.
The report’s authors called on the World Health Organization and member states to declare climate change a global health emergency, and for health to be centered in global talks to reduce emissions and transition away from fossil fuels. The next major opportunity is in November at the 31st United Nations Conference of the Parties on climate, known as COP31.
“The evidence is undeniable: climate change is one of the greatest threats to health facing humanity,” said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, director-general of the World Health Organization, in a statement with the report.
The report’s authors emphasized that global investments in clean energy have brought some relief: From 2016 to 2023, cleaner air avoided an estimated 323,000 annual deaths in a little more than half of countries surveyed, with leading gains in China and the U.S. But globally, that was balanced out by increased deaths in the other 46 percent of countries.
The average number of people dying each year from extreme heat has grown in the last decade. In 2023—the most recent year with complete data—heat was linked to a record 710,000 estimated deaths. That’s more than the lives lost to HIV or malaria in the same year. And more than 70 percent of those deaths are attributable to human-caused climate change, according to the report.
Between 2016 and 2023, climate change is estimated to have caused almost 3 million heat deaths, the authors found.
Heat also has serious impacts on people’s livelihoods, and carved an estimated $1.07 trillion of potential income out of the global economy as high temperatures kept people from work, the report concluded. Southeast Asia and Africa were hit hardest, as were the agriculture and construction sectors.

More than half of the world’s land was impacted by extreme drought for at least a month last year, the second-highest level on record after 2023, with serious implications for food security and sanitation. In the decade since the Paris Agreement went into effect, incidence of extreme drought has grown more than 700 percent faster than it did in the previous 10 years. Extreme rainfall is also becoming more common, ramping up risks of floods, landslides and waterborne disease.
This year and next, an El Niño supercharged by climate change is likely to bring more death and destruction along the same unequal lines. It’s critical to prioritize early warning systems and make sure health systems around the world are equipped to respond, Romanello added.
“In the upcoming months, we have to be very vigilant,” she said. “We’re talking about very extreme events that could have lethal consequences.”
Meanwhile, global efforts to get wealthier nations to support developing ones in mitigating and responding to climate harms, like the U.N. Loss and Damage Fund, have languished. Four years after the fund was created, Nepal became the first country to get approval for an emergency allocation this month
The report comes out just weeks before COP31, where government, business, science and civil society leaders will gather to review climate goals. That includes those from the Paris Agreement, from which President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. for the second time at the start of this year.
Diana Picon Manyari, international climate senior director at the global organization Health Care Without Harm, wants health professionals to have a seat at the table at COP31. Manyari would like a focus on both adaptation and mitigation in the healthcare sector, and better financing options for healthcare systems to address climate impacts.
“The commitments are not enough [and] whatever is out there is very difficult to access,” Manyari said of financing.
Jeni Miller, executive director of the Global Climate and Health Alliance, wasn’t surprised by the Lancet Countdown’s results: They match what she’s hearing from her international network of healthcare workers. She emphasized that all the decisions made at COP have an impact on human health. That includes addressing the root cause of climate change—fossil fuels.

ac7df6c28a05.text: Senate leaders could be guessing who will control the chamber well into November, thanks to a slew of tight races and state-specific voting rules. Why it matters: A GOP majority would ease the pressure on Senate Majority Leader John Thune to move quickly on nominations, while a Democratic majority would give Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer more leverage in the lame-duck session. If the chamber splits 50/50, leaders will have to start negotiating their power-sharing agreement. Zoom in: Four states could leave the majority in limbo. Alaska: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) is trying to fend off former Rep. Mary Peltola (D). Alaska election results have taken weeks to finalize because of the vast state's transportation challenges, mail ballots and ranked-choice tabulation. The Trump Justice Department is preemptively trying to block results from being finalized if Sullivan narrowly loses. Maine's ranked-choice voting could lengthen the vote tallying if neither Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) nor Democratic nominee Troy Jackson gets more than 50% in the first round. Kansas' three-day grace period for mail-in ballots could delay results in the race between Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton and Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.). It is far closer than expected. In Texas, a dragged-out recount could be coming. A candidate can request one if the margin is less than 10% of the winner's vote total — which is likely to happen between state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) and state Rep. James Talarico (D). The candidate who requests it has to pay. The clock: Congress currently plans to leave for the holidays on Dec. 18. But if Republicans lose both the House and Senate , Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) wants senators to stay in town through the holidays (yes, Thanksgiving and Christmas) to work on a massive GOP reconciliation package they can pass without Democratic support. The big picture: Congress has a long to-do list either way, including funding the government past Dec. 11, passing emergency defense spending and potentially raising the debt ceiling. It needs to pass the National Defense Authorization Act, Farm Bill and permitting reform, reauthorize the warrantless wiretap authority under FISA Section 702 and confirm nominations before they expire at the end of the year. The bottom line: "I'm guessing that's a possibility this year," Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) told reporters today about working in D.C. through the holiday recess.

85f1976054cd.text: White evangelical Christians have been among President Trump’s most loyal supporters for more than a decade, and our new PBS News/NPR/Marist poll shows that most still approve of him. Stephanie Sy: White evangelical Christians have been the bedrock of Donald Trump's support for more than a decade, and they largely still are. In the latest PBS News/NPR/Marist poll, 66 percent say they approve of the job Trump is doing as president, 26 points higher than the number of Americans overall who say the same. As Trump rallies his base ahead of the midterm elections, nearly three-quarters of white evangelicals also plan to back Republicans for Congress. For Trump, it's a bond that once seemed unlikely. In 2016, candidate Trump rocketed to the top of the Republican primary, a thrice-married New York real estate mogul caught on tape bragging about groping women and accused of relationships with more than one porn star. President Donald Trump: I stand before you today to fulfill one of my highest and most important duties under the United States Constitution, the nomination of a Supreme Court justice. Stephanie Sy: But, as president, he accomplished what has long driven many Christians at the polls, his appointment of three conservative Supreme Court justices, which led to the historic overturning of Roe v. Wade and a rollback of abortion protections for millions of American women. Estep acknowledges his congregants don't all vote alike, but making abortion illegal is one issue where they are mostly aligned. Pastor Erik Estep: To vote according to what our faith prescribes us to vote. Some people have different perspectives, but there's not much of a different perspective when it comes to issues of abortion and life. I think the Bible's pretty clear. Stephanie Sy: But even among evangelicals, Trump's support has slipped, reflecting an overall fraying of his coalition. His approval rating among those that voted for him has dropped 12 points since the start of his second term. That falloff is particularly steep among Latinos and young voters in other recent polling. Even at Village Church in South Carolina, some are wavering. Cynthia Carroll, South Carolina Voter: I was a Republican. I voted Donald Trump into -- as president. And now I'm more on the fence between conservative and a Democrat. Stephanie Sy: Until recently, that loyalty had survived some striking moments, like when conservative Charlie Kirk was assassinated last year and his widow, Erika, chose to forgive his killer. Erika Kirk, CEO, Turning Point USA: I forgive him because it was what Christ did and is what Charlie would do. Stephanie Sy: President Trump took a different stance. President Donald Trump: That's where I disagreed with Charlie. I hate my opponent. Stephanie Sy: And this spring, the president posted an AI image of himself appearing as a Christ-like healer. President Donald Trump: I did post it. Stephanie Sy: After Christian leaders labeled it blasphemous, Trump deleted it, explaining he thought the image portrayed him as a doctor, which he also is not. Robert Jones, CEO, Public Religion Research Institute: I think part of it is really about a vision of the country that he has promised them. Stephanie Sy: Robert Jones, president of the Public Religion Research Institute, says the evangelical support Trump does still enjoy is rooted in a certain vision of America. Robert Jones: The message is, we're a white Christian country. We're losing that identity. But if you stick with me, I'm going to make sure that we keep that identity. Stephanie Sy: But voters who identify as Christian may have more options this election. Christian faith leaders are running for the Senate as Democrats in Kansas and Texas. In reliably red South Carolina, where the Senate race is unusually tight. Republicans are trying to energize evangelical support for Darline Graham by focusing on transgender issues. President Donald Trump: The Democrat who Darline is running to defeat is a far left political hack who supports transgender for everybody and believes in telling confused children they're trapped in the wrong body. Stephanie Sy: During a recent campaign rally in the state, Trump painted Democrats as enemies of conservative values. Robert Jones: So when you have, like, that willingness to like literally demonize your political opponents, and then you have got a group that has been attached to you by party and religion, it sets up a kind of toxic environment. Stephanie Sy: For his part, Pastor Erik Estep does not endorse specific candidates or a party in his sermon. Pastor Erik Estep: We think that it falls on pastors. If you want people to respond and to get out and to be to be heard, well, there has to be some sort of motivation. Stephanie Sy: What motivates his congregants this year may well be critical on Election Day. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.

887a84ce72f8.text: Indonesia is battling its worst wildfires in more than a decade, made worse by El Niño. Many were deliberately set to clear land for farming, including palm oil plantations. More than 12,000 schools across Indonesia have closed because of the toxic haze. Nathaniel Undas, a school principal and photographer, has been documenting the fires on social media. Amna Nawaz: Indonesia is battling its worst wildfires in more than a decade, made worse by El Nino weather patterns. Many of these fires were deliberately set to clear land for farming, including palm oil plantations. Rain this week brought some relief, but the rainy season isn't expected until next month. More than 12,000 schools across Indonesia have closed because of the toxic haze, which has also spread to neighboring countries. In Central Kalimantan, where children have been out of class for weeks, one school principal and photographer has been documenting the fires on social media. He spoke to us from an empty classroom at the Golden Christian Middle School. Natanael Undas, Photographer: My name is Natanael Undas. I'm a school principal Palangkaraya, Central Kalimantan. It is a kind of rain forest and then a lot of native trees. We got a lot of fruits. We got a lot of tree for timber. But now the sky, it turns yellow. It turns like hell. The last time I saw the blue sky was in August '20. The haze come to our city. And then the fire goes closer, closer, closer and closer. And then, like the last week, it was a really huge fire in the city. I'm really sad, because my student lost a lot of school hour and learning experience. If you go outside in a school hour, probably at 8:00, 9:00 a.m. in the morning, they go outside, they play with other friends without a mask and thinking it's just like a school holiday in the middle of yellow sky. This fire is not natural disaster at all. It is manmade disaster. We're hoping the rain will come soon. Last night, there was a huge rain, even only for 17 to 25 minutes. We're longing to inhale the smell of rain, the smell of air, the smell of wet leaves, the smell of wet land. Last night, when it was raining, I open a little bit of my door, and I try to smell the rain. It's like a smelling the perfume that's mixed with smoke. It's still poisoned, so I need to close it. Not many people knows about what really happening right now, what we are experiencing, especially what we are inhaling. A lot of children are suffering because of respiratory issue. I don't want my daughter having the same experience. I don't want to lose this generation. We still can save this.

5060f9921bf8.text: This year, the 26th president's legacy received a remarkable new tribute: the opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in the Badlands of North Dakota, a landscape that helped shape his lifelong commitment to conservation. Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown recently paid a visit for our arts and culture series, CANVAS. Geoff Bennett: Finally tonight, a birthday salute to Theodore Roosevelt. The nation's 26th president one of its most consequential was born on this day back in 1858. And, this year, his legacy received a remarkable new tribute, the opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in the Badlands of North Dakota, a landscape that helped shape his lifelong commitment to conservation. Our senior arts correspondent, Jeffrey Brown, paid a visit for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Jeffrey Brown: It's a spectacular setting nestled in the rugged Badlands of Western North Dakota, a breathtaking tribute to the life and legacy of Theodore Roosevelt. It's a landscape that deeply impacted T.R., who once said he'd never have become president if not for his time here. And it continues to inspire and move people today. Craig Dykers: We wanted it to feel that it belonged, so that it didn't feel that it just dropped out of the sky. Jeffrey Brown: Yes. Craig Dykers: At the same time, we wanted it to feel fresh and new and different from anything anybody had seen before. Jeffrey Brown: Craig Dykers, co-founder of the international architecture firm Snohetta, helped design the new 93,000-square-foot Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library. Craig Dykers: There's a sensation of what the landscape means that you learn when you move through it. Jeffrey Brown: After settling on this remote location, Dykers camped alone for 12 days in the Badlands searching for inspiration. Craig Dykers: In the wilderness here, the more you go into it, the more you're able to experience what he called lonesome freedom, or lonely freedom. And that's an interesting idea, that you're alone, but you feel free. Normally, we think of being alone as a scary thing, especially in a place that's wild. Jeffrey Brown: Beautiful, but potentially very scary out there, right, if you're alone. Craig Dykers: Yes, if you're alone, but, at a certain point, you and the context around you become one. Jeffrey Brown: The son of wealthy and prominent New Yorkers, Teddy Roosevelt first came to the small town of Medora to hunt bison in 1883. He returned the following year as a heartbroken 25-year-old after writing in his diary: "The light has gone out of my life." Edward O'Keefe: The Women Who Created a President": Theodore Roosevelt came to North Dakota at a time of incredible stress and distress in his life. He had lost his wife and his mother on the same day of different causes in the same house. He healed and he recovered in the Badlands of North Dakota. Jeffrey Brown: Edward O'Keefe is the CEO of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library Foundation, a nonprofit that raised more than $500 million to complete the project. O'Keefe, author of a biography of T.R. and who now leads public broadcasting's WNET Group in New York City, says Roosevelt's time in North Dakota would shape the rest of his life. Edward O'Keefe: He found resilience in nature. He mourned, and he was depressed when he was in Dakota. And he finally got to live that life that he'd only read about in books. Theodore Roosevelt felt that North Dakota saved his life. Jeffrey Brown: So far, large crowds have poured in since the library opened July 4, offering visitors a chance to learn about a president who left an indelible, if complicated, impression on American life. A champion of conservation and protector of public lands, Roosevelt was also a champion of military might and expansion abroad. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt is like a Rorschach test. What you see in him says more about you than it does about him. Republicans, Democrats, independents, everyone loves T.R., right? That's the beauty of Theodore Roosevelt. He brings people together. Jeffrey Brown: And while it's a presidential library in name only, Roosevelt's personal papers are mostly scattered elsewhere, some of his most famous speeches light up the walls, and visitors can see photos and artifacts from every part of his life, from his student days at Harvard, to a hat and single-action Colt revolver from his time as a New York City police commissioner. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt later said, it's better to wear out than to rust out. And he did it every day of his life. He lived only to 60 years old, and those were very, very packed 60 years. Jeffrey Brown: Other highlights include his custom-tailored Rough Rider uniform worn during the Spanish-American war. AI ACTOR: I wanted every guest to feel the worth of their talents. Jeffrey Brown: And there's even an AI hologram of Roosevelt designed by Microsoft that takes questions. Mr. President, what do you hope people visiting your library take away from it? AI ACTOR: I hope visitors leave knowing a single thing. We have power to protect wild places just as I did. Edward O'Keefe: Theodore Roosevelt wrote a letter in 1918, a year before he died. He said: "If I could keep one memory of my entire life, it would be my experiences as a rancher and a cowboy in Dakota." Jeffrey Brown: Using heavy timber, rammed earth walls, and Many materials native to the region, Dyker says the library was designed to give visitors a chance to reflect, all while taking in the surrounding natural beauty, from a walkable roof above, to rocking chairs below. Craig Dykers: If you look at the shape, it has a shape that's characteristic of the low-lying Badlands in the distance. It's not the same, but it has the feeling of something you might find out here. Narrator: Here we have a group of beings who are not able to protect themselves. Jeffrey Brown: The library also uses educational videos like this one to address some of Roosevelt's troubling legacies
