The port-call situation is wearing out Navy warships
Diego Garcia is the only safe place for ships fighting Iran, but the remote atoll can’t provide the maintenance they need.
A few years ago, a port call in the Middle East might mean bottomless-mojito brunches in Bahrain, hitting the indoor ski slopes in a Dubai megamall, or a desert safari in Qatar. But since Operation Epic Fury began eight months ago, U.S. warships in the theater have basically had just one option: Diego Garcia, some 2,500 miles away.
It’s not great for morale, but the consequences go beyond disgruntled sailors who tire of fishing off the British island in the Indian Ocean. The remote coral atoll lacks the pierside infrastructure that many Gulf, Mediterranean, and Pacific ports can offer. As the Navy stretches its fleet with longer deployments and fewer port calls, warships are losing the ability to do crucial mid-cruise maintenance.
“When a ship is deployed overseas for longer than the nominal seven-month deployment period, that increases the amount of time for equipment on the ship to break, get worn down, or worn out. As a result, when the ship finally does make it back to the United States, it might need more maintenance and repair work than it would have needed if the deployment had not exceeded seven months,” said Ron O’Rourke, who retired this year after more than 40 years as a naval analyst for the Congressional Research Service.
“That can increase the time and cost to do the maintenance and repair work, and an increased time needed to do the work could prevent other ships from entering maintenance and overhaul as scheduled. This can lead to a cascading effect in delaying maintenance on other ships.”
A Navy officer with expertise in maritime security agreed, noting that “even deployed ships need time alongside”—that is, moored directly to a pier or tender vessel for what’s called voyage repair availability—“to fix broken things, remediate rust, paint, etc. If these ships are kept out for 10 to 12 months, they’ll be missing other scheduled maintenance events and be much more broken than they should be when they get home.”
The Navy itself nodded to the problem in a recent press release about the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln, which is changing homeports to receive overdue depot-level maintenance after a nearly 11-month deployment.
“Regularly scheduled depot-level maintenance maximizes the lifespan of our Navy vessels and keeps our fleets lethal, modern, and ready to defend the nation.”
The Lincoln’s 321-day deployment—and the carrier Gerald R. Ford’s 326-day deployment before it—set records for consecutive days at sea and length of deployment, respectively. But a few Arleigh Burke-class guided missile destroyers are on track to far surpass those numbers. And Navy officials recently told families in Yokosuka, Japan, that for the foreseeable future they should expect all ships to deploy for 10 to 12 months.
A Navy spokesperson said they would “not discuss specific readiness rates, operational requirements, force-allocation deliberations, or future force movements. However, we remain committed to regular maintenance to maximize the lifespan of our Navy vessels and keep our fleets lethal and ready to defend our nation.”
‘It’s empty’
Instead of the luxury hotels and hundreds of restaurants sailors can visit in ports like Dubai and Bahrain, Diego Garcia has a military supply base and a small town with a handful of restaurants. And since virtually every ship deployed in the region is using the island for port calls and resupply, store shelves don’t always stay stocked.
The guided-missile destroyer John Finn, which left Japan in January, pulled into Diego Garcia after months at sea.
“Everybody’s going to the ship store and it’s empty,” a sailor’s spouse told Defense One. “You can find ice cream, but you’re not going to find your necessities that you need to function.”
The ship had pulled in because it was “empty,” the spouse said, after having spent all of its weapons in the campaign against Iran. “So they had to spend that week resupplying.”
The spouse of a sailor on the Mustin, another guided-missile destroyer, said her husband was able to get socks but not shoe polish at the exchange on base during the only port call the ship has made since leaving Japan in April.
“He got off like, preparing to be able to get the stuff that he needed right now, and he goes, ‘They don’t have shit,’” she said. “They didn’t have anything.”
For the Mustin crew, the port call seemed like a welcome respite from their months at sea, until they were told just before getting off the ship that they would not return in August as originally planned, but stay deployed until April 2027, the spouse told Defense One.
“The sad part is, they were actually in good spirits,” she said. “And then I know things went really rowdy in Diego Garcia because they were given the bad news literally the day before they pulled in. … There was one of the nights in Diego Garcia that two sailors ended up in the ER with alcohol poisoning. And so then they lost their last night of liberty because of it.”
O’Rourke said the British island “can provide an opportunity to be on land for a while, and to engage in certain R&R activities. But the options for doing R&R things at Diego Garcia are a lot more limited than they are at other ports, such as Singapore or somewhere in the Mediterranean.”
Ralph Cossa, chairman of the Pacific Forum, was less diplomatic.
“Please shoot me if that’s the only R&R I’m going to get in 10 months,” he said.
Mail delays
Sailors have asked their families and friends to send them supplies, but mail is taking three to six months to reach the destroyers, the spouses said.
The Mustin spouse sent her husband six boxes at the end of June; he received one in September and the rest in October. The John Finn spouse said it took four months for a few packages to reach her sailor, and some that “took even longer than six months to get out there.”

Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.
Official data released in the last week, external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.
No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.
The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.
The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.
The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.
Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.
The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

9707f03ffdf3.text: By — Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/dolores-huerta-labor-and-civil-rights-icon-dies-at-96 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dolores Huerta, labor and civil rights icon, dies at 96 Nation Oct 28, 2026 12:36 PM EDT Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase "Sí, se puede!" that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96. Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home. READ MORE: For feminists, the deaths of Parton and Steinem days apart deliver a double dose of grief She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women's rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Huerta's resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation's most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to "Yes, it can be done" — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change. WATCH: Still an Activist at 82, Dolores Huerta Calls Herself 'a Born-Again Feminist' Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign. This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement's co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died. Dolores Huerta of the United Farmworkers joins Dick Gregory, National Organization of Women President Patricia Ireland, the Rev. Jesse Jackson and actor Danny Glover during the 1996 "Fight the Right March" organized by NOW. Photo by Lou Dematteis/Reuters From the early 1970s on, Huerta's life partner was Richard Chavez, César's brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages. Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life's work and unravel all the progress made for workers. When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: "It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I'll say it that way." Homegrown activism Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who went on to win a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California. Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism. Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students' poor living conditions. READ MORE: Labor rights leader Dolores Huerta says she was sexually abused by César Chavez "I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children." Huerta's early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years. She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year "Delano Grape Strike." With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers. WATCH: Communities rebrand César Chavez Day as abuse allegations taint his legacy Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations. On the campaign trail She met Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and became a volunteer on his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her moments before he was shot. The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing for farmworkers' rights. Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating. In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush's opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco. Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer's baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. The Scoop
PsiQuantum is building its first product. It isnât a quantum computer, but it could become a superpower for AI data centers.
The company has been working for a decade on building quantum computers that use photons as âbitsâ of information and has built its own optical chips that control light particles with extreme precision. That ability to manipulate light could turn out to be a marketable tool in the next phase of the AI race, where data centers, bottlenecked by the limits of copper wiring, are switching to using fiber optics instead.
PsiQuantum says it has been showing potential customers a prototype of a new âoptical circuit switchâ that could be used to route optical signals from GPUs across data centers much more efficiently.
Know More
The AI boom wouldnât have happened without the ability to network hundreds of thousands of AI processors together. But all that networking is also the data centerâs weakest link. While GPUs can crunch numbers at blazing speeds, they are bottlenecked by the comparatively slow copper that carries the output of that math from GPU to GPU.
Thatâs especially true during the training process of increasingly large AI models that require the most coordination between large numbers of GPUs.
The next generation of data center racks are more often using optical cables to carry the data between GPUs. But optical information must be converted into an electrical signal in order to be routed to its destination, then converted back into light, before itâs converted once again when it reaches its destination.
All those conversions happening billions of times per second in the largest data centers require optical switches that generate heat, energy and bulk.
PsiQuantum says its new device can do that without ever having to convert the photons into electrical signals. It could be used to create speed-of-light connections between server racks in AI data centers that generate almost no heat and consume negligible energy.
The only major hyperscaler currently using purely optical circuit switching in an AI data center today is Google, which built a system that uses tiny mirrors, known as MEMS, to direct the light signal.
Robert Soderbery, executive vice president of PsiQuantum, said in an interview with Semafor that separate data center racks will effectively behave as one, using PsiQuantumâs device. Data could flow between GPUs in separate server racks at the same speed and latency as they would between GPUs interconnected inside a single rack. That would be a huge advantage because today server racks are reaching the limit of compute density, size and energy efficiency.
PsiQuantum isnât alone. The battle to convert data center networking to photonics has been raging since the ChatGPT moment kicked off the AI race. Earlier this year, photonic computing company Lightmatter helped launch an initiative to standardize optics in the data center space. Nvidia has been spending billions on investments in optics computing companies like Lumentum and Coherent.
For now, the GPU reigns supreme but data centers are seeing a lot more of the light.

US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta has died at the age of 96, her family has announced.
Huerta campaigned alongside fellow labour leader Cesar Chavez for farm workers' rights in the 1960s and 1970s, founding the United Farm Workers Union (UFW) with him.
Through her foundation, Huerta had continued her activism work addressing immigration and voting issues.
"As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family," family spokesman Erik Olvera said on Wednesday.
Earlier this year, Huerta said Chavez, who died in 1993, had "manipulated and pressured" her into having sex and on another occasion forced her in the 1960s.
That was after the New York Times published an investigation detailing allegations from Huerta and two other women, who said Chavez groomed and sexually abused girls involved in the labour movement.
Huerta said the two encounters with Chavez resulted in pregnancies that she chose to keep these secret, arranging for the children to be raised by other families.
Chavez's family said in a statement at the time that they were "devastated" by the reports and praised the women's "courage to come forward".

9c882b45720e.text:
Davidâs view
The day Jeffrey Epstein died, I was at the Iowa State Fair hearing from presidential candidates, and he was not exactly on their minds.
When left-wing podcasters asked 2020 hopefuls if theyâd probe the circumstances of the convicted sex offenderâs death, a few looked rattled. Theyâd prepped for so many questions, but not this. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn. was an exception, questioning how a man on suicide watch could hang himself. She also had to explain, for some reporters, what she was talking about: âThis was a sex trafficking scheme.â
Voters no longer need refreshers on Epstein. Democrats have run hundreds of ads this cycle linking their opponents to the disgraced financier, worth tens of millions of dollars. Iâm not the first take-slinger to ask whether this is the âEpstein election.â
Iâm here to answer with the reason why the message is working. This is the most expensive midterm election ever. Weâve witnessed the biggest donation in American history by one man (Elon Musk) to help one candidate (Ken Paxton). For the first time, off-year elections have attracted more cash than was spent to win the presidential race two years earlier.
The very wealthy can spend unlimited sums on campaigns, and while plenty of candidates denounce this â âoverturn Citizens Unitedâ will thrill the audience at any Democratic town hall â thereâs no serious effort to pass a constitutional amendment that would shrink that voice. Thatâs where Epstein comes in.
Many Americans are predisposed to think that wealthy people earned their money and that itâs churlish to try to take it away from them. But itâs easier than ever to argue that some ultra-wealthy people are strange, selfish, and even evil. Democrats, the GOP pollster Patrick Ruffini wrote this week, exploited the âconspiratorial, anti-system tendencies in the electorateâ and found a much sharper weapon to swing at Republicans.
If this pays off for Democrats, serious credit will be due to California Rep. Ro Khanna. As a co-chair of the 2020 Bernie Sanders campaign, he saw how clarifying it could be for audiences to hear that billionaires were hoarding wealth while most people struggled. After President Donald Trump promised to release Epstein case files but didnât, Khanna and Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., found the votes to force it last year.
The files didnât take down the Trump presidency. But Khanna found a framework for anti-billionaire populism in battling the âEpstein class.â
âThe Epstein class has become a symbol [of] how the wealthy and powerful rig the system to avoid accountability and enrich themselves,â Khanna told me as he campaigned for the Democratic challenger in a Wisconsin seat Trump won by 5 points.
This theme aligned with what Democrats wanted to do anyway: run against Republicans as pawns of the ultra-wealthy. Why wouldnât the GOP slow data center construction? Billionaires. Why wasnât Congress bringing down costs for regular people? Billionaires.
When Trump was on the ballot, it helped Republicans that he was perceived as so wealthy that other billionaires couldnât influence him. Democrats struggled to land the anti-plutocrat attacks that worked against Mitt Romney because prominent billionaires and corporate leaders refused to support Trump.
That changed after Trump returned to power last year, and Democrats got comfortable again with populism. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who picked up the âEpstein classâ term from Khanna, pointed to its presence at Trumpâs inauguration: âThey are the elites they pretend to hate.â
If Democrats have a good Tuesday, their willingness to run against vast wealth and suggest that thereâs something evil about it will have proven essential. âIf youâre a billionaire, Ohio looks picture-perfect,â Ohioâs Amy Acton says in one of her final ads â one of several, from her allies, that go after GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy for the crime of flying a private jet.
And when former President Barack Obama headlined a Michigan rally with Abdul El-Sayed, an attendee shouted affirmation back at him: âObamaâs not on the Epstein files, either!â
El-Sayed pointed and smiled at the man. He let the applause ring out.
Room for Disagreement
Republicans have some substantive rebuttals to this line of attack. Hadnât the president jawboned other billionaires into funding child investment accounts? Wasnât everyone invested in tech stocks getting richer?
Not as rich as the people who had money already. In fact, the best counter to the anti-billionaire line has proven to be â¦ turning it on Democrats.
In Wisconsin, and other places where LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman has funded Democratic PACs, Republicans attacked Hoffmanâs friendship with Epstein and asked why Democrats werenât giving back his money. When Abdul El-Sayed fundraised with members of the Soros family, Republicans said his campaign trail rhetoric about money in politics was a ruse.
Notable
- Katie Phang, a journalist whoâs sued DOJ over redactions in Epstein file releases, wrote in the Guardian about their impact on the elections.
- Politicoâs Playbook looked at whether you could call this the âEpstein election,â with Democratic strategists very happy that candidates adopted their âcorruptionâ framing.

ec0d7a6134fe.text:
The Scoop
Even with the political wind at their backs for this midterm, Democrats still arenât sparking enthusiasm among low-propensity voters. So when doorknockers for the countryâs largest hospitality union fan out in swing states, they donât start by mentioning the party.
UNITE HERE, which boasts more than 300,000 members across the country, tells its organizers to zero in on votersâ personal financial situations before seeking support for Democratic candidates. In Texas, a doorknocker for the union might reference last yearâs Hilton Americas-Houston hotel strike before pivoting to telling a voter that Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa supported workersâ drive for a higher wage.
âThatâs more what we find effective, because there is an apathy about Democrats in general,â Gwen Mills, UNITE HEREâs president, told Semafor. âWe talk about the agency that workers and working-class people have to change their lives through their union, and then through voting. Thatâs a different angle into having a conversation about the election.â
Itâs a sign that Democrats still have work to do nationally to rebuild their brand, and it also reveals the messages voters are hearing right before Election Day on pocketbook issues that are dominating the national mood.
UNITE HERE is well-known for its heft in Nevada, where the hospitality union has played a massive role in Democratsâ turnout machine over the past two decades. Itâs still playing in the Silver State, working to flip back the governorâs office from GOP control and hold the stateâs three battleground House districts.
The union is also working to bring its economic message to more than a million households across a broader array of races in Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Maine, Michigan, Mississippi, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Texas. UNITE HERE has focused its persuasion project on reaching low-propensity voters â the bloc that often swings elections â by talking about workersâ issues.
Low-propensity voters, pollsters have found, often think the system is âriggedâ against them and are highly skeptical of both parties.
âWeâre talking to people who really feel left behind by the political system,â Mills said. âTheyâre working-class voters. And I think they see, whether they voted for Trump or Biden, right, or for Democrats or Republicans, theyâre like: âThis system is failing us.ââ
The campaign is taking UNITE HERE to unusual places, like Floridaâs 27th District, which GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar won by 20 points in 2024. The union is running a Spanish-language canvass there in support of Democrat Eliott Rodriguez, a tough slog in South Florida where the Republican brand is still strong.
But though the union wants to win that race and other battleground seats, its work in Florida isnât just about the midterms. Mills described a hope to get out ahead of larger demographic shifts already underway in American politics.
âWhen the Census happens in 2030, youâre going to have a shift in the electoral college â¦ [moving] seats in Congress out of states like New York and California, into states like Florida and Texas, and really across the Sun Belt,â Mills said. âWeâre certainly focused on building the infrastructure in those places.â
Room for Disagreement
The hospitality union is not explicitly partisan and said that it could support pro-union Republicans in a future election. But not this year.
âIn the past, we certainly supported Republicans, and we could in the future,â Mills said. âBut thereâs a particular moment here, and folks who arenât standing up to the brutality of these policies that are being passed donât get excused.â
Burgessâs view
Millions of dollars of ad buys can only do so much to reach voters. Itâs doorknockers like those working for UNITE HERE â and conservative organizations like Americans for Prosperity â that are doing the hard work behind the scenes to persuade voters.
No one factor will be decisive, but if thereâs an archetype of this yearâs swing voter, itâs the folks this union is trying to reach: low-propensity voters who hate both parties.
Notable
- UNITE HERE and state AFL-CIOs and their affiliates are targeting swing voters in several states with the âContract with Working Americans,â a populist economic platform they devised independently of the national AFL-CIO, Semaforâs Brendan Ruberry reports.

9a35ccd40e0b.text: By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press By — Areej Hazboun, Associated Press Areej Hazboun, Associated Press By — Audrey Horowitz, Associated Press Audrey Horowitz, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israelis-await-final-election-results-as-netanyahu-rivals-weigh-joining-forces-with-arab-parties Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israelis await final election results as Netanyahu rivals weigh joining forces with Arab parties World Oct 28, 2026 11:58 AM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Anxious Israelis watched election results near completion Wednesday after the highest voter turnout in over a quarter-century, as no clear winner emerged and weeks of negotiating could lie ahead for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an array of opposition parties trying to unseat him. READ MORE: No clear winner in Israeli election, exit polls indicate, as Netanyahu's fate hangs in the balance Arab-led parties made a historic showing, but it's not clear if other opponents of Netanyahu's far-right government would form a coalition with them for a majority of seats in parliament. Issues around the Palestinians and their descendants remain incredibly sensitive in Israel. Netanyahu seeks to remain the country's longest-serving prime minister. In defiant comments after the vote — which showed his Likud party losing ground since the 2022 election — he dismissed as treasonous the idea of partnering with Arab parties. Please check your inbox to confirm. On Wednesday, Netanyahu warned against a "dangerous government" that might include them. He won't work with the Arab-led parties, whose constituents make up 20% of Israel's population, and they have also ruled out any partnership with him. READ MORE: Why it could be weeks or months before Israel's election winner is known His top challenger, centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has left the door open to partnering with Arab parties under certain conditions, including their recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and of Hamas as an extremist group. But it's not clear whether some of Eisenkot's likely partners who have ruled out such an alliance will change their minds to force Netanyahu from office. Israeli voters choose parties, not individuals. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%. The official count does not indicate how many seats each will have in parliament, the 120-seat Knesset. Emerging results indicated that neither Netanyahu's nor Eisenkot's coalition blocs would reach the 61 seats needed for a majority; local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties. Netanyahu faces a setback but not outright defeat Nearly 78% of eligible voters turned out, the highest since 1999. Final results are expected by the end of the week, and will capture about a half-million absentee ballots yet to be counted from military personnel and diplomats. Voting reflected unease over Netanyahu's alliance with the far-right and anger in a war-weary nation over military draft exemptions for the significant ultra-Orthodox Jewish population; the Likud party's share of the vote declined from 23.4% in 2022. But results suggest opponents were unable to capitalize on the grief caused by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack to decisively push him from office. WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election One far-right partner losing support was national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. For many Israelis, he represented the worst strain of Netanyahu's government, openly taunting Palestinian detainees and asserting that many in Gaza are "not even people." Vote-counting suggested Likud would remain the largest party and best placed to be tapped to form a government by Israel's president, Isaac Herzog. The president, however, isn't required to task the leader of the party holding the most seats. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections," Herzog said Wednesday. The most obvious path to a parliamentary majority could involve Eisenkot partnering with Arab-led parties — which have 14.9% of the votes counted — but that's politically challenging. In a speech early Wednesday that focused on national unity, Eisenkot pledged to form a government and promised "a new era — an era of hope." If no one can put together a majority coalition, new elections could be held early next year. Israel held five elections between April 2019 and November 2022 because of a similar stalemate. It is unclear whether thousands of Israelis living abroad would again fly back home to vote, and whether Arab voters would again surge to the polls. Minority governments also are possible, but they must rely on cooperation from parties outside the government to pass legislation. Arab-led parties could hold the key Confronted with Arab parties' strong election showing, Israelis have renewed a debate about identity. "We have no future here if we do not stop being afraid," said Yair Golan, whose Democrats party supports bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition. "We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes." Israel's Arab citizens are descendants of Palestinians who remained in the state after its creation in 1948. They often face discrimination and are viewed with wariness because of their solidarity with the Palestinian cause. That suspicion intensified after Oct. 7, even though Arab citizens were also among those killed and abducted. dd6746a93cf3.text: Dolores Huerta , the pioneering labor organizer who co-founded the United Farm Workers and coined the rallying cry "Sí, se puede," died Wednesday at 96, her family announced on her Instagram account. Why it matters: The civil rights legend helped lead strikes and boycotts, fought to expand rights for Hispanic Americans and became a powerful kingmaker in politics. What they're saying: "We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96," her family wrote in a statement posted on Instagram . "As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family. We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy." This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

32901d0fcf13.text: By — Joseph Wilson, Associated Press Joseph Wilson, Associated Press By — Iain Sullivan, Associated Press Iain Sullivan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/dozens-dead-in-spain-after-high-speed-train-slams-into-another-stopped-on-tracks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dozens dead in Spain after high-speed train slams into another stopped on tracks World Oct 28, 2026 11:41 AM EDT URDA, Spain (AP) — One high-speed Spanish train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and shredding carriages in the country's second deadly rail collision this year. The regional government for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people needed medical treatment in hospital. Rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies. READ MORE: Barcelona commuter train crash kills 1, days after deadly train collision in Spain The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies. Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain. One train, run by the state-owned RENFE company, ran into the tail of the other train owned by private company IRYO that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track in a rural area between two villages. READ MORE: What to know about Spain's housing protests sparked by an 87-year-old woman's eviction David Gómez, a construction worker, was working with his brother and another colleague nearby when they heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País. "People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought," until emergency services arrived, he said. "As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg." Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia. Until this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain's dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992. It was a source of national pride. Transport minister says crash was due to 'inexplicable' decision Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the accident was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame. Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m. Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed. Puente said they were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track. "I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said. Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car torn into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope. Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area. "It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said. Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO. "We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook." Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood. Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train. IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities." The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, said civil protection authorities had asked his officials to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo." "Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families." Spain's King Felipe VI visited the crash site. He and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident. "We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo)," the royal couple said. "We share in the grief of the familie

c0f99ccc17cc.text: By — Leah Willingham, Associated Press Leah Willingham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/education/cornell-faculty-to-begin-voting-on-no-confidence-measure-over-handling-of-sexual-assault-allegations Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cornell faculty to begin voting on no-confidence measure over handling of sexual assault allegations Education Oct 28, 2026 11:39 AM EDT Cornell University faculty will meet Wednesday to conclude debate and begin voting on a proposed no-confidence resolution in the university's administration following widespread frustration over its response to a woman who reported she was gang raped at a campus fraternity house in 2024. READ MORE: Woman who accused Cornell students of rape says university president's response made her feel 'unsupported' The meeting comes after an Oct. 14 Faculty Senate meeting at which angry members confronted Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff about the university's handling of the allegations. The meeting was closed to the media, but in an audio recording obtained by The Associated Press, Kotlikoff acknowledged some missteps, defended his leadership and asked for more time to push for cultural changes in student social life and make reforms. He urged faculty to have confidence in his leadership, pointing to an independent investigation into the university's handling of the case that he said could lead to meaningful reforms. Please check your inbox to confirm. A woman identified in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe filed a lawsuit last month alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints. All seven men have denied her allegations. WATCH: Fraternity culture under scrutiny in wake of Cornell allegations The criminal investigation by Cornell's police department stalled after the district attorney declined to pursue charges. In a New York Times interview, Kotlikoff said he never followed up to learn what had happened to the woman or the investigation. Asked by a faculty member whether he read the Cornell Police Department's report on the rape allegations, Kotlikoff acknowledged he had not, but said that was because the police investigation was confidential and university policy is that top administrators shouldn't have a role in criminal investigations. "I really reject the idea that I had no interest in it or was not concerned about it," Kotlikoff said. He insisted experienced leadership was necessary to confront problems. Replacing a president would harm Cornell's reputation, Kotlikoff said. READ MORE: Cornell president admits he never followed up on gang rape allegation ahead of no-confidence debate Faculty also questioned Cornell's handling of a disciplined student's return to campus, including his assignment to a shared dorm room with a roommate unaware of his disciplinary history. After Kotlikoff left the Oct. 14 meeting, a string of faculty speakers said they had lost confidence in the administration's ability to combat sexual assault on campus. Some Faculty Senate members warned that a hasty no-confidence vote would do little to address the underlying problems. Wednesday's meeting is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. and will be closed to the public and media. Electronic voting will open afterward and remain open through Nov. 6. Individual votes will be anonymous. A no-confidence vote by the faculty would be largely symbolic, but could send a message to the university's trustees, who ultimately decide who leads it. Kotlikoff became the university's interim president in July 2024 and took the job permanently last year. He's faced challenges including a dining and custodial workers strike, ire over his decision last year to pay $60 million to resolve Trump administration civil rights investigations, and accusations from activists that his administration stifled campus protests. - Published
Two trains have collided in Spain just south of the capital Madrid on Wednesday morning.
Rail operator Adif says the incident occurred between a Renfe train and another of the Iryo company, which covers the Madrid to Seville route.
So far at least 68 people are confirmed to have died in the incident.
Here is what we know about the crash so far.
Where and when did the crash happen?
The two trains collided just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) between municipalities Mora and Orgaz, and about 140km (100 miles) south of Madrid.
The accident happened when a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to the south of the country collided with another train that was apparently stationary. The crash caused at least two carriages to fall down an embankment.
Broadcaster RTVE, quoting the transport ministry, said a Renfe train rear-ended an Iryo train.
Renfe is Spain's national state-owned railway company while Iryo is a private high-speed railway operator.
All train traffic on this line has been stopped at stations along the route, Adif said.
Renfe said services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia remain suspended.
A passenger on board one of the trains told local media there was a heavy impact about 40 minutes into the journey.
What caused the crash?
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train "due to causes that are still unknown.
Transport minister Oscar Puente has said a computer failure led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control centre takes over," he said, adding it was the control centre which decided to allow the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
That decision, Puente said, was made "under inexplicable circumstances". It resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks further ahead.
How many passengers were on board?
More than 500 people were believed to be on board both trains.
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the government of Castilla-La Mancha region, told TVE that one of the trains - managed by the Iryo company - was carrying 146 passengers plus one baby, while the Renfe-managed train had 397 passengers on board.
A former government minister was also among those reported missing.
The Spanish Confederation of Business Organizations (CEOE) posted on X that, FÃ¡tima BÃ¡Ã±ez - who heads the organization's foundation - was on board one of the trains involved in the crash.
The Castilla La Mancha regional government said 64 people are now confirmed to have died.
Speaking separately to Spanish media, he warned the death toll could increase further.
Eighty people are being treated for injuries, according to authorities, with 50 of the casualties said to be in a serious condition, and 15 more in a critical condition.
How have the authorities responded?
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has said "the whole of Spain is grieving" and that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart".
"The pain is immense," he said on a visit to the crash site.
The government was "trying to determine what was the origin of this tragedy, of this terrible accident," he added.
"We will get to the bottom of this, and if there has been any negligence, it will come to light.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."
SÃ¡nchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A spokesperson for the EU said the bloc was ready to help Spain if needed.
A huge emergency response is under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash, Spanish media have reported.
A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de TransfusiÃ³n said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and AlcÃ¡zar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.
Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.
The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.
A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.
The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.
The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

b4907d52bf2a.text: TEL AVIV, Israel — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's electoral coalition opened a sizable lead over Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc with 85 percent of the vote counted. But while Netanyahu outperformed exit polls, which had Eisenkot's opposition coalition ahead, neither bloc will clear a 61-seat majority. That sets the stage for weeks of wrangling over the country's next government. Why it matters: Netanyahu will emerge from the election down but not out. His bloc is on pace to secure 53 seats — 11 fewer than he currently commands. But Eisenkot's bloc trails with 48 seats, leaving both men without a clear mandate to lead a government. While Eisenkot could theoretically swear in a government with the support of Arab parties — which are on track to secure a record-breaking 19 seats — such a scenario is highly unlikely. The intrigue: The actual vote count significantly boosted Netanyahu's standing compared to initial exit polls, which showed Eisenkot's bloc ahead. President Trump told Axios in a brief interview Wednesday that at first he received "horror reports" about Netanyahu's prospects. But "he's in pretty good shape now," Trump said. "I heard my endorsement made a big difference for Bibi," he added. Asked whether he is going to get involved in an effort to form a Netanyahu-led unity government, Trump said he hadn't thought about it. "I will take a look," he said. State of play: There are 500,000 votes left to be counted, from soldiers, diplomats, prisoners and others who voted outside their designated area. These votes could slightly shift the blocs' seat totals or the allotment of seats within each bloc. But they are unlikely to change the overall balance of power. Driving the news: Israeli President Isaac Herzog will begin consulting next week with the different parties before issuing a mandate to either Netanyahu or Eisenkot to form a government. "We must do everything possible, especially after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to arrive with an open mind," Herzog said on Wednesday. If neither side can assemble a majority, a new round of elections would be scheduled as early as April. Between the lines: Herzog could try to persuade Netanyahu and Eisenkot to form a unity government, but Netanyahu doesn't seem interested in that. On Tuesday night, he called for a "strong right-wing government." Netanyahu will likely try to convince one of the opposition leaders to cross over to him. All of them, however, committed publicly before the election not to do that. Under another scenario, Eisenkot could try to form a minority government with outside support from the Arab parties. But such a government could collapse quickly and lead to a Netanyahu victory in the next elections. On the other hand, allowing Netanyahu to remain on as a caretaker prime minister until the next elections could also lead to defeat for the opposition bloc in the next elections. It would give Netanyahu's bloc more time to organize and ease its divisions. For Netanyahu, staying as caretaker prime minister until new elections are held could be the best option. It would leave him with almost full powers to direct Israel's national security and foreign policy and move forward with renewed war against Iran. What to watch: The opposition will likely take over key positions in the Knesset after the new parliament is sworn in next week. That would allow Eisenkot and his partners to install a Knesset speaker, control the legislative agenda and pass laws they agree on — such as forming a national commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the October 7 attacks.

9787c344d78d.text: With less than a week until a potentially historic midterm election , the political discourse is being dominated not by war or seismic shifts in technology, but by the Cheesecake Factory . The big picture: Culture wars regularly swarm American political discussions, especially when the jibes are personal. Former President Obama's passing joke over the weekend about Cheesecake Factory decor did just that — by criticizing President Trump 's personal taste and style. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama said, poking fun at the president's controversial White House renovations . Zoom in: John Murphy, professor emeritus at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who studies political rhetoric, tells Axios that the first time he heard Obama's comment, he "really did think, 'this is going to go somewhere.'" That's both because of the messenger and the butt of the joke: Obama "can get under Trump's skin like no one else in the world can," he says. Obama knows all too well how seemingly trivial moments can blow up; in 2014, he wore a tan suit instead of a black one to discuss foreign policy, and years later his sartorial choices remain a political talking point. The tan suit has its own Wikipedia page , and still nets pop culture references . State of play: Days after Obama's quip, the news cycle and social media are still serving up the joke, and the White House posted "Lo-fi" beats accompanied by a cartoon image of Trump in front of a Cheesecake Factory. Conservative critics used the jab to paint Obama as elitist. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , a multimillionaire, criticized Obama outside a Cheesecake Factory, saying he "had a great meal, and I would tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try." Murphy notes that framing comes from a classic red v. blue playbook to paint Democrats as "elitist." "It's a conscious strategy, I think, on the part of conservative media to gin up culture-war arguments," he says. The other side: Trump's pushback, however, has centered less on the class divide seized by some members of conservative media — and more on his White House renovations. "We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America," Trump told reporters Monday. He continued, "Guys like Obama don't see it ... he doesn't see filth. He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building," later adding, "for you to say it's a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president." The White House referred Axios to Trump's previous comments when asked for comment. The bottom line: The fight has also drawn in the restaurant chain itself: Rick McCormack, its former longtime vice president of design, lamented "the pettiness of politics" and told CNN he was disappointed to see the company caught in the dispute. Go deeper: How the Cheesecake Factory got dragged into a midterms food fight

b280382f69ff.text: By — Daniel Kozin, Associated Press Daniel Kozin, Associated Press By — Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Mauricio Savarese, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-defeated-brazilian-candidate-flavio-bolsonaro-arrives-in-u-s-amid-investigation Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Defeated Brazilian candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in U.S. amid investigation World Oct 28, 2026 10:54 AM EDT MIAMI (AP) — Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil. Watch Bolsonaro's arrival in the U.S. in the video player above. The stunning move came after 48 hours in which Bolsonaro refused to concede to Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and then threatened to attempt to annul the election result. READ MORE: Brazil's Flávio Bolsonaro and his family will get U.S. visas after presidential election loss Bolsonaro's father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later. On Monday, the U.S. said that it would grant visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family. Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, visited the White House in May. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Bolsonaro first fled from Brazil to Argentina and then Ecuador alongside his wife and two daughters, Argentina's migration authority said Wednesday — a day after the 45-year-old senator and his family were granted United States visas by the Trump administration. Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. The court had ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday — two days after he lost the vote to Lula. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport. WATCH: Lula prevails in Brazil but Flávio Bolsonaro refuses to concede Argentina's migration authority said Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. Tuesday. They entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina's northeastern province of Misiones. "Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country," the Argentine migration authority said on X. The authority said that at 11:30 p.m. local time, shortly after clearing immigration control, the four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador. The move is almost certain to cause a big diplomatic rift between Lula and Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro's campaign. Bolsonaro lands in Miami Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro's landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport. The plane carrying Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami at around 9:30 a.m. EST. Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told several dozen supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia before the plane landed that he didn't have precise information about Bolsonaro's whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil. READ MORE: Lula bucks regional shift to the right and denies Trump a powerful ally in Brazil "I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true," Lula said. "This act of leaving Brazil is shameful." Paulo Figueiredo, a close Bolsonaro ally who lives in the U.S., said in a short statement that he can't confirm information from foreign authorities, but added "Flávio Bolsonaro is well, in security and resting with his family." Figueiredo also said there would be a press conference Thursday in Miami to discuss the case. Representatives of Brazil's government didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press. President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling him and his family "fine people." "The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from campaigning in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate, but stressed that he didn't endorse the election results. Leaders all over the world and the Organization of American States, or OAS, endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round. On Tuesday, Milei's administration spokesman Adrián Ravier said "there is no asylum request (from Bolsonaro) and there is nothing more to add." Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving Brazil The defeated candidate was served with a Supreme Court order to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later. Flávio Bolsonaro said on Monday in a video that he was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court. Brazil's Supreme Court

55100058e3e5.text: If Democrats gain full control of Congress next week, as many polls and prediction markets suggest they will, private equity could once again find itself in the political crosshairs. The big picture: Private equity has become a rhetorical punching bag for a number of Democratic House and Senate candidates, including in debates and on the stump, as an affordability bête noire. Most of this has related to housing, both single-family and mobile homes, but also has extended to health care. What they're saying: "It's no doubt that housing is way out of control and a big part of that is because private equity has come into Maine," said Troy Jackson in an Oct. 6 debate with Sen. Susan Collins. "I do think we have to go after private equity, make it so that they can't buy these things and charge outrageous prices." Chris Pappas, running for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire, said during a campaign stop at a mobile home community: "We need to... address the housing crisis that we're seeing, including addressing the corporate private equity influence that we're seeing in housing that's making it less affordable and is causing a lot of consternation here at this park." Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) decried PE ownership of residential care facilities during a public event, saying: "Those people know nothing about health care." State of play: Congress passed a bipartisan bill this past summer to restrict PE ownership of single-family homes, with the Treasury Department last week issuing related regulations . The legislation became law despite not being signed by President Trump, who supported it but was in a snit over the Senate not passing his voter identification bill. Zoom in: A Democratic sweep would likely result in Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) taking the Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee gavel, which means she'd go from writing strongly worded letters to holding hearings and guiding legislation. "Americans are sick and tired of private equity's playbook of rolling through industry after industry, jacking up prices and leaving local businesses and workers in the dust," she tells Axios. "After we passed a bipartisan law this year to ban private equity from buying up homes, candidates everywhere are campaigning on reining in private equity in the next Congress, whether in hospitals, mobile home communities, residential care facilities, or other industries." It's also worth noting that Warren has Republican allies when it comes to some of these issues, having worked with Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) on a stalled health bill that has been more endorsed by Senate candidate James Talarico. The bottom line: Private equity has a very successful track record in beating back federal legislation that could hurt its bottom line. What to watch is if past proves to be precedent.

ed7ab4200989.text:
- Published
Israel looks to be in political deadlock.
With 85% of votes counted after Tuesday's election, neither the incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, nor the bloc of his key challenger Gadi Eisenkot look set to have a majority.
In order to form a government, it looks likely one of the leading parties would have to break their campaign promises - meaning the most probable outcome may well be new elections.
Here are four possible scenarios.
National unity government led by Netanyahu
Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?
Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.
Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".
But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.
Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government"- remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.
One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.
This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.
Eisenkot-led coalition with Arab parties
This would be a seismic shift for Israeli politics. Only one independent Arab party has ever formally been part of a coalition, in 2021, and it didn't last long.
Eisenkot and every other Jewish party in his bloc bar one have already ruled out entering government with them. But right now, it's the opposition's only path to a majority.
The Arab parties were the story of election night. They look to have defied expectations and could gain a record 19 seats - helped by an unprecedented turnout from Israel's Arab population, who account for about one-fifth of the country and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout last night, inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, has shaken things up.
The United Arab list, who are currently projected to win around 7 seats, have said they'd join an opposition government, while The Joint List, who are projected to win 12 seats, have said they'd support one from outside.
However, the only Jewish leader advocating this scenario right now is The Democrats' Yair Golan. And a coalition like this would be very fragile, especially on issues like Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The fact there is such a unified front from the Jewish parties against Arab participation points to Israel's deep divisions.
Netanyahu-led majority, with right-wingers from opposition
Could Netanyahu persuade the right-wing parties in Eisenkot's bloc to break away and join his coalition?
The two most likely candidates for this are Naftali Bennett - joint-leader of the Beyachad political alliance - and Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party. They are both right-wingers who are hardline on security, and share some political ground with Netanyahu.
But both campaigned explicitly to oust him, and to extend military conscription to the ultra-Orthodox - bringing them into direct conflict with the two ultra-Orthodox parties already part of Netanyahu's government. So it's difficult to see them joining forces.
Some have suggested Bennett and Lieberman's parties could replace the ultra-Orthodox parties, but current electoral math suggests that grouping may not have the seats needed for a majority.
New elections
If none of the above scenarios can be negotiated, the default outcome would be new elections.
Many would see this as a tacit win for Netanyahu, who would remain as caretaker PM until the new elections take place - which he may believe he has a better chance of winning.
Some analysts think the high Arab turnout would not be replicated again - especially if their record representation in parliament led to no change - and it could also mobilise more right-wing voters in a second poll. Netanyahu may also bet that the estimated 70,000 Israelis who flew home from abroad to vote, and are thought to skew against him, wouldn't do so again.
Additionally, several right-wing parties who failed to pass the electoral threshold of 3.25% may attract fewer votes or may not even run, thereby bringing more votes to Likud and its allies.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.
