52d049e2e35e.text: The most-aired ad in the closing stretch of Mississippi's Senate race features a Jeffrey Epstein survivor attacking GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith for voting against releasing files related to the convicted human trafficker. Why it matters: In the past week, Hyde-Smith has been outgunned on the airwaves. AdImpact data shows that only one of the eight most-aired spots portrays her positively. Five of the ads either positively portray her Democratic challenger, Scott Colom , or attack Hyde-Smith for her Senate record, largely painting her as an out-of-touch senator who cares more about her rich donors. The other two ads are for down-ballot races. Zoom out: The Epstein survivor ad has aired more than 1,200 times over the last week, costing the left-leaning New Deal for All super PAC over $329K, per AdImpact. In the ad, Jena-Lisa Jones condemns Hyde-Smith for her vote on the Epstein files and urges Mississippians to vote against her to protect their children. That vote, which passed 51-49 last year, indefinitely postponed an amendment that would have required the full release of the Epstein files by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. "I do want transparency, and I support releasing information that can legally be released while protecting Epstein's victims. But a procedural vote on one amendment is not the same thing as saying the Epstein files should remain secret," Hyde-Smith said in a statement to the Mississippi Free Press. Hyde-Smith's campaign cut its own attack against Colom, calling him the "transgender defender" and naming him the "most radical Senate candidate of our lifetime." The ad played over 2,800 times across Mississippi and Memphis, Tenn., television markets in the 30 days since its Sept. 10 debut, costing the senator's campaign over $854K, per AdImpact. Hyde-Smith's campaign appears to have pulled back on the ad, spending less than $150,000 to air it between Oct. 19 and Oct. 26. The bottom line: Hyde-Smith is still expected to win, but the race is far tighter than anyone expected. As President Trump said during a rally for Hyde-Smith in Corinth, Miss. on Monday: "I'm here because Cindy is doing great, but I've just got to make sure."

26f497c3a961.text: Democrats will happily tell you how good they feel about retaking the House on Tuesday — just as soon as they stop hyperventilating into a paper bag. Why it matters: They've been burned too many times on Election Day to feel anything more than "nauseously optimistic," as one House Democrat put it to Axios. The polls point to a decisive Democratic victory on Nov. 3, yet fears of a massive polling error or some other eleventh-hour disaster are giving party members sleepless nights. "One woman at a rally in New Jersey told me last week that she was 'nauseously optimistic,'" Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios. "That may capture a lot of people's last-minute jitters." A House Democrat who has spoken to leadership told Axios: "They feel optimistic. You know, guarded. Guarded optimism. Where we're going to end up, you never know." State of play: Democrats are targeting dozens of Republican-held seats they think could flip, some of which President Trump carried by 10, 15, even 20 percentage points in 2024. Democrats' House Majority PAC, for instance, went on the air Wednesday in retiring Rep. Elise Stefanik's (R-N.Y.) district, which Trump won by 21 points. They also began spending against Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.), who won his last reelection with 60% of the vote. HMP is so bullish it has moved money out of the races to replace retiring Reps. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) and Darrell Issa (R-Calif.), which they believe Democrats are on track to win handily. "I am cautiously optimistic we win between 20-25 seats," Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told Axios. Democrats' landslide scenario puts them closer to 40 or 50 pickups, which would be a historic night for the party. Yes, but: Mid-decade redistricting in Republican-controlled Southern states is all but certain to cut into those gains. The GOP is expected to easily flip redrawn seats in Tennessee and Louisiana where the incumbent Democrats chose to retire rather than face uphill reelection battles. Democratic leadership is also nervous about several Democrats who opted to run in their new seats, including Reps. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), Darren Soto (D-Fla.) and Shomari Figures (D-Ala.), according to three lawmakers familiar with their thinking. What they're saying: All of the nearly 20 House Democrats who spoke to Axios on Wednesday expressed some degree of confidence about the election. "I've been to 26 states this campaign, and I'd say Democrats have been riding a wave of tremendous optimism and activism over the last several months," said Raskin. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) told Axios she is feeling "legitimately good" and that "the cautious optimism is there only because of … history." "The optimism is real and I think for good reason," said Rep. Johnny Olszewski (D-Md.). But virtually everyone also offered reasons for keeping their expectations tempered. "Dems have been burnt by good polling before," Rep. Dave Min (D-Calif.) told Axios. Min also said Democrats are "hyper-aware of the election tampering that Trump and his goons are engaging in right now," something several other lawmakers echoed. "We're bracing for all manner of drama before, during and after the election," said Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.). The other side: "The Democrats are trying to deflect from the revelation of their secret, corrupt plan to stack Alaska's ballot," said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis, referring to a New York Times report about the drafting of spoiler Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan. The Justice Department has sued to delay certification of Alaska's Senate election if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses. "If these are the types of tactics Democrats need to use to win elections, maybe they should reexamine their radical policies," Bis said. Other Democrats worry that an eleventh-hour spending spree by Republican donors and super PACs will give the GOP a critical boost in the final days of the campaign. "Elon Musk's $366 million infusion to Republican coffers ... has definitely filtered down into a lot of the close House and Senate campaigns and paid for a wall of propaganda," said Raskin. Another House Democrat told Axios that there is "some anxiety about the super PAC money from Rs," which is "mostly coming" from candidates in battleground districts. Zoom in: Lawmakers also pointed to race-specific dynamics that have helped certain Republicans outrun national headwinds. The battle between Democrat Cait Conley and Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) is "razor-thin close" despite Kamala Harris carrying the district in 2024, a House Democrat from New York told Axios. A House Democrat from Michigan told Axios that Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's weakness atop the ticket is "hurting" Democratic campaigns in the state's battleground House districts. A House Democrat from Texas told Axios the party will likely fall short in several winnable seats there because of either poor recruitment or insufficient investment from the national party. The bottom line: "There are two ways to run — scared and unopposed," said Scholten. "We're running in tough elections all across the country, and we're going to run hard through the tape in every single one."

- Published
At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.
Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.
In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.
The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.
The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.
Nine researchers from the UK, Nepal and India looked at areas up to 50km (30 miles) downstream from Himalayan rivers, as well as around 1,360 glacial lakes.
They found significant development in these areas - including an expansion of tourism facilities, infrastructure development and real estate.
It's clear in Pokhara, a major tourism hub at the foot of the Himalayas that's grown significantly in the past 30 years to cater for a massive increase in visitors.
Mayor Dhana Raj Acharya says it's a huge challenge to deal with the risk posed by the Seti Gandaki River, which stems from the Annapurna mountain range and flows right through the city. Many old buildings are just 5m (16ft) from river banks, he says, despite new rules requiring them to be further away.
"Where we move them, and how we do that, is the real challenge."
To the north is the world-renowned Annapurna trekking region that has also seen a major increase in settlements along river banks - some hit by recent floods and landslides.
Phurpa Chhiring Lama, who runs a homestay there, feels helpless. Normally all of his 20 rooms are occupied at this time of year - the peak trekking season - but now only five are. "We have been doing this business for more than 40 years, but we've never seen this kind of disaster."
Krishna Gauchan, whose hotel is close to the glacier-fed Modi river, is worried too. "This river can flood if the glacier collapses or if the glacial lake bursts out and we are living in constant fear."
Tourism investors promote some of these spots as destinations without factoring in the risks, suggests Khagendra Poudel, a geographer at a local campus of Tribhuvan University. It's similar to what's happening in parts of north India's Himalayan valleys which host major pilgrimages.
The president of the Hotel Association Pokhara admits tourism businesses have expanded "without any proper planning" in the region and been promoted "haphazardly".
"By the time disasters hit, it is too late," says Laxman Subedi. "As a professional body we are trying to create awareness among tourism entrepreneurs and investors."
But it's not just tourism. The regions surrounding the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have seen a significant rise in the construction of hydropower plants.
"As river valleys become increasingly populated, development decisions being made today will shape disaster risk for decades to come," warns the study's lead author, University of Leeds glaciologist C Scott Watson.
And even more buildings may be under threat than those identified by the researchers.
The study categorised buildings at risk as all those that were within 50 vertical metres (164ft) of a river or glacial lake's surface.
But during the catastrophic flooding on 26 August, locals in Rasuwa district say the river level had risen by 70m (230ft) at some points - so even buildings that were relatively far from the river banks were hit and buried by debris-sludge.
The risks in all of these areas are largely driven by warming in the Himalayan region, which scientists say is happening at twice the global rate. This has sped up the melting of glaciers, icefields, snowpacks, and ground that's normally frozen all year.
This can, in turn, destabilize mountain slopes which are also frequently shaken by earthquakes, unleashing devastating disasters downstream.
The rapid melting is also filling up and expanding glacial lakes until they burst, causing deadly floods. Nepal alone has documented around 30 of these events since 1940.
Another issue is that rising temperatures cause rain to reach high altitudes where it used to only snow, leading to slope failures, rock and ice falls, and other disasters.
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah raised the dangers of climate change at his recent UN General Assembly speech, where he said his country was paying a "colossal price" for a crisis it did not create.
"Every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause."
Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado who was not involved in the study, says it should serve as a "springboard" to bring about more effective early-warning systems and other precautionary measures.
But achieving that will be a challenge. Campaigners say building regulations aren't implemented on the ground and through the years, development has been haphazard in too many places.
Roads, hydropower projects, hotels and market towns have expanded on the low, flat land along rivers, which is accessible and buildable, says Prof Surya Raj Acharya, an urban planning expert and registrar at the University of Nepal.
Those responsible have often ignored safeguards including keeping off the river bank, he adds.

d37326e03c17.text: President Trump headed to Ohio to rally voters in a race that could determine control of the Senate. That stop comes after dueling rallies in another key state offered a snapshot of the divisions shaping the midterm elections. Liz Landers reports. Amna Nawaz: President Donald Trump heads to Ohio tonight to rally voters in a race that could determine control of the Senate. Geoff Bennett: And that stop follows dueling rallies in another key battleground state, Texas, that highlighted sharp divisions driving this year's midterms. Our Liz Landers reports. Liz Landers: Last night, a political showdown in a usually deep red state, Trump and Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico holding rallies just miles apart in Lubbock. President Donald Trump: And the other guy does not deserve it. He doesn't represent your values. State Rep. James Talarico: On November 3, we are going to do something extraordinary. We are going to do something historic. Liz Landers: The president mocking the Democrat with insults and a nickname. President Donald Trump: Seven days from now, the people of Texas are going to defeat Democrat communist James Talafreako. Liz Landers: Talarico using the timing of the dueling rallies and that nickname to fire up the crowd. State Rep. James Talarico: I know that we're not the only show in town tonight, and I appreciate all 4,000 of you that showed up here this evening. (CHEERING) State Rep. James Talarico: That's a lot of Talafreakos in one room. So... (CHEERING) Ken Paxton: Let's go win Texas. Liz Landers: Talarico's opponent, State Attorney General Ken Paxton, also taking swings. Ken Paxton: So let me tell you about the other guy. I think you've heard of him, James Talarico, the most radical Democrat to ever run in Texas history. (BOOING) Liz Landers: All for a key seat in a state that is not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than three decades. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to retake the majority in the U.S. Senate. Another state that captures the fault lines shaping this year's midterms, Pennsylvania. Just two years ago, the state was central to Trump's return to the White House, but now anxieties over the economy and corruption have crumbled support for Trump and the Republican base. Linda Markle, Pennsylvania Voter: The Republican Congress does not have a spine. They've abdicated their powers to one person, one person only. And that's not democracy. Liz Landers: But for others, the president and his party still have their support. John Tim Betts, Pennsylvania Voter: Probably President Trump. I mean, I'm sorry people don't like him, but I think he's doing more for us than anybody else has. Liz Landers: But how big is the battleground for Senate control? A new New York Times/Siena University poll shows Democrats may be making surprising gains, in reliably red South Carolina, Republican Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother Lindsey Graham's seat, tied with Democrat Annie Andrews. Darline Graham in South Carolina today: Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC): Nobody outworks South Carolinians. That's the formula, and it's working, and we're going to keep it going. Liz Landers: In North Carolina, where a Democrat hasn't been elected to the Senate in nearly 20 years, former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley by double digits, centering his campaign on affordability. Fmr. Gov. Roy Cooper: And these tariffs are chaotic. They're not -- they're essentially a tax, folks. We need to overturn them. I will work to do that when I get to the United States Senate. Liz Landers: Also in North Carolina today, Vice President J.D. Vance making the case for Republicans. J.D. Vance: North Carolina, you send a message to Washington that we are sick of being ignored, we are sick of being left behind, and we are going to put America first for a change. (CHEERING) Liz Landers: Both parties have less than one week left to make their closing arguments to voters. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Liz Landers.

4611d1e054d0.text: By — Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/un-condemns-u-s-economic-embargo-of-cuba-though-more-nations-sit-out-amid-trump-push Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter UN condemns U.S. economic embargo of Cuba though more nations sit out amid Trump push World Oct 28, 2026 6:50 PM EDT UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The U.N. General Assembly condemned the U.S. economic embargo of Cuba for the 34th year on Wednesday, even as Washington's campaign to influence the outcome led to a number of countries voting against the resolution or sitting out the decision for the first time. WATCH: Trump at GOP rally in Florida revives idea of military intervention in Cuba after Iran The vote was 130-17, with 25 abstentions — a notable decrease in support from last year, when more than 160 nations supported the measure and only 12 abstained. While such resolutions at the U.N. General Assembly are not legally binding, they do reflect world opinion. For the first time in 34 years, Western countries like Germany, Italy and Latvia were among those that refrained from voting. Bosnia, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Lithuania, Morocco, North Macedonia, Paraguay and Slovenia are among those member states that voted no — most for the first time. It marks a stunning shift in international support at a time when the small island country weathers outages, shortages and other deepening financial troubles as the Trump administration looks to force changes to Cuba's political system by increasing an already punishing economic campaign. President Donald Trump last week once again raised the specter of U.S. military intervention, saying American warships could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war. "A great power is attacking through economic war a member state of this organization," Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said ahead of the vote. "Cuba is not a threat. The blockade is a threat." U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told member nations that, "your vote today is the only thing standing between the corrupt, kleptocratic communist regime and using this body and your vote for another propaganda victory at the expense of the Cuban people." Tensions between Washington and Havana have spilled over into fiery public spats at the United Nations. On Tuesday, Waltz and Rodríguez got into a shouting match on the floor of the General Assembly while debating the embargo resolution. Watch the clip in the video player above. Shortly after Waltz had begun his criticism of the socialist government, Rodríguez walked down to the podium where the U.S. envoy was addressing the hall and called him a liar while trying to get a point of order from the official presiding over the session. "This individual needs to back away from this podium. He's not going to intimidate me in the United States of America," Waltz said as U.N. security and personnel tried to intervene. "You understand who you're dealing with? This is America. Back up." In a post on X, Rodríguez reminded Waltz where he was making his remarks, saying he's at the U.N., not at a national security meeting at the White House. "With his crude lies at the UN General Assembly, the U.S. government has launched another desperate attempt to justify its economic aggression against Cuba and its criminal energy blockade," he continued. On the sidelines of the GA hall, Waltz accused a member of Cuba's delegation of attacking an American diplomat who was filming him. He said Secretary of State Marco Rubio has ordered the official sent home. The State Department on Wednesday confirmed to the AP that the individual accused has left the U.S. A week earlier, a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, took place outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behavior of the island's government. It all reflects a clear break from the traditional diplomatic decorum expected at the U.N. and the new phase of contentiousness between the U.S. and Cuba. The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960 after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations. As a result, the Caribbean country has spent decades facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba. The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island, leading to widespread power outages that impact basic services such as water supply and internet and telephone services. Associated Press writer Matthew Lee in Washington and Dánica Coto in San Juan, Puerto Rico, contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press

765210bfec18.text: In Israel, nearly all the votes have been counted in Tuesday's election. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies emerged as the largest bloc, but lost seats and fell short of the majority needed to form a government. The results leave Israel facing the prospect of political gridlock. Nick Schifrin reports from Tel Aviv. Geoff Bennett: In Israel, nearly all the votes have been counted in yesterday's election. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies emerged as the largest bloc, but lost seats and fell short of the majority needed to form a new government. The results leave Israel facing the prospect of political gridlock. Nick Schifrin joins us now from Tel Aviv. So, Nick, last night the opposition bloc was leading based on exit polls. Now that the votes have been counted, where do the party stand? Nick Schifrin: Well, you're right, Geoff. The polls essentially inverted the final results. As you said, Netanyahu's Likud Party won the most seats of any party, and his coalition also won the most seats, even if, as you pointed out, they did lose their majority. Now, as of now, with the vast majority of votes counted, they -- Netanyahu's bloc has 53 seats, well short of the 61 it needs for a majority in the Parliament or Knesset, but more than the 48 seats that the opposition Change bloc won. One of the most significant outcomes of this election is the 19 seats that as of now the Arab parties won. They are also anti-Netanyahu. So you could conclude that the majority of the country rejected the current government, but that is not how Israeli politics work. It is Netanyahu's coalition that has the most votes, which means, as of now, there's not only weeks ahead of us of negotiations, but there's no clear direction that the country has chosen to go, even though, Geoff, voters on all sides told us that the country is at a crossroads. Geoff Bennett: And what are the scenarios, Nick, for what could happen next? Nick Schifrin: So, next week, Israel's president will invite one of the blocs to try and form a majority government. When it comes to Netanyahu, he would have to persuade one of Eisenkot's coalition partners to defect. But a Netanyahu official told me today they consider that impossible. Or he could form what's known as a unity government with Eisenkot. This has been done before, especially in times of war. But Eisenkot and all of his allies have ruled it out. They are vociferously anti-Netanyahu. Now, Eisenkot does have his own path. Note again, the Change bloc in blue and the Arab parties in green combined have more than 61 and could create a government together. But Israelis have been resistant to Jewish parties needing Arab parties to be part of the ruling coalition, especially after October the 7th, and Eisenkot calls his coalition -- quote -- "Zionist." But we will see what happens because there is a technical way for those Arab parties to support Eisenkot from the outside. As for Netanyahu today, his campaign accused Arab voters of -- quote -- "stealing the election," an allegation police responded to by saying there is no investigative substantiation to the claims. And last night, Netanyahu called for the Arab parties to be excluded. Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister (through interpreter): We must form a right-wing national strong government. That is what must be done. We must not, must not endanger Israel and establish a government that is backed by anti-Zionist Arab parties. Nick Schifrin: Finally, Geoff, the fourth and perhaps most likely scenario at this point, one that many Israelis do not want, neither side gets to form a government or neither side succeeds in forming a government, and Israel heads to more elections. Geoff Bennett: And what might all of this mean for Netanyahu and his political future, Nick? Nick Schifrin: Well, Netanyahu stays prime minister, even if he's supposed to act with restraint. But analysts here say that he could choose to take the country to war. A U.S. official confirms to me that Netanyahu pushed for attacks on Iran before the Israeli election. Israeli defense officials have also said that, and that led to this extraordinary warning last night from Gadi Eisenkot. Gadi Eisenkot, Israeli Prime Minister Candidate (through interpreter): I call on the heads of the security establishment and the civil service, remember that you serve only the state and the interests of the Israeli citizens. Stand firm against any attempt to challenge you. Netanyahu, do not dare use Israel's security for your own political needs. Nick Schifrin: Now, U.S. officials have also said, including President Trump in public, that the U.S. could go back to war with Iran after the U.S. midterm elections. And that would presumably give Netanyahu more leverage as these coalition talks play out, and which shows, really no matter what happens, Geoff, whether Netanyahu is able to form the coalition or not, we are still in a country dominated by Netanyahu and the opposition's inability to sell a majority of the country on the idea of a post-Netanyahu Israel. Geoff Bennett: Nick Schifrin reporting again for us from Tel Aviv. Nick, our thanks to you.

d01e894acb39.text: There is shock, anger and mourning in Spain after the second fatal train crash this year. At least 68 people have died in what is now the deadliest collision there in more than a decade. William Brangham reports. Amna Nawaz: In the day's other headlines: There is shock, anger and mourning in Spain after the second fatal train crash this year in what's now the deadliest collision there in more than a decade. At least 68 people have died. William Brangham has our report. William Brangham: A normal morning train journey in Central Spain today ended in a field of twisted steel. Near the town of Urda, about 90 miles south of Madrid, a high-speed train bound for Seville slammed into another train that was stopped, knocking them both off the tracks and shearing at least one apart; 147 people were aboard the stopped train. From inside, survivors could see out the windows at the destruction they'd narrowly missed. On the other train, nearly 400 passengers were thrown into chaos. Rafael Barcelo, Train Passenger (through interpreter): We were having breakfast, having a coffee, and we felt a huge impact. We were all thrown into the air. I am reasonably OK. My friend is quite worse. William Brangham: Many are now looking for their loved ones. Woman (through interpreter): My husband was in the train that left Madrid, and we just rushed here as soon as we heard about the accident. We came here and no one tells us anything. I don't know anything. William Brangham: Firefighters and a military unit climbed through the wreckage, digging by hand through shattered seats and crushed steel. Authorities said this is Spain's deadliest rail accident in more than a decade, but it's not the first one this year. In January, on the same high-speed line, a train operated by the same carrier derailed and struck another, killing 46, and ignited a debate over whether Spain is doing enough to keep its railways safe. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faces national elections next month, went to the scene and promised action. Pedro Sanchez, Spanish Prime Minister (through interpreter): We are going to get to the bottom of this. If there were failures in the safety system, we will address them decisively. William Brangham: All high-speed service between Madrid and the southern province of Andalusia has been suspended. But in a country that built one of the world's larger high-speed networks, with the promise that its cities could be linked quickly and safely, today, that promise lies in pieces for the second time in a year. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham.

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent nearly twice as much to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review as public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent more than $56 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent close to $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.
“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure and clean energy projects.
“I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY, policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure, has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis found.

That definition includes facilities that house the physical infrastructure used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet—which describes many data centers.
Yet data centers are conspicuously absent from the list of excluded controversial projects, which includes high-speed rail, the Delta Conveyance Project, nuclear power and oil and gas facilities.

fa2f10db349d.text: In our news wrap Wednesday, the Federal Reserve held interest rates unchanged even as officials acknowledged that inflation remains elevated, the federal judge overseeing the prosecution of former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro died at the age of 92 and hundreds of passengers aboard a cruise ship found themselves stranded in Cambodia after their trip was cut short due to high fuel prices. Amna Nawaz: Also today, the Federal Reserve held interest rates unchanged, even as officials acknowledged that inflation remains elevated. In its statement, the Central Bank said today's decision gives officials time to gather more information on how to address rising prices. Last month, the Fed raised rates for the first time in three years. And, today, two Fed officials called for an additional hike. Speaking to reporters, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh addressed those dissenting views and brushed off any notion that politics played a role with the midterm elections just days away. Kevin Warsh, Federal Reserve Chairman: We just came out of a heck of a family fight, a serious, sober discussion. I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment. I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics. Amna Nawaz: Warsh also said that he plans to reduce the number of meetings devoted to setting interest rates starting next year. Alvin Hellerstein, the federal judge overseeing the prosecution of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, died today at the age of 92. He appeared at a hearing in that case just this month. It will now be randomly handed off to another judge, as will his other cases. The New York native spent nearly three decades on the bench, where he oversaw cases involving nine 11 victims and Donald Trump's hush money lawsuit, among many others. Colleagues described him as personable to the people in his court and careful with procedure. A court official says Alvin Hellerstein died of natural causes. In California, a federal judge says the top U.S. prosecutor in Los Angeles is serving in the role unlawfully. Bill Essayli was also barred from overseeing certain cases. He's technically the first assistant U.S. attorney, but the judge said that, in reality, he's the -- quote -- "de facto United States attorney." And such a role can only be filled on an acting basis for 120 days without Senate confirmation. In a statement, Essayli said he disagreed with the ruling and that the case will ultimately be decided by the Supreme Court. Hundreds of passengers aboard a U.S. cruise ship found themselves stranded in Cambodia after their trip was cut short due to high fuel prices. The MV Odyssey was about two years into a three-year global voyage when its owners pulled the plug, citing rising energy costs due to the Iran war. Its Florida-based operator says it's working on temporary living arrangements for passengers. Some paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for a suite on the ship, and there was widespread disappointment at the trip's early termination. Steve Skulnich, MV Odyssey Passenger: We got thrown off the ship yesterday. They ran out of money. They don't have any money for fuel, so they told us we all have to get off. Russ Borman, MV Odyssey Passenger: A lot of people now have no place to go. This was their home. They put all of their money -- sold their home back in the U.S. or Australia or wherever they're from, but now they have nowhere to go. Amna Nawaz: According to Cambodian officials, the ship had been carrying more than 200 passengers, most of them Americans, and 156 crew members. The vessel itself is docked at a Cambodian port with no planned departure date. Well, "LIFE" magazine is making a comeback, returning to print next month as a quarterly publication. Launched in 1936, "LIFE" became a fixture on the nation's collective coffee table with its trademark red box logo and commitment to visual storytelling. But media habits changed over the years, and the magazine ceased publication nearly two decades ago. Model and entrepreneur Karlie Kloss is backing "LIFE'"s reboot, which will also include a Web site, social media presence and videos. But it faces an increasingly challenging media landscape that is vastly different from its mid-century peak. A group of investors led by billionaire Nelson Peltz is offering to buy Wendy's for around $1.4 billion. That amounts to a nearly 20 percent premium over the stock's closing prices yesterday before the offer. The burger chain has struggled in recent years amid competition from the likes of In-N-Out Burger and Five Guys, as well as a recent spike in beef prices. Shares of Wendy's ended 15 percent higher today after the news. Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks posted modest gains after the Fed held steady on interest rates. The Dow Jones industrial average added nearly 100 points. The Nasdaq rose about a quarter-of-1-percent. The S&P 500 also ended in positive territory.

72e2df262aa5.text: Another member of Brazil's Bolsonaro family has found haven from possible prosecution by fleeing to the U.S., where they have an ally in President Trump. Just three days after losing Brazil’s presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro, who faces multiple criminal investigations, defied a Brazilian court and left the country. Stephanie Sy discussed more with Brian Winter of America's Quarterly. Geoff Bennett: Another member of Brazil's Bolsonaro family has found safe haven from possible prosecution in Brazil by fleeing to the U.S., where they have an ally in President Trump. Just three days after losing Brazil's presidential election, Flavio Bolsonaro, who faces multiple criminal investigations, defied a Brazilian court and left the country. And, today, he issued a statement saying that he is the rightful leader of Brazil. Our Stephanie Sy is here with more. Stephanie Sy: Geoff, it's been a dramatic few days in Brazil's politics, starting with president Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise comeback in Sunday's presidential election. Even though he won by more than four million votes, Bolsonaro refused to concede. On Monday, a judge ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports and banned him from leaving the country. But, on Tuesday, he and his family crossed by land into neighboring Argentina, then flew to Ecuador. And, today, he was granted entry into the United States, landing at an airport near Miami. For more on all this, I'm joined by Brian Winter, editor in chief of "Americas Quarterly." Brian, thanks for joining the "News Hour." So Bolsonaro issued a statement this afternoon saying he is facing a politically motivated witch-hunt and that he is the true elected president of Brazil. How do you think this is going to motivate his base? And how do you think this may play out? Brian: It's an open question, Stephanie. We will have to see. But the early indications from Brazilians, including some on the right, are that this is not a strategy that is likely to work. It's hard to set up a parallel government or a government in exile. Flavio Bolsonaro compared himself in this statement to Juan Guaido, who was the Venezuelan president-elect who assumed that role at least in exile for several years and was unable to dislodge Nicolas Maduro from power. It's important to note that Flavio Bolsonaro's own party, the Liberal Party in Brazil, recognized the results of Sunday's election as legitimate. Other allied countries with the Trump administration in South America have also done so in the last couple of days. So I'm not sure that Flavio Bolsonaro is going to find the audience to be quite as receptive as he's hoping, either in Brazil or in the rest of South America. Stephanie Sy: And yet some are arguing that asking Bolsonaro to surrender his passports just a day after the election does look like political retribution and is the result of bias within the judicial system in Brazil. Is that a legitimate concern? Brian Winter: You know, it's hard to tell simple stories about Brazil, in part because it's a country where some institutions work exceptionally well. Others have shadows. One of them is the Brazilian Supreme Court, which has been embroiled in corruption and fallen into some of the political polarization that we have seen in Brazil over the last 10 years or so. And so, yes, there are questions about whether there are political elements in this case against Flavio Bolsonaro, although most legal observers think that the cases themselves are legitimate. Stephanie Sy: The Bolsonaros have been cultivating relationships within the Trump administration really for years, and that certainly came into play today. Let's listen to what President Trump said earlier this morning. He was asked about whether he approved of Flavio coming to the U.S. election. President Donald Trump The election was very strange and I thought it was terrible. It's gotten bad reviews. You look at what happened to their market. Would I approve of it? Yes, I would approve of it. Stephanie Sy: Brian, is this appropriate? Should the U.S. be providing political refuge for politicians and influencers who may be trying to evade legal processes in their home countries? Brian Winter: Well, look, the Bolsonaro family has been among President Trump's closest allies in South America over the last 10 years. The only other sort of competition in that space is Javier Milei, the president of Argentina. The connections between the families are real. There are figures like Steve Bannon and Jason Miller in President Trump's orbit who have made themselves specialists, let's say, on Brazilian politics over the last couple of years. So I see President Trump trying to accomplish two different objectives with these statements that he's made over the last couple of days. One of them is trying to at least give some support to the Bolsonaro family, who he considers ideological fellow travelers. But I also interpret President Trump's statements as a clear effort to keep a bit of distance with the Bolsonaro family for two reasons, one, because the Bolsonaro family has now lost two consecutive elections in Brazil and may no longer be the future of conservative politics in Brazil. And, two, because there's a big commercial and investment relationship between Brazil and the United States, the two biggest economies in the Western Hemisphere. President Trump has carefully noted that he has a good relationship with Lula and has said several times in recent days, he said, "I didn't take sides in this election." Stephanie Sy: All right, that is Brian Winter, editor in chief of "Americas Quarterly," joining us. Thank you. Brian Winter: Thank you.

5bca2255e33c.text: The race for the Senate has moved from off-the-radar a year ago to a dramatic, hard-to-predict finish where Democrats stand a chance of retaking the chamber. The contest will come down to just over a dozen races across the country. Lisa Desjardins takes a look at the map and what might happen. Geoff Bennett: The fight for control of the U.S. Senate is coming down to a hard-to-predict finish, where Democrats see a possible path to reclaiming the chamber in a year where that seemed like a long shot. Our Lisa Desjardins joins us now from the super screen to break down the map, the key contests, and what it will take for either party to win. All right, Lisa, so where does the race for the U.S. Senate stand? Lisa Desjardins: It is unpredictable and it is also incredibly dramatic. Let's jump right in with Cook Political Report's view of things to help us out. First of all, Democrats, right now, they are defending four vulnerable competitive seats. However, for Cook, three of these, you see them in the dark blue, they don't think are likely to go to Republicans. There is, however, a toss-up seat for Democrats, Michigan. That's number one on their watch list. How about Republicans? Look at this. Their job is much harder. You can see they're defending far more places, and far more of them are that light color. That means that they are toss-ups or a state that is about to lean potentially for Democrats. Now, in order to take over the Senate, the magic number, I want everyone to remember this, is four. Democrats need a net gain of four seats here. To do that, you can read the map as well as I,they have got to win in some of these deep red states, but they are competing there. I want to give everyone a sense of how extraordinary this is by looking at the 2024 presidential results of some of these states where Democrats are competing this year. Ohio, where there's a toss-up race, look at that. Trump won by 11 points. Let's go not far away over to Iowa, also a state that is in competition this year. Trump won that state by 13 points. And go just down the way to Kansas. Look at that. Trump won Kansas by 16 points just two years ago, but, right now, Senate Democrats think they might be able to pick this or other deep red states up to turn over the Senate entirely. Geoff Bennett: So Democrats, as you say, need to pick up four seats. What's the path to do that or the Republican path to block it? Lisa Desjardins: All right. This is your cheat sheet for election night. Remember this. Again, four seats is the magic number. Let's talk about where each party may have some likely or potential pickups. First, where can Democrats pick something up? North Carolina. Both parties will tell you that they do think this is likely to go from red to blue this year. Now, how about likely pickups for Republicans, per The Cook Political Report? There are none right now. There are some potential hopes that Republicans have, but right now there are none that are forecast to go their way. So this leaves the ball game right here, everyone, in the toss-ups. Look at these seats. These seats are the ones likely to determine the fate of the U.S. Senate. Now, how do you figure this out on election night? Again, it does come back to that magic number. Democrats need to pick up four. So it's actually a little bit simple. Let's imagine North Carolina goes, as it's expected to, for Democrats. That's one. Now it comes down to Michigan. If Democrats keep it, that means they need to pick up three seats among these swing states. If Democrats lose Michigan, they have got to pick up four. And that's what it comes down to. Geoff Bennett: And how does that compare to the map two years ago? Lisa Desjardins: Right. This is far more seats. In fact, we have 14 competitive seats right now versus nine two years ago, so a lot more. Geoff Bennett: Lisa Desjardins, I don't know how you do it, but you always do. Thanks so much. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

01b4e12407d3.text: To discuss how the midterm races are shaping up in the final days, Amna Nawaz sat down with Democratic strategist Mo Elleithee and Republican strategist Doug Heye. Amna Nawaz: Well, for more on how the races are shaping up in these final days, we turn now to the insights of Democratic strategist Mo Elleithee and Republican strategist Doug Heye. Good to see you both. Doug Heye, Republican Strategist: Good to be with you. Mo Elleithee, Democratic Strategist: Hi. Amna Nawaz: Less than a week to go for that final day of voting in these midterm elections. So far, as you both seen and have said, the indicators are good for Democrats. It's a matter of how good a night it will be. So, Doug, what are Republicans bracing for? Is it a blue wave, a blue tsunami, a blue ripple? What do you expect? Doug Heye: First, they're prepared to lose the House of Representatives. Every conversation I have had with Republicans has been that seems to be a done deal. The question is, is, what is that margin? And we don't really know at this point. And it goes to ultimately what is turnout going to be. And that then goes to the United States Senate. And I can't talk to a single person who can tell you anything that is solid or predictable about what's going to happen in pick your seven states. Amna Nawaz: Mo, what are you -- how are you looking at it? Mo Elleithee: Yes, I think that's exactly right. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Mo Elleithee: The margin in the House is going to matter for governing, right, for running the House? If it all goes as expected. Speaker Jeffries needs a little bit of a cushion, because we have now seen several consecutive speakers who have had incredibly small margins. But the Senate, I think it's a coin flip at this point. I think Democrats are in a really good position, much stronger position. I think they will, at the very least, pick up seats. The question is how many. Lisa was talking about the need for four. I think a lot of people are hoping that it's actually five just in case John Fetterman decides after the new year to have some fun with the math. Amna Nawaz: What do you think are the most likely seats for Democrats to pick up from the Senate? Mo Elleithee: I think North Carolina is done. Amna Nawaz: I think Ohio is looking really good. I think Kansas is looking better and better. Texas is a coin flip. People are feeling really good about Alaska as well. Doug Heye: And everyone I talk to, R or D, when you ask about specific states, they sort of make that face that Mo made. I don't really know what's going to happen in Iowa. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Doug Heye: I don't really know what's going to happen in Michigan. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Doug Heye: There are a lot of states like that. Amna Nawaz: Well, that may be your answer when I ask for this next question as well. But I want to point to what The New York Times showed in their latest poll about South Carolina this morning, a reliably red state there, but the Senate race between Darline Graham and Annie Andrews is now effectively tied. Doug, is that an outlier or a warning sign for Republicans? Doug Heye: It's a real warning sign. It's a warning sign in this race for two reasons. One, Darline Graham just hasn't been a candidate that's really caught fire, been incredibly weak and weak support from within the party. But it also tells us where Donald Trump's numbers are in South Carolina, like they are everywhere else. And when I was at the Republican National Committee in 2010, our magic number for Obama was 46. If Donald Trump were at 46 percent approval right now, we're not talking about Iowa or Michigan or Maine or a lot of these other states. It'd be a very good night for Republicans. His numbers are just so critically low, even in South Carolina. Amna Nawaz: Can a Democrat win in South Carolina, Mo? Mo Elleithee: I think they can. I mean, look, we all have -- every Democrat has memories of Lindsey Graham's last race against Democrat Jaime Harrison, where the polls showed it was tied headed into Election Day and he ended up winning by double digits. The big difference is that Lindsey Graham was so popular among South Carolinians. Darline Graham is not. By a double-digit margin, the voters are saying they don't think she's qualified to be in the United States Senate. Candidate quality really, really matters, and that's the underlying factor beyond the national numbers, beyond the president's number. You see where Republicans are really struggling across the country is because they nominated really bad candidates in those states. Amna Nawaz: Well, you mentioned Alaska, and I want to put to you another big headline today related to that Senate race, more reporting from The New York Times that Democrats actively recruited a spoiler candidate in Dan J. Sullivan to join the Senate race to boost the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola. He, of course, has virtually the same name as the Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. Late today at Joint Base Andrews, President Trump called on Peltola to resign from the race. He also said this to reporters. Take a listen. DONALD TRUMP, President of the United States: It's a fraud, and they said they didn't do it, and they did do it and they got caught. And, in fact, it was the plot by the Democrat Party. And, frankly, they should be -- I think they should be prosecuted. To me, that's voter fraud at the highest level. Amna Nawaz: Mo, how do you look at this? Is this unethical but legal? What happened here? Mo Elleithee: It's boneheaded but legal. It's dumb but legal. I don't like it when parties do this. I don't like this in Alaska. I didn't like it when Republicans were funding the petition drives to get Green Party candidates on the ballot in a number of states. I hate this. Now, the reason it's boneheaded is because this is one of those stories where the headlines are going to be worse than the impact. Dan Sullivan number two isn't going to have that big of an impact on this race. He didn't in the primary. Ranked-choice

a34958f724e5.text: Nearly 40 million votes have already been cast for races that will determine not only who controls Congress, but also governors, mayors and city councils. For many years, PBS News has relied on the Associated Press to keep track of results, and we will again next Tuesday. Deema Zein takes a closer look at how the AP counts the vote. Geoff Bennett: Nearly 40 million votes have already been cast ahead of Election Day. And that's for races that will determine not only who controls Congress, but also governors, mayors, and city councils. Amna Nawaz: For many years, PBS News has relied on the Associated Press to keep track of results. And we will do so again next Tuesday. Deema Zein takes a closer look at how AP counts the vote. Deema Zein: Elections are run and ballots are counted by thousands of local jurisdictions across the country. The Associated Press is tracking results in thousands of races. Knowing how many voters actually showed up is critical to knowing when a race is over. To explain what it takes to count the vote, I'm joined by David Scott, vice president of election services at the Associated Press. David, thank you for joining me. David Scott: Happy to be here. Deema Zein: So I want to jump right in. Election Day is a big operation. How many races are you tracking? David Scott: So in this year's general election, we will tabulate close to 7,000 races across national races for Congress, state legislative races, local races for mayor, some city council, some school board. So it's an enormous effort. Deema Zein: And, as we said, elections are locally run. So how many people does it take for AP to gather results? And is this done in person, online, both? David Scott: Both, all. Wherever we can get vote count, we're looking for it. And that's actually one of the hallmarks of what we do is multiple sources. So we will employ. 4,000 stringers this year, reporters essentially, who go to local election offices and wait for results to be posted or they talk to election officials as they are releasing ballots. We also know that those results are posted online in many places. Some states and some counties have electronic feeds. So we are looking wherever we can get those and we take all that data and we match it up. Is what the stringer is hearing from election officials, the same things on the Web site? It adds a layer of accuracy to our vote count and to what we're reporting on election night. We like to say that what we do at AP on election night is the single largest act of journalism there is. Now, there's lots of big stories, but there will be close to 5,000 people working for AP on this election night, all trying to answer that question of who of Americans picked to lead. Deema Zein: Wow. And as you're tracking these results in calling races, you're also estimating the number of votes cast. So I want to ask, how do you determine the actual size of the electorate? David Scott: It's a big math problem, right, because we don't know in advance, but we get a lot of help from election officials. So, in many states, they say ahead of time how many advanced ballots have been returned, how many have been cast. On the day of election, many states, many counties will post details or tell our reporters, this is how many people have voted at the polling place on Election Day. And so we use that information, that data to make an estimate of how many people have voted and what the turnout will be in every race. Deema Zein: How have the elections now changed over the years, in both how people have voted and how you count the vote? David Scott: Well, the biggest change is that people vote before Election Day. 1972, 95 percent of Americans voted at their neighborhood polling place on Election Day. And that number is now less than 50 percent. A lot of people, most people are voting before Election Day. The biggest change has been the rise of mail balloting, early in-person voting, just the different ways that you can cast a ballot. Deema Zein: David Scott, vice president of election services at the Associated Press, thank you for joining us. David Scott: Happy to be here. Amna Nawaz: And we will have those live election results next Tuesday, November 3. Join us and our reporters and our panel of experts for analysis as the votes are counted. Our coverage begins at 7:00 p.m. Eastern.

0e2465df87e2.text: Following partisan battles over political maps, nearly 35 million Americans will vote in congressional districts redrawn ahead of this year's midterms. As the nation marks its 250th anniversary, Judy Woodruff explores the origins of gerrymandering and why this centuries-old practice remains one of the most powerful tools in American politics. It's part of her series, Crossroads: America at 250. Geoff Bennett: Nearly 35 million Americans will vote in congressional districts that were redrawn ahead of this year's midterms following partisan battles over political maps. As the nation marks its 250th anniversary, our Judy Woodruff explores the origins of gerrymandering and why this centuries-old practice remains one of the most powerful tools in American politics. It's part of her ongoing series Crossroads: America at 250. Judy Woodruff: The items on these cards are rare political artifact, protected by Library of Congress curators who carefully brought them out of their Archives. Woman: What you're seeing today is a copy of the original Boston Gazette, where you see the actual first appearance of the gerrymander cartoon. Judy Woodruff: What year was this? Woman: And this was March 26, 1812. Judy Woodruff: 1812. At the time, Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry had approved redrawn districts in the state in a bid to keep his party in power. As the story goes, a newspaper editor saw a salamander in the map's outline, combined it with Gerry's name, and a new word entered the American political vocabulary, gerrymandering, or, as it became, gerrymandering. Nick Seabrook, UNF: This is, I would argue, probably the very first example of a viral meme in American politics. So it spread around The Federalist newspapers in the New England era, and then over the subsequent year it was reprinted in almost 100 newspapers across the country. Woman: It's depicted as this mythical salamander beast. Judy Woodruff: The library also has the wood blocks used to print this piece of history. More than two centuries later, gerrymandering is flourishing and playing out in state after state. The latest round of mid-decade redistricting intensified last year when, at President Trump's request, Texas redrew its congressional maps to try to add five Republican seats. After that, other states entered the fight. California Governor Gavin Newsom called a special election to redistrict and pick up more Democratic seats. Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-CA): They want to rig these elections and they want the power that gerrymandering provides, because they know what Donald Trump knows. He's going to lose the midterms. President Donald Trump: The Democrats, or as I call, the Dumocrats, because they are dumb in so many ways, they have redistricted for years, and now we took our shot, and it looks like we're going to pick up a lot of seats. Nick Seabrook: The motive for gerrymandering is almost always power. It's a product of polarization, of Democrats and Republicans not just disagreeing, but actively hating each other. Negative partisanship is such an incredibly strong force in our politics today. Judy Woodruff: Nick Seabrook is the author of "One Person, One Vote: A Surprising History of Gerrymandering in America." He says the practice of manipulating district lines to protect political power is actually older than Gerry. It began with George Burrington, a colonial governor of North Carolina in the 1730s. Nick Seabrook: His attempt to manipulate the districts of the colonial assembly was motivated by a desire to try and prevent the columnists themselves, who elected the lower house of that legislature, from pushing back on the taxes and fees that his administration was charging to try and expand the footprint of the North Carolina colony. Judy Woodruff: So he had a motive, or motives, for what he was trying to do. Nick Seabrook: He did, yes. Judy Woodruff: Does that qualify as redistricting or gerrymandering as we know it today, manipulating? Nick Seabrook: I would say this was certainly gerrymandering because there was no -- there was no legal obligation for him to make any changes to these districts. He approached it purely as an exercise in maximizing his own political power. Judy Woodruff: This year, that maximizing of political power has ended up with mid-decade redistricting in nine states, Texas, California, Utah, Ohio, Tennessee, Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, and North Carolina. From the colonial days of George Burrington to today, North Carolina has been one of the most gerrymandered states in the country. When congressional maps are redrawn, they sometimes split communities right down the middle. That's the case in the small town here of Sharpsburg, North Carolina, where three counties come together. I'm standing at the northernmost edge of the Third Congressional District, but if I take just a few steps across these railroad tracks, you will see I have moved into the First Congressional District. When Republican state lawmakers redrew these and other lines last year, they said they were trying to pick up one more Republican seat in Congress. Several counties shifted from one district to another, changing the demographics of both, spreading out eligible Black voters and weakening their electoral power. The city of Wilson is one of the communities plucked out of the First District and placed in the Third. For the 50,000 people who live here, the question is, what will the switch mean for their voice in Congress? Castonoble Hooks has lived in Wilson his entire life. Castonoble Hooks, Wilson, North Carolina, Resident: This is a traditional Black area, where most of the original Black residents still live. Judy Woodruff: He remembers the days of Jim Crow laws, when the town was segregated. Castonoble Hooks: What disenfranchisement taught us is that if you're not a part of the political process, you are left behind. Judy Woodruff: Today, Hooks is a regular fixture at the senior center where he teaches chess and encourages his neigh

a15777630d9a.text: Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor leader and civil rights icon, died Wednesday from cancer at her home in Bakersfield, California. Amna Nawaz looks back at Huerta's life and legacy. Amna Nawaz: Finally tonight, we remember the life and legacy of Dolores Huerta, the pioneering labor leader and civil rights icon. Huerta died today from cancer at her home in Bakersfield, California. Leaders from around the country paid tribute, including in California, where flags were lowered to half-mast in her honor. "Yes, we can," Dolores Huerta's belief and words that helped build a movement. Dolores Huerta, Activist: It means activism. It means that people can have the power to change things in their lives, change things politically, and it means that every person should feel their own power and know that they can make a difference. Amna Nawaz: Her rallying cry power at the United Farm Workers union and more widely, the labor and civil rights movements. Dolores Clara Fernandez was born in 1930 in New Mexico. As a young schoolteacher in the San Joaquin Valley, her students' poverty inspired her to start organizing farmworkers, as she told the "News Hour"s Ray Suarez in 2012. Dolores Huerta: These children that were my classroom were the children of the Dust Bowls, the little Opie and Archie kids, and they were coming in there also and kind of hungry and threadbare. I thought that was so wrong. So I thought, well it's better to just get up and start organizing the farmworkers and I decided then to quit. Amna Nawaz: She eventually joined forces with Cesar Chavez in California's Central Valley to found what would become the United Farm Workers Union. The union joined the Filipino workers' strike against grape growers over low wages and working conditions that lasted five years. As the union grew, it organized multiple major strikes and boycotts through the '60s and '70s, and it helped negotiate contracts with big growers to win benefits for those in the field, as chronicled in this 2017 documentary "Dolores." Dolores Huerta: We will take economic pressure, strikes, boycotts to force recognition and obtain collective bargaining rights. The social and the economic revolution of the farm workers is well under way, and it will not be up until we receive equality. Amna Nawaz: Geraldo Cadava, a professor of history and Latino studies at Northwestern University, says Huerta's presence on the ground was key to her emerging voice. Geraldo Cadava, Northwestern University: She was a huge kind of influence. She was on the ground from the beginning. She was knocking on doors with Cesar Chavez. She was visiting farm workers in their homes. She was with them in the fields. So she was a real fighter and leader and influencer within the movement. Amna Nawaz: She spent almost four decades as the union's vice president and as the second in command to the charismatic Chavez until his death in 1993. But for decades, Huerta had kept a stunning secret to herself. Chavez had raped her during those early years. Huerta only went public earlier this year. Dolores Huerta: I had to protect the movement. I think that we accomplished a lot with the movement. So I don't know. Should I have spoken out sooner? I don't know. But at least I'm glad that I'm finally getting this off my chest finally. Amna Nawaz: An investigation from The New York Times found that Chavez had sexually abused multiple women, some of them children. Huerta told The Times that Cesar Chavez's assaults resulted in two pregnancies that she concealed, two children she gave up for adoption. She later was in a long-term partnership with his brother, Richard Chavez, and had 14 children overall. The revelations shocked the world, especially many in the Latino community. Throughout her life's work, she suffered again and again. Huerta was jailed 22 times over union demonstrations and was once critically injured after she was beaten by police. She was active in politics for decades as well, volunteering for Senator Robert F. Kennedy's presidential campaign. Huerta was on stage with him when he was assassinated in 1968. Years later, she campaigned for Presidents Clinton, Obama, and Biden. In 2012, President Obama awarded Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Barack Obama: On a personal note, Dolores was very gracious when I told her I had stolen her slogan, "Si, se puede," "Yes, we can." Knowing her, I'm pleased that she let me off easy, because Dolores does not play. (LAUGHTER) Maria Teresa Kumar, Founder and Executive Director, Voto Latino: Dolores Huerta was a giant. Amna Nawaz: Maria Teresa Kumar is the president of the political organization Voto Latino. Huerta was a mentor of hers. Maria Teresa Kumar: When Voto Latino first started, one of the biggest challenges was how to navigate a space that didn't necessarily welcome women. This was after the first wave of anti-immigrant sentiment, and Dolores stepped up and she came to us and provided us counsel. She provided us cheering, she provided us strategy, and she provided us, I think, just generous, generous friendship. Amna Nawaz: Dolores Huerta never slowed down. The labor leader, civil rights icon, and feminist activist was still rallying well into her late 90s. Dolores Huerta: Every one of our segments of society that are trying to make positive change, that are fighting for social justice, this is what we have to do, come together, organize push back, take that direct action, and then we can make the world a better place. Amna Nawaz: Dolores Huerta was 96 years old.

An eight-year-old girl has been seriously injured in a wolf attack at a German wildlife park.
She was inside an enclosure at the JohannismÃ¼hle park in Brandenburg, south of Berlin, with a staff member and two other children when the attack happened, police said.
They said in a statement that the "precise circumstances of the incident are the subject of an ongoing police investigation".
The girl was taken to hospital by helicopter after the incident on Wednesday. No one else was injured.
The park, in the town of Baruth/Mark, has been closed temporarily and is set to reopen on 2 November, according to its website, which did not give further details.
The park keeps grey and arctic wolves, along with other animals including the brown bear and lynx.
The girl was injured by at least one animal and suffered head injuries, according to German newspaper Bild.
It reported that the incident happened before the park opened at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT) and that the girl could have been taking part in a special visit.
JohannismÃ¼hle offers small group tours to allow visitors to spend time with some animals, with its site mentioning feeding wolves or petting a llama.
The incident comes after a number of other animal attacks at zoos and wildlife parks in Europe.
A keeper at a Dutch zoo died this week after being mauled by a leopard, and a man was killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park earlier this month.

Sisak, Associated Press By — Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/alvin-hellerstein-federal-judge-who-handled-cases-on-trump-maduro-and-9-11-dies-at-92 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Alvin Hellerstein, federal judge who handled cases on Trump, Maduro and 9/11, dies at 92 Politics Oct 28, 2026 5:49 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Alvin K. Hellerstein, a Manhattan federal judge who presided over cases involving President Donald Trump, former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and the 9/11 attacks during nearly three decades on the bench, has died. He was 92. Hellerstein died Wednesday morning while surrounded by his family, Chief Judge Laura Taylor Swain said in a statement. His funeral is scheduled for Thursday at Riverside Memorial Chapel in Manhattan. READ MORE: New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture Swain remembered Hellerstein as a "distinguished jurist" and praised his "energetic and dedicated service" to the court, which continued until his death. Please check your inbox to confirm. "He is greatly appreciated and will be sorely missed," she said. Just two weeks ago, Hellerstein presided over the arraignment of Maduro and Maduro's wife, Cilia Flores, on torture charges that were added to their ongoing narco-terrorism conspiracy case. Maduro, who was captured alongside his wife in January in a surprise U.S. military raid in Caracas, twice defied Hellerstein's request to enter a plea. Irked, Hellerstein took matters into his own hands, interjecting that "a plea of not guilty will be entered on behalf of Mr. Maduro." At Flores' Oct. 8 bail hearing, Hellerstein coughed and struggled to speak at times, telling lawyers: "I have a voice problem. As long as you can understand — hear me, I'll keep going." Nevertheless, he was resolute that he'd preside over Maduro and Flores' trial, which he'd scheduled for next June. "We were saddened to learn of Judge Hellerstein's passing and offer our condolences to his family," Maduro's lawyer, Barry Pollack, said. Analisa Torres, the judge taking over the case, was part of an international monitoring delegation for Venezuela's 2006 presidential election, won by Maduro's late mentor and predecessor Hugo Chávez. A federal judge since 2013, she previously served on the state bench in Manhattan. A New York native and Columbia Law School graduate, Hellerstein served in the U.S. Army Judge Advocate General's Corps and worked as a Manhattan litigator before President Bill Clinton appointed him to the federal bench in 1998. He kept a robust docket even after moving to senior status in 2011. Rulings left Trump's conviction in place In August, in one of his last significant rulings, Hellerstein again spurned Trump's effort to erase his hush money conviction, rejecting the president's bid to move the case to federal court and have it dismissed on presidential immunity grounds. "Paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity," Hellerstein wrote, referring to the $130,000 payoff to adult film actor Stormy Daniels at the heart of Trump's case. It was the third time Hellerstein had denied Trump's requests to move the case. The first time was after Trump's March 2023 indictment; the second followed Trump's May 2024 conviction and a subsequent U.S. Supreme Court ruling that presidents and former presidents cannot be prosecuted for official acts. Hellerstein revisited the matter after the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that he erred by failing to consider "important issues relevant" to Trump's request. The panel expressed "no view" on how Hellerstein should rule. In 2020, Hellerstein sprang Trump's estranged former lawyer and fixer Michael Cohen from prison after the Justice Department revoked his home confinement to thwart his efforts to publish a book or talk to the media. The government's action, he ruled, was retaliatory and a First Amendment violation. 'This is different. This is 9/11.' In the aftermath of the 2001 attack on the World Trade Center, Hellerstein presided over dozens of wrongful death, injury and property damage lawsuits — a two-decade-long effort that shaped his legacy on the bench. Some of the judge's former clients died in the attack and, lawyers say, he showed great empathy to victims and their families, meeting with them for hours in his chambers and rejecting what he felt were low-ball settlement offers. In March 2010, Hellerstein rejected a proposed settlement that would have paid at least $575 million to thousands of people who fell ill working in the toxic ash of the trade center. He acknowledged he was breaking with tradition by getting so involved. "Most settlements are private. A plaintiff and defendant come together, shake hands, and it's done with," he explained. The judge usually has no part in saying yes or no. "This is different," Hellerstein said. "This is 9/11." Others were dismayed when, in 2008, Hellerstein ended an effort to force New York City government to keep searching for human remains in debris moved from ground zero to a Staten Island landfill. High-profile cases until the end Hellerstein's other notable cases included the criminal trials of Charlie Javice, who was convicted last year of defrauding JPMorgan Chase out of $175 million by exaggerating the customer base for her financial aid startup, and hedge fund founder Bill Hwang, who was convicted in 2024 of securities and market manipulation fraud in a scheme that cost banks billions of dollars.
