In 2016, current Democratic candidate for Congress Leticia Gutierrez lived six miles from a refinery owned by the Brazilian oil company Petrobras in Pasadena, part of the greater Houston area. The plant accrued thousands of dollars in fines from the Texas Commission on Environment Quality for violations including the release of dangerous air pollutants like sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides that coated the significantly Hispanic area bordering the plant, where Gutierrez and her two children lived.
Her eldest son developed an upper respiratory illness as a child and, according to Gutierrez, it wasn’t until she spoke to several pediatricians that she was able to identify the source of her son’s ailment as pollution from the nearby petrochemical facilities along the Houston Ship Channel. A decade later, the same environmental issues that plagued Gutierrez’s community have become central to her campaign platform as she makes a bid in a newly redrawn congressional district that is reliant on fossil fuel to power its local economies by providing more than one million jobs.
“I’m all for making money, but it shouldn’t be on the backs of our children’s health,” Gutierrez told Inside Climate News.
As Election Day approaches, Gutierrez and her Republican challenger, Alex Mealer, have taken clear stances on the industry and its impacts. Gutierrez has focused much of her campaign on the disparate health and environmental ramifications that spawn from living near petrochemical facilities. Mealer, a former oil and gas finance executive, emphasizes her plans to expand employment at those facilities and strengthen the district’s fossil fuel businesses.
This will be the first general election since Texas’ 9th district was redrawn to favor Republicans last year. The election could determine control of the House. A recent poll from the University of Houston shows Mealer, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump in the primary, with a six point lead over Gutierrez, and 10 percent of voters still undecided. Mealer defeated state Rep. Briscoe Cain in the Republican primary runoff. Gutierrez secured her own party’s nomination against five opponents in March.
According to Renee Cross, the senior executive director and a lead researcher behind the poll at the University of Houston’s Hobby School of Public Affairs, the gap between the candidates is considerably narrower than expected, particularly in a newly redrawn district.
“It went from a +26 Democrat district to a +9 Republican. Well, +9 is not tremendous, but it still gives the edge to Republicans,” Cross said. “So the fact that Gutierrez is only 6 points behind is pretty remarkable, not only based on those voting trends but also based on the amount of money that Mealer has had to advertise to get people aware not only of her, but aware of her opponent’s alleged weaknesses.”
Gutierrez and Mealer fall on opposite sides of the oil and gas industry, with Mealer alleging that Gutierrez’s concerns for refineries’ effects on public health will undermine job growth in the oil and gas sector that powers the state of Texas. Gutierrez has denied the assertion.
“My response has always been the same, even as I’ve been doing this work prior to me campaigning: advocating for cleaner air and cleaner environmental standards actually creates jobs,” Gutierrez said. “It doesn’t do away with them. As a matter of fact, this Trump administration’s rollback of a lot of the protections have been put in place for decades by Republicans,” she said, referencing former President George H.W. Bush’s 1990 amendments to the Clean Air Act.
Mealer has expressed plans to expand domestic energy production in an effort to knock down gas and electricity costs and boost local economies. She’s also announced plans to grow the Houston Ship Channel, which accounts for 18.5 percent of the state’s GDP.
Throughout the campaign, Gutierrez has courted working class families, drawing on her background as a single mother and the immigrant daughter of farm laborers. She has pledged to tackle affordability and environmental issues, like the disproportionate impact of poor air quality near Port Houston. Labor organizations, including the Texas Gulf Coast Area Labor Federation and the Texas chapter of the Service Employees International Union, have endorsed her.

The Texas Health and Environment Alliance declined to comment on the election but said the organization has worked with Gutierrez for years and witnessed her advocacy in the Houston area.
Though Gutierrez has never held public office, in her role as government affairs director at the advocacy group Air Alliance Houston, she supported legislation designed to improve environmental standards in the region, including Senate Bill 763, which called for a more efficient review of air quality standard permits.
In her role at Air Alliance, she also supported HB 1730, which proposed a collaborative health study from the University of Houston to determine the health outcomes caused by forever chemicals in partnership with the Railroad Commission of Texas, the TCEQ and the Department of State Health Services. According to Gutierrez, following a fire at a storage tank in 2019, chemicals from the foam used to combat the blaze seeped into the Houston Ship Channel, raising the contamination level above that allowed by the EPA.
Mealer, who did not respond to requests for comment, has remained relatively quiet on climate and environmental issues in her own campaign, a decision that Cross said makes sense given that, while Mealer has maintained a strong positive position toward the oil and gas industry, residents in the 9th district still grapple with its health effects, including higher cancer risks.

Reeling rods, pulling pots and hauling nets this summer, fishermen from Greece to the U.K. discovered unexpected visitors popping their heads above the surface.
In the Aegean, it was silver-cheeked toadfish—an invasive pufferfish with powerful, prominent teeth. In the English Channel, it was the unprecedented arrival of uncommon common octopuses. And in the Adriatic, it was the aggressive and aptly named blue crab.
Across the continent’s seas and straits, warming waters and decades of overfishing are throwing marine ecosystems off kilter and sending species swimming in new directions. For the fishermen landing unfamiliar tentacled and scaled sea creatures, the novel arrivals haven’t always been welcomed on deck.
“The fisheries I found 30 years ago were more or less the species that archeozoologists found in [archaeological] remains many thousands years back. But today, this is changing really fast,” said Anastasia Miliou, the science director at Archipelagos Institute of Marine Conservation, a Greek nonprofit.
“Fishermen are [already] having a hard time because of a lack of fish. Changing temperatures and the new invasive and alien species don’t make it any easier,” said Miliou, noting the surprising spikes in certain stocks were adding financial pressure for artisanal fishermen struggling to survive.
This summer was Western Europe’s warmest on record. Above the waterline, a wave of wildfires, droughts and heat-related deaths ravaged the continent. The blue-jewelled depths of the Aegean and even the more-bracing North Sea and Baltic basins also experienced mass heat.
Globally, June to August 2026 saw the highest mean sea surface temperature on record. In Europe, this included sea surface temperatures more than 3.6 and 5.4 degrees Fahrenheit (2 or 3 degrees Celsius) above the last three-decade average.
As global ocean heat content rises for the ninth consecutive year, “ectothermic” fish—species unable to regulate their own temperature that depend on finding suitable surrounding conditions—are on the move.
These newcomers across the continent have brought economic challenges to fisheries who have, at times, struggled to adapt.
In Greece, the arrival of the fatal-if-consumed toadfish and their large, sharp gnashers has significantly damaged fishing gear as the rabbit-like front teeth chomp nets.
“It’s got to the point where we might go out fishing one day and then spend the next three days fixing our nets,” Giorgos Kyriakakis, a Cretan fisherman, told Greek public broadcaster ERT in June. “They eat our catch and damage our nets—that’s very costly.”
Over the summer, Greek fishermen were offered almost $6.00 (€5.33) per kilo to catch the invasive species by the Agriculture Ministry.
Off Britain’s southern shores, eight-legged, suction-cupped common octopuses have arrived from breeding grounds in the Channel Islands and northern France in record numbers. The largest population bloom in 75 years, the arrival is tied to temperature increases, according to researchers at the Marine Biological Association.
The newcomers have proven both a blessing and a curse. Staggeringly lucrative catches have been recorded for those able to catch the creatures. But for traditional shellfish fisheries, the landings of brown crabs, European lobster and king scallops have dropped dramatically.

With octopods expected to stay in U.K. waters, the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs held its first “octopus conference” earlier this month.
“They are both a threat and an opportunity for fishermen and a massive challenge for fisheries management,” said Mike Cohen, CEO of the National Federation of Fishermen’s Organisations, at the event. “The sudden arrival of this fast-growing, short-lived and highly predatory species into British waters upends a lot of our established knowledge and expectations about our coastal ecosystems.”
In many cases it’s more than just warming water. It’s also the consequences of rampant overfishing.
“We forget to put in the equation the human [fishing] impact because in the Mediterranean, and especially here in the Aegean Sea, our seas are very overfished,” said Miliou, explaining that this creates gaps in the ecosystems.
“When the new species arrive here, they find a lot of space to grow because the native species are no longer there,” added Miliou, highlighting that many invasive species hitch a ride in the ballast water of ships transiting the Suez Canal.
Europe’s not alone.
More than 125 fish species in Japanese waters were found to have moved north to cooler waters, according to an eDNA study released this week by the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology.
“Fishermen across Japan are already finding differences in the types of fish they reel in compared to a few decades ago,” said the paper’s lead author Timothy Ravasi in a press release.
“A sudden influx of new types of fish means you need new techniques, tools, and knowledge to catch them, which is especially hard on small, family-based fishing businesses,” Ravasi said, noting people might not be able to make their culturally or historically significant dishes.
With European fish moving north to cooler confines—and also deeper to colder, darker depths—fisheries management will have to adapt. And as El Niño hits the Pacific Ocean, fish stocks are likely to be further disrupted the world over.
“Healthy marine ecosystems have their own mechanisms to restore balance and resist the spread of invasive species,” said Miliou, who remains optimistic.
“Nature will remake the balance as long as we let it. Right now we’re not letting it.”

As the most heavily forested state in the country, about 94 percent of Maine’s forests are privately owned, so focusing on their carbon benefits has both immediate ecological and economic effects.
By creating specific programs and collaborations, the state has been strategic in using its resources to reach its climate goals and has made thoughtful partnerships for years ahead. The story of Maine demonstrates how individuals can collectively make a greater impact and how international alliances can contribute toward global stewardship.
In a four-year climate action plan called “Maine Won’t Wait,” the state sets out four pillars to focus on: drastically reducing greenhouse emissions, strengthening resiliency by adaptation, protecting jobs at risk from climate change and creating clean energy jobs and supporting all of Maine’s residents, even in rural communities.
On the economic side, Maine’s Forest Products Council reported that in 2024 the state’s timber industry produced $8.3 billion for Maine’s economy, representing 3.45 percent of the state’s GDP. Maine’s paper and timber industry also accounted for 29,000 jobs across 16 counties.
But Maine’s 18 million acres of forests also protect the watershed, soil and biodiversity as the largest unfragmented tract across the eastern United States, essential for species migration.
One thing is certain: Maine’s forests are indispensable. In 2021, the state created the Forest Carbon Task Force and implemented a range of programs and legislation to support Maine’s forests and build climate resiliency. Now, as reporting deadlines are approaching, the state can see exactly how successful these conservation efforts have been.
In March, the Maine Forest Service introduced the WoodsWISE Resilience Program, which supports private woodland owners and encourages climate-focused stewardship. The program, which works alongside an existing program called the WoodsWISE Incentives Program, is now funded by two grants totaling $9 million from the Inflation Reduction Act and the U.S. Forest Service Landowner Support Program. One grant requires documentation of pre- and post-treatment inventory and carbon modeling.
Nicole Rogers, formerly the Maine Forest Service landowner outreach forester, said that through the WoodsWise program, landowners can apply for eight approved practices that have climate or carbon benefits. To participate, woodland owners need 10 to 1,000 acres of forest and must agree to work with a practice plan focused on the area of practice implementation that meets their forest’s specific needs for 10 years.
“Our program is a tool for landowners wanting to take action in their own forest,” Rogers said in an email. “By offering financial incentives, landowners have the opportunity to do thoughtful silviculture with a reduced financial burden.”
According to Rogers, since March, more than 150 landowners have participated in the WoodsWISE Resilience Program. Through this program, a trained consulting forester works with each landowner on a plan specific to their forest’s needs so they can gain support while navigating the changes from climate change.
The program focuses on good stewardship, which can mean many things, depending on the forest. It can range from invasive species removal and thinning an overcrowded, young forest; to removing specific trees to encourage regeneration, or removing trees that carry disease or fungus.
“These practices can be costly for a private landowner, so the program aims to reimburse 60 to 90 percent of the financial burden for landowners based on their underserved status by creating an indiviudalized plan the woodland owner agrees to follow for the next 10 years. This could result in up to $20,000 per participant and another program is set to open later this year with a higher landowner cap. With programs like these, the state of Maine could see a collective benefit.”
By purposefully using landowners’ forests, Maine has an advantage in reaching carbon neutrality. According to research by the University of Maine, the state’s forests offset at least 60 percent of overall greenhouse emissions annually. Philip Bartlett II, the former chair of the Maine Public Utilities Commission, said that electricity generation in Maine is already fairly clean, with a mix of renewables in use throughout the state.
Bartlett said it’s important to look long-term when meeting climate goals, and agrees that good forest management practices are key for Maine. He said that, to his knowledge, no fast clear-cutting is being done, and forests are managed for growth and harvesting, creating opportunities for carbon sequestration.
The challenge, he said, is the state’s vastness, which makes residents rely on fuel for transportation and oil to heat their homes. Bartlett said recent international dynamics have emphasized the need for a diversified portfolio of renewable resources to stabilize electricity prices.
“I think what we’re seeing now is that reliance on fossil fuels is really what is driving a ton of volatility and really high prices during certain parts of the year. So the only way you’re going to tackle that is to figure out how to diversify that portfolio,” he said.
Catherine Wolfram, a professor of energy economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Sloan School of Management, said Maine’s implementation of carbon markets aligns with how Europe and other countries are operating.
She said that while compliance markets run by governments in which polluters are essentially taxed for carbon emissions are “extremely robust and extremely effective,” much of the criticism of carbon markets comes from the voluntary markets where companies buy and sell carbon offsets without formal monitoring, with corruption and manipulation sometimes a factor.
While Wolfram said these potential problems are solvable, she said the issue of large areas of forests being used as carbon sinks is more complex when businesses are also dependent on the area fo

Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity.
He said Ethiopia and Russia had agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow.
The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats.
Abiy, who described Russian President Vladimir Putin, "as a close friend of Ethiopia", said Ethiopia had now become the first country in subâSaharan Africa to own this kind of "advanced combat technology".
"If we fail to build this capability, surviving as a country in our region will become difficult. Countries with sufficient preparation are not easily defied," he said.
Russia and Ethiopia have signed several military agreements in recent years, including a deal in 2021 to train and improve technology for the military.
Abiy explained that Ethiopia signed an agreement with Russia several years ago to procure the Suâ35 jets and Sâ400 systems, citing global air force trends and security threats facing the country.
The Suâ35, he noted, was equipped for both airâtoâair and airâtoâground combat, with the ability to detect and neutralize incoming cruise missiles at distances of up to 200km (124 miles).
Military intelligence analyst Qalaab Segatu told BBC Amharic that Ethiopia's acquisition of additional warplanes was a key indication that "it was preparing for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts".
According to him, the jets are highly manoeuvrable and capable of covering large areas, with radars capable of ensuring air superiority and long-range scanning.
When combined, the fighter jets and air defence systems "create a significant capability to protect and defend major cities and critical infrastructure such as the Renaissance Dam, providing key strategic air superiority", Qalaab said.
Abiy said in addition to the advanced capabilities of the aircraft from Russia, the use of drones was equally important in strengthening deterrence.
Ethiopia has extensively used military drones, including those sourced from Turkey and China, in recent conflicts.
"We need to build capacity not only with drones, but also with the fourth generation capabilities of the Su 30 and Su 35 [aircraft]," Abiy said.
The latest acquisition of military hardware from Russia comes after the current conflict in northern Tigray started last month between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which it denies.
Tensions between the two countries have also persisted as Abiy terms Ethiopia's lack of direct sea access an "existential question", which Eritrea views as a direct threat to its sovereignty.
Eritrea gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long war with Ethiopia, with the latter losing access to the sea.

9bab8b48cf61.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/hegseth-fires-the-pentagons-top-military-planner-even-as-trump-considers-new-iran-strikes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Hegseth fires the Pentagon's top military planner even as Trump considers new Iran strikes Politics Oct 29, 2026 4:51 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, the latest in a series of generals to be ousted and one that comes even as President Donald Trump is weighing renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. He is the second general to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the "J5," under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced to retire last October. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. The move was reported earlier by The Atlantic. A spokesperson for the Joint Staff said "the Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation" and they "wish him and his family the best." WATCH: A look at Hegseth's attempts to reshape the Pentagon Typically, the J5 director and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president. Sylvia's firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran. Trump has vowed to "finish the job" in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said new strikes are an option after the midterm elections next week. U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action after Tuesday's elections as well as for the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter said. They say Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes. A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as the commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the J5. He is the latest in nearly two dozen generals, admirals and other military leaders to be fired, forced to retire or otherwise depart under Hegseth's tenure — almost all of which have not been publicly explained by the Pentagon. That includes the civilian secretaries of the Army and Navy as well as some top uniformed officers for the military services. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment late Wednesday. Hegseth said last month that he ordered the military to double the cuts to the overall number of top officers to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. There are currently roughly 800 flag and general officer positions. "I call it accountability and long overdue," Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30. Some members of Congress have criticized cuts to the ranks of generals as a "purge" that will take years to rebuild. "He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military," Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth, said last month. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it." Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani in Washington and Samy Magdy in New York contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 1149d7eccad6.text: The 2026 midterms already face a messy pileup of lawsuits and ballot battles, raising fears about election confidence before voters even finish casting ballots . Why it matters: Election challenges aren't unusual, but as the Trump administration continues to make false claims about widespread voter fraud, officials are juggling fights over voter lists, mail-ballot rules and election certification challenges. What they're saying: "The types of challenges that we are seeing pre-election, this close to election day, are very unusual, and mostly because they are coming from the federal government," Jonathan Diaz of the Campaign Legal Center told Axios. "These lawsuits are frivolous," Diaz said, adding they could "create doubt in the minds of the public about the legitimacy of the election process." "It shouldn't be allowed to happen, and it was done in conjunction with Schumer and everybody else. It's called VOTER FRAUD. It should not have been allowed to happen." The other side: The White House referred Axios to comments President Trump made to the media. The Department of Justice did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Here's some of the ways chaos and uncertainty have shaped the 2026 midterms: California In the Golden State, the Trump administration asked state election officials to set aside ballots from roughly 20,000 registered voters whom the DOJ suspects are noncitizens. A federal judge rejected that push Wednesday night, warning that the administration lacked sufficient evidence to justify potentially disenfranchising eligible voters. The judge noted that the DOJ had made similar claims in neighboring Nevada, where election officials determined that 185 voters the DOJ had flagged as noncitizens were actually U.S. citizens. Diaz told Axios that, from his perspective as a voting-rights advocate, the California battle is "not a real lawsuit. It's a political press release that they just happened to submit to the court." The other side: The White House directed questions about the ruling to remarks Trump made Thursday, in which he said "California is very corrupt," and the state's elections are "extremely corrupt." He did not provide evidence for his claims. Washington On Monday, the two U.S. attorneys' offices in Washington state asked the state to set aside ballots from more than 400 people they allege were illegally registered to vote. The letter mirrors similar demands sent to California before the Trump administration sued. Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs fired back Wednesday, tearing into the U.S. attorneys for making the request so close to Election Day and calling the timing "profoundly disappointing." Hobbs said a preliminary investigation confirmed that the federal list includes U.S. citizens and is unreliable. He asked prosecutors to provide individualized proof of ineligibility. North Carolina Nearly 4,000 mail-in ballots, or about 6%, processed in North Carolina through Oct. 24 have been flagged for problems that, if not fixed, could invalidate voters' choices. Time is running out for those voters to address the issues, and hundreds have yet to respond to notifications about their ballots. The rejections appear to stem in part from new guidance issued by the GOP-controlled state Board of Elections requiring the inner ballot envelope to be sealed, even if the outer envelope is already sealed. Alaska In Alaska's Senate race , two men named Dan Sullivan are on the ballot, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan. New reporting from The New York Times on Wednesday alleged that aides to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola helped recruit the other Dan Sullivan in an apparent attempt to confuse voters and siphon votes away from the incumbent senator. Peltola's campaign denies any involvement. Alaska Gov. Sir Patrick Stewart: The life of a legendary actor
Legendary Star Trek actor Sir Patrick Stewart has died, aged 86. Stewart died at his home in Los Angeles on 28 October after suffering with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia, according to a statement shared on his social media.
âHis sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,â the statement reads.
In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick won multiple Emmys and Golden Globes, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.

- Published
Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86, was a stage and screen great who balanced Hollywood stardom with an equally stellar career in classical theatre.
While many actors are typecast, he moved effortlessly from Shakespeare and Dickens to the command of the USS Enterprise and his famous wheelchair in X-Men.
In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick received multiple awards, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.
One of the world's most versatile actors, he mastered both comedy and tragedy, science-fiction and historical drama - despite the entertainment industry's traditional dislike of bald heads.
Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield in the West Riding of Yorkshire on 13 July 1940.
His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.
His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had shredded his mental health.
"My father was a very potent individual," Stewart later recalled. "It was said that when he strode on to the parade ground, birds stopped singing."
But Alfred Stewart had become a quick-tempered man, suffering from what would now be called post traumatic stress.
He was prone to drink and often took out his frustrations on his family - although Patrick himself was never the target of his fists.
Young Patrick's love of drama developed at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.
He found the predictability of dramatic performances a welcome change form the turmoil of his home life.
He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a journalist and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.
He also threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."
But he found it impossible to concentrate on both his job and his acting. Eventually his editor told him to choose between journalism and the "foolhardy" acting.
Stewart picked up his typewriter and walked out.
At the age of 18, he had the traumatic experience of losing all his hair, a huge blow to an aspiring actor and self-conscious teenager - who worried that girls would no longer find him attractive.
He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company - playing a variety of roles across the company's repertoire.
And when not appearing as Oberon or Enobarbus, he made his TV debut as a fireman in a 1967 episode of soap opera Coronation Street.
His Broadway debut came in 1970 as Snout in Peter Brook's critically acclaimed production of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Over the next two decades, Stewart appeared in a variety of television roles without threatening to become a major star.
In 1974, he played Lenin in the BBC's 13-part drama series The Fall of Eagles.
He was a conspiratorial Roman soldier in the hugely popular I, Claudius and a Soviet spy in Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy and Smiley's People.
In 1984, Stewart left the RSC and moved to the National Theatre. Now in his mid-40s, he had only ever been unemployed for three weeks, but was rarely cast as a main character.
He'd landed a number of minor film roles: including playing Guinevere's father in Excalibur, a minstrel in Dune, and a riding instructor in Little Lord Fauntleroy.
And he was the voice of a small character in the animated film of Richard Adams' novel The Plague Dogs.
But even he described the first half of his career as "sound but never spectacular".
Then came the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
A producer named Robert L Justman was intent on reviving the Star Trek franchise, and was looking for a successor to William Shatner's legendary James T Kirk.
He had hoped to find a sexy, hirsute Frenchman to play the role - but chanced upon Stewart giving a lecture to his wife's Shakespeare class in Los Angeles.
Justman turned to his wife. "I said I think I've found our new captain," he said.
Stewart was intrigued but dubious.
He knew nothing about the original Star Trek and his great friend Sir Ian McKellen, told him not to throw his stage career away on a wild goose chase into space.
But in need of a boost to his finances, Stewart signed a six-year contract, firmly believing the show wouldn't last and he'd be back on the boards before long.
"Everybody told me it would be a flop," he recalled. "A friend of mine said, 'Get a suntan, make some money, go home.'"
He was, however, pleased that the producers didn't mind his baldness.
He'd tried wearing a wig in early screen tests, but it looked ratty and - in the end - Star Trek's founder Gene Roddenberry told him to ditch it.
"In the 24th Century, they wouldn't care if Picard was bald," he said.
Stewart, who was billed by the New York Times as "an unknown British Shakespearean actor", found it hard adapting to his new job.
After his stage experiences, he found the 20 hours a day on set tiring, and he also struggled to work with a fairly laid-back and fun-loving US cast.
His decision to call his fellow actors together and give them a lecture about behaving more seriously failed to gain him popularity.
"It was really awful, being dressed down by the captain," said Brent Spiner, who played Data, the android. "We really thought, 'Well, please, get over it'."
Eventually Stewart softened, insisting that every member of the cast told at least one joke a day.
Despite his initial scepticism, Star Trek: The Next Generation both survived and prospered - making its star a very wealthy man.
Captain Picard was supposed to be French, but displayed a surprisingly English regard for both Shakespeare and Earl Grey tea.
And, after playing all those Shakespearean princes and dukes on the London stage, Stewart became fiercely proud of him, and of the show's ability

The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" â which some American journalists will be invited to witness â the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson â an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months

9e4e991dc3fd.text: Alaska's tight Senate race is facing a new controversy over two candidates named Dan Sullivan appearing on the ballot — a twist that's drawn attention from President Trump . The big picture: The controversy is adding uncertainty to one of the nation's most competitive Senate contests, with control of Congress on the line in next week's midterm elections. Catch up quick: The New York Times reported this week that Democratic operatives with ties to Mary Peltola's Senate campaign helped recruit a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan to challenge Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan. Trump accused Peltola and Democrats of election fraud and called for criminal prosecution, though the Times did not establish that any laws were broken. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered an investigation into Peltola's campaign over the NYT report. House Republicans are also launching an Alaska Senate race probe. Though the presence of two Sullivans in the Senate race has been known for months, the Times' report adds a new wrinkle to a dispute that's already reached the courts. Here's what to know about the controversy. The same-name Senate race controversy The controversy centers on two candidates with nearly identical names appearing on Alaska's Senate ballot: Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan and unaffiliated challenger Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. The ballot will show registered Republican "Sullivan, Dan S." and unaffiliated candidate "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." Peltola and Republican Gerald Heikes will also be on the ballot. The challenger initially filed as a Republican but later changed his registration to undeclared. He will appear on the ballot without a party label. Flashback: Concerns about the duplicate names have existed for months. In June, a top Alaskan election official ruled that candidate Daniel J. Sullivan was ineligible to run on the state's primary ballot. The official said she found the candidacy was "filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality," per the Associated Press. The Alaska Supreme Court later ruled that state election officials lacked the authority to disqualify Sullivan based on their concerns about his motives, allowing him to appear on the ballot. The court did not determine whether his candidacy was intended to mislead voters. Trump reacts to Alaska controversy Flashback: Last week, the Justice Department sued Alaska, seeking to block certification of the Senate election if the incumbent loses by a margin potentially attributable to voters confusing the two Sullivans. Both Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have asked a federal judge to dismiss the case. Alaska officials are seeking dismissal of the lawsuit, arguing that it has no legal basis and that the federal government lacks authority to intervene in a matter governed by state election law. Zoom in: The new NYT report , published this week, cited texts, interviews and documents showing that Peltola's aides worked with Democratic operatives to recruit candidates who could siphon votes from the Republican senator. Per the report, a staffer was told to review every "Dan Sullivan" in the state, leading the team to Dan J. Sullivan, the retired schoolteacher who was registered as a Republican. Peltola's campaign and the DSCC denied recruiting Sullivan, per NYT. The latest: The NYT report sparked a reaction from Trump this week, who wrote on Truth Social that the recruitment by Peltola's campaign was done "in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election," in his call for Peltola and the other Sullivan to be prosecuted. Gov. Dunleavy ordered a state investigation on Oct. 28 into the allegations, and House Oversight Chair James Comer launched a congressional probe on Oct. 29. What they're saying: "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight," a spokesman for the Peltola campaign tells Axios. "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." The other side: In a statement to Axios, Nate Adams, a spokesman for Dan S. Sullivan, accused Peltola, her advisers and Democratic operatives of coordinating with the DSCC to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse voters. "We always knew this was a coordinated effort to mislead Alaskans, and Mary Peltola was counting on it staying buried until after the election. Now that she's been caught red-handed, she still won't come clean," Adams said. "Instead, she's doubling down on the lie and is now attacking the same media outlets she's been misleading for months." How Sullivan confusion could affect the Alaska race Why it matters: Alaska's ranked-choice voting system could limit the impact of voter confusion for the two Sullivans. How it works: Ranked-choice voting allows voters to rank multiple candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-place votes, the lower-performing candidates are eliminated and their supporters' votes go to the next-ranked choice. If Dan J. Sullivan is eliminated, ballots listing the incumbent as the next remaining choice would transfer to him. But voters who mistakenly select Dan J. Sullivan without ranking the incumbent could still cost the Republican votes in a close race. By the numbers: Dan J. Sullivan received 2.5% of the vote in Alaska's August primary, compared with 41.4% for the incumbent and 49.5% for Peltola.

77cbe8745971.text: By — Mark Kennedy, Associated Press Mark Kennedy, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/patrick-stewart-star-of-stage-and-star-trek-dies-at-86 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Patrick Stewart, star of stage and 'Star Trek,' dies at 86 Arts Updated on Oct 29, 2026 4:52 PM EDT — Published on Oct 29, 2026 4:02 PM EDT Patrick Stewart, the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises, has died. He was 86. Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following "a brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart's diagnoses had not been previously disclosed. WATCH: Patrick Stewart reflects on his life and legendary career in new memoir, 'Making It So' While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the "X-Men" and "Star Trek: The Next Generation" series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of "A Christmas Carol" and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter's "No Man's Land" and Samuel Beckett's "Waiting for Godot" in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen. He achieved some of the best reviews of his career when he finally tackled Macbeth for the first time. The production, under the direction of Rupert Goold, debuted in May 2007 at England's Chichester Festival Theatre, switched to London's West End and then moved to the Brooklyn Academy of Music before transferring to Broadway in 2008. Stewart's performance earned him his sole Tony Award nomination. The Times of London said his Macbeth was "an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humor." The Daily Telegraph said he had turned in "a truly great performance" and The New York Times said it was "a must-see." "Nearly 50 years I've waited," Stewart told The Associated Press in 2008. "I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn't have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job." Starship commander grew up without a toilet Raised in Mirfield in Yorkshire, a working class corner of northern England, the future 24th century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house. Stewart joined an amateur drama group at 12 and memorized Shakespeare for fun as a teen. He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, launching a career as a character actor. He had been bald since he was 19 — alopecia runs in his family. His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of "repeated violence against my mother," as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. "Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it." In his memoir, "Making It So," Stewart wrote about how he and his older brother Trevor braced for the nights when their dad came home drunk and angry, and attacked their mother. "Sometimes it was with an open hand, other times a closed fist. Always he aimed for her head." The son would later become a patron for Refuge, an organization that provides shelter for domestic abuse victims. Loving Shakespeare proved fruitful as Capt. Picard "The stage would prove to be a safe space, a refuge from real life in which I could inhabit another person, living in another place and time," he would write. Stewart was accepted into the Royal Shakespeare Company and stayed for 14 years, playing everything from Mark Antony to Henry IV to Shylock to Oberon. "People who were not in the company would say to me, 'Give it a break. Why don't you go somewhere else?' And I would say, 'To do what?'" he told the AP. "Telly?" Stewart eventually left to look for more varied work, including the 1981 film "Excalibur." He had just done a production of "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?" in 1987 when an interesting offer came along. "I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail." It didn't, of course. Thanks to Stewart's rich baritone and noble bearing, the "Star Trek" franchise ran for seven years, 178 episodes and produced four feature films. He was known for his slogan "Make it so." His adoration for Shakespeare would serve him well when he began to play Jean-Luc Picard, a 24th century starship commander. "There is a formality to the way they speak and comport themselves that remind me of numerous Shakespearean situations I'd been in onstage. I should play Jean Luc, I realized, as if he were a character in 'Henry IV,' which is about brave men," Stewart wrote in his memoir. Despite the Borg and Klingons, Stewart still managed to make room for blank verse. He established the Paramount Shakespeare Company, a workshop on Saturday and Sunday mornings for any actor interested. (Stewart revisited Picard in the TV series "Star Trek: Picard.") Stewart died just a few days after Walter Koenig, another "Star Trek" icon, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov on the original NBC TV show from 1966 to 1969. The show gave him higher visibility, which led to more work, including roles in the films "Conspiracy Theory," "L.A. Story" and on Broadway, where he starred in "The Tempest," "The Caretaker" and David Mamet's "A Life in the Theater." He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in June 2010. Stewart was also an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee. A brave and commanding persona. But sexy? In July 1992, he and supermodel Cindy Crawford were on the cover of TV Guide's "Top Turn-Ons," based on a readers' poll. In his memoir, Stewart wrote: "Absurd." 7a625e82e517.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-blocks-trump-administrations-medicaid-work-requirement-rule-forcing-proof-of-medical-frailty Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge blocks Trump administration's Medicaid work requirement rule forcing proof of medical frailty Politics Oct 29, 2026 3:53 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Chronically ill people on Medicaid won't be bound by new work requirement rules that the latest Trump administration guidance requires in order to qualify for "medically frail" exemptions, a federal judge ruled Thursday. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston gave a partial victory to a coalition of 25 states and the District of Columbia, which sued the Trump administration in June over the new Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services guidance linked to the 2025 law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill." READ MORE: As states face stricter Medicaid work requirements, Nebraska is an early test The law says the definition of medically frail must include people who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders, have certain disabilities that significantly impair daily activities, or have serious or complex medical conditions. But the CMS rule went further, requiring people in those categories to show that their conditions also "significantly impair" their ability to comply with the law's work requirements. The plaintiffs argued that the stricter rule would prevent eligible Americans from accessing the care they need — and oversteps the text of the law itself as well. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The states have met their burden of showing irreparable harm for which monetary damages would provide inadequate compensation — they face the burden of costly and intensive alterations to their eligibility verification systems," Stearns said in his 16-page ruling. Notably, while the ruling will make it easier for some Medicaid recipients with qualifying medical conditions to obtain an exemption from the new work requirements, Stearns' decision does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful. Additionally, Stearns upheld two other federal restrictions on how states can verify medical frailty: including the requirement that states reject proof of patients' medical frailty if the diagnosis is more than a year old. He also upheld a policy allowing states to accept only one self-attestation per continuous period of enrollment. Explaining why he upheld the portions in favor of the government, Stearns said "the government provided a non-frivolous rationale for adopting each provision and explained why it did not find the States' concerns of disenrollment compelling." Representatives from the Department of Health and Human Services and CMS did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment. The new Medicaid restrictions are part of Trump's big tax and policy law in 2025. The change affects those covered through an expansion in most states that gave more lower-income people access to the government's safety net healthcare program. Starting Jan. 1, expansion enrollees aged 19 to 64 must show that they work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or are in school at least half the time. There are exceptions for those considered medically frail or in addiction treatment programs, among others. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. With less than a week to go until the US midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress for the next two years, more than 43 million Americans have already voted.
Data from the University of Florida Election Lab indicates that four to five million early votes have been cast each day, representing a much higher rate than in most previous elections.
Texas has seen the highest above-average turnout rate so far, says Prof Mike McDonald, who runs the Election Lab database. Hispanic communities are also seeing a much higher turnout than usual.
Overall turnout appears on track to outpace 2020, or even 2018, which beat the 1914 record for overall turnout in a midterm election.
Texas has already surpassed its 2022 numbers by around 1.75 million voters, says McDonald. More than 5.8 million ballots have already been cast in the Lone Star state, which has emerged as a key battleground that could decide which party controls the Senate for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.
Data from states that require voters to register a political affiliation indicates an increase is votes cast by Democrats, while Republican early voting numbers remain generally similar to 2022.
Early voting is also up among voters who chose to not register with a specific party, McDonald says, however the data does not show which candidates they chose.
Figures on Thursday, external show that 44% of early ballots have been cast by Democrats, and 31.2% by Republicans. A further 24.7% were attributed to voters who had no party affiliation. However, that's just for the roughly half of states that require voter affiliation.
Three states require voters to submit their race when they register - North Carolina, Georgia and Florida. Data from these states shows an increase in votes cast by Hispanic and black communities, while voting among white people is on par with 2022 early voting figures.
"That makes sense because communities of colour are more frequently part of the Democratic coalition, and whites are more frequently part of the Republican coalition," McDonald says.
Texas does not require voters to provide party affiliation or race. But the data still shows a surge in voting by some counties on the border with Mexico, which are comprised of more than 90% Hispanic people.
"When I look at those counties, what I see is some of them are going to beat their 2022 turnout in just the early vote alone," says McDonald.
Early voting has boomed in recent years, driven by the Covid pandemic when more states began offering early voting options, including both in-person and by mail.
In the 2020 election, when voters were picking both the next president as well as their lawmakers, more than two-thirds of all ballots were cast early. Half of those early votes were also cast by mail.
Voters increasingly prefer to vote in-person, even when voting early, says McDonald. They are also returning their ballots earlier than in previous elections.
He adds that he believes this could be due to concerns about postal voting, but says there is not data to indicate what could be causing this. Postal votes are more likely to be disqualified due to errors, he notes, and says some voters could be concerned about meddling in the US Postal Service.
Some officials have already confirmed records being broken. On Thursday, the city of Minneapolis said that it has set an early voting record for a non-presidential election.
Early voting will soon taper off, as states start cutting off early voting as an option in the days before the election on Tuesday, 3 November.

Republicans wonât attach their names to this prediction, but many of them expect Tuesdayâs midterms to hand Democrats at least one chamber of Congress. And theyâre already bracing for President Donald Trumpâs healthcare agenda to get bogged down by a divided government.
The slowdown could happen in a number of ways, GOP aides working on health policy told me â depending on how big an election night Democrats have. At a minimum, Republicans anticipate that a new House majority will haul Trump administration health officials into oversight hearings on a litany of topics, like the still-growing measles outbreak, the presidentâs slashing of global health aid, and the implementation of Medicaid work requirements.
Those hearings would be designed to trip up administration officials. But even if they donât yield embarrassing headlines, Republicans are prepared for healthcare policymaking to get hairier. âPreparing for oversight and obstruction from Democrats will take 50% of our time and mean less ability to push for reforms and regulation,â a former GOP congressional staffer said.
Two top Trump health officials have left in the last week alone: Senior health adviser Calley Means and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Deputy Director Jennifer Shuford. The midterms could complicate the confirmation prospects of several others still awaiting their Senate votes, including Chris Klomp, tapped as No. 2 at HHS, and Heidi Overton, picked to lead the Food and Drug Administration.
The former Republican staffer put it bluntly: âGod forbid we lose the Senate â weâre not getting any nominees in.â
Even a tiny Senate GOP majority could hand outsized power over health confirmations to a single Republican, like abortion-access supporter Lisa Murkowski of Alaska or libertarian-leaning Rand Paul of Kentucky.
Healthcare bills with bipartisan potential, like measures on hospital price transparency or food labeling, might still find room to break through. But as one former health official told me, itâll be âmostly gridlock.â

5c7e5a4ad6d4.text: By — Tim Sullivan, Associated Press Tim Sullivan, Associated Press By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/how-trumps-immigration-crackdown-sparked-a-backlash-that-could-undermine-republicans-campaigns Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter How Trump's immigration crackdown sparked a backlash that could undermine Republicans' campaigns Politics Oct 29, 2026 3:23 PM EDT MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — When Donald Trump was running for president two years ago, Americans' television screens were filled with images of migrant chaos. There were tent camps on both sides of the border, caravans of people trudging through Central America and concerns about newcomers overwhelming social services. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. That turmoil faded as President Joe Biden tightened immigration enforcement after Trump clamped down even more. Now any chaos is on American streets, where violent and even deadly clashes have defined a deportation campaign that's designed to fulfill hardliners' goals of uprooting anyone in the country illegally. The shift helps explain why Trump's effort to fulfill his promises has turned into a backlash, undermining one of the core issues that fueled his return to the White House. While Trump maintains some support for his handling of the border, polling shows voters disapprove of his approach to immigration, a striking turnaround that could undermine Republican attempts to maintain control of Congress in the midterms. WATCH: How immigration policies shaped America and evolved throughout its history "The American people supported strong border security," said Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who has become a prominent critic of the administration's policies. "What they got instead was shredding the Constitution, mass deportations and killing American citizens on the streets of Minneapolis." Trump's allies say the president is the victim of his own success. "The disaster at the border and the impunity of people just walking over and being released into the country was hard to ignore," said Mark Krikorian, executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies. Trump dramatically reduced illegal border crossings, Krikorian said, "and that's often politically bad." Krikorian praised Trump for adopting low profile but highly effective sweeps that have achieved month after month of record arrests. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested almost 51,000 immigrants in the country illegally in August, according to the Department of Homeland Security, up from 49,000 in July and 43,000 in June. An estimated 660,000 people have been deported in the past fiscal year, according to the Migration Policy Institute, short of the administration's goal of 1 million annually. Biden's immigration policies remain a regular target for Republicans this year. Trump said at a recent Florida rally that Democrats let migrants "pour across our borders from all over the world." "If they win in the midterms, they'll do it again," he warned. Trump returned to White House with deportation pledge In 2024, Trump warned repeatedly of an immigrant "invasion." "They're poisoning the blood of our country," he said of people crossing the border illegally. He insisted, falsely, that immigrants were behind spikes in crime and eating household pets. Even as Trump drew criticism for his rhetoric, his focus on the issue resonated with voters who had seen illegal immigration soar during the Biden administration, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023. Trump's victory seemed poised to reshape immigration politics. Forty-six Democrats in the House and a dozen in the Senate joined Republicans in voting for the Laken Riley Act, a bill named after a Georgia student killed by a man in the country illegally. The law requires detention without bond for noncitizens accused of murder and other violent crimes. After Trump took office, he cranked deportations into higher gear. Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident, was one of the people caught up in that net. Despite a court order forbidding it, the administration sent him to his native El Salvador, where he was confined to that country's notorious central prison that was also used to house other Trump deportees. The U.S. Supreme Court directed the administration to "facilitate" Abrego Garcia's return, and Van Hollen flew to El Salvador to meet with him. Some Democrats questioned the wisdom of confronting Trump on an issue where the president was so popular, the senator recalled. Now his party is more emboldened on the issue. "We've gone from some of that sniping on the sidelines to a clear vote among Democrats to defund ICE," Van Hollen said. Minneapolis crackdown leads to backlash The early face of the Trump crackdown was top Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino, who swaggered through raids in tactical gear and deployed forces to Los Angeles and Chicago, where he led a helicopter raid on an apartment building. But Minneapolis was the turning point. More than 2,000 federal officers were sent to the city, and scenes of masked agents spilling from convoys of unmarked vehicles became commonplace. Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets. Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37 — were killed during confrontations with agents. In the weeks that followed, the White House pushed aside Bovino and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Michael Pretti, Alex's father, said this week that the family is still troubled by the bystander videos of the shooting. He had a holstered gun that he was legally allowed to carry, and none of the footage shows him brandishing the weapon or at

A man who had already been found guilty of firebombing a group of protesters advocating for the release of Israeli hostages in the US state of Colorado has now plead guilty to federal hate crime charges.
Prosecutors said Mohamed Sabry Soliman threw Molotov cocktails at the group of demonstrators in June 2025 - injuring at least 12 people, one of whom died.
He plead guilty in May to 101 state charges, including first-degree murder - resulting in a sentence of life in prison - but initially pleaded not guilty in the federal case.
Prosecutors want Soliman to be sentenced to life in prison plus 50 years over the federal charges, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
He is due to be sentenced in January.
United States Attorney Peter McNeilly said the sentencing recommendation was driven by what the victims wanted.
In light of the plea, McNeilly said Soliman had dropped motions seeking to keep his family from being deported from the US in case they needed to be witnesses in his case.
Authorities said Soliman planned the attack for a year, watching videos on explosives before driving from his home in Colorado Springs to the Boulder protest.
While he hurled the Molotov cocktails at the crowd on 1 June, 2025, he shouted "Free Palestine". The group were members of Run for Their Lives in Colorado, which met weekly to support the release of Israeli hostages taken by Hamas during the 7 October attacks.
Karen Diamond, 82, died from injuries caused by the attack three weeks later. Her family said her husband, Lou, was also severely burned and had to recover for a month in a hospital burn unit.
Soliman, an Egyptian national, told police after he was arrested that he wanted to "kill all Zionist people", according to court documents.
He came to California in 2022 on a non-immigrant visa that expired in February 2023, according to CBS.
The firebombing escalated concerns about antisemitic violence in the US, taking place shortly after a fatal shooting outside a Jewish centre in Washington DC.

A Toronto jury has found self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski guilty of fraud, after hearing evidence he stole millions of dollars of investor money and spent it on private jets and other luxuries.
The jury quickly reached its verdict on Thursday, convicting the 27-year-old with one count of fraud over C$5,000 ($3,600; Â£2,900), after just hours of deliberation.
Throughout trial, Crown prosecutors called over a dozen witnesses, including investors whom Pleterski had cheated, and accountants and financial experts who testified on his scheme.
Pleterski pleaded not guilty and represented himself at his trial, cross-examining only one witness. He presented no evidence and did not testify.
The Canadian man was charged in May 2024 with one count each of fraud and money laundering following a 16-month joint investigation between Durham Regional Police and the Ontario Securities Commission.
The laundering charge was later dropped.
At the time, Durham Regional Police Chief Peter Moreira said it was potentially the biggest-ever fraud case in the region.
During Pleterski's trial in Ontario's Superior Court, Crown prosecutors presented ample evidence of his lavish spending using investor funds, according to local media.
He is believed to have taken more than C$36m from investors, and spent about half.
They said he used the money sent to his company AP Private Equity Limited to buy multiple trips on private jets and spend about C$5.6m on luxury vehicles.
Prosecutors also said he used the money to spend C$45,000 a month on a lakefront mansion in Burlington, Ontario, while racking up C$4.9m in credit card bills.
Bankruptcy proceedings had shown Pleterski also bought a McLaren and BMW for his parents - who had given him C$50,000 as a crypto investment - along with a Louis Vuitton bag, Burberry coat and a 2017 Bentley Bentayga.
Crown prosecutor Akshay Aurora said during closing arguments on Wednesday that "Pleterski was no 'Crypto King'".
"He was a thief. A thief who stole investor money and used it as he pleased," Aurora told the jury, according to CBC News.
Things came crashing down for Pleterski ahead of his May 2024 arrest.
In December 2022, he was kidnapped in the middle of the night in downtown Toronto, with his captors demanding a large sum for his release.
"I'm sorry, I really am, I didn't want to or mean to ruin anyone's life," a bruised and bloodied Pleterski said in a video obtained by CBC News.
He was released three days later, after being tortured, including with waterboarding, cigarette burns and beatings with golf clubs.
He returns to court on 13 November for a sentencing hearing.

Army pilots are trying virtual reality to stay more alert in flight
The 101st Combat Aviation Brigade is testing the NeuroTrainer as a possible readiness tool for their aviators.
The 101st Combat Aviation Brigade is testing a virtual-reality headset to see if it can make helicopter pilots more alert.
For the next eight months, the unit will incorporate the Oculus-based NeuroTrainer into their flight-training regimen, to measure whether pilots’ reaction times improve.
“In the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade, our pilots operate in unpredictable environments where split-second decisions dictate mission success,” Col. Anthony Marston, the unit’s commander, told Defense One. “By putting our aviators through the targeted exercises using the NeuroTrainer, we want to see if it can measurably improve their processing abilities.”
Pilots will do three headset sessions a week, playing two games for at least six minutes. One game requires them to catch orange balls while dodging projectiles, and the other challenges them to identify a robot teammate outside of their immediate field of view, then swat a ball in that teammate’s direction.
“All the VR-based exercises are designed to challenge and improve reaction time, situational awareness, and quick-decision making,” said Capt. Drew Lightsey, a spokesman for the 101st CAB.
During the initial phase of the program, unit pilots will do a round on the NeuroTrainer and then get in a helicopter simulator to measure their cognition, a news release said.
“It had a little bit of a learning curve to start,” said Chief Warrant Officer 2 Eric Low, a CH-47 Chinook maintenance test pilot. “Once you start to get the hang of it, it felt like a video game. I like how it challenged different aspects of hand-eye coordination and the ability to track multiple objects at the same time.”
The second phase begins at week 15, when 70 pilots will be evaluated on their long-term results.
“Evaluators will consider the speed at which aircrews perform emergency procedures in the simulator and a qualitative assessment asking open-ended survey questions on how participants felt they improved after using the system over time,” Lightsey said.
Down the line, the NeuroTrainer could become a tool for pilots to use on days when they aren’t flying, or for staff pilots who don’t fly frequently but need to keep their skills sharp.
“I think this device could bring awareness to some of the underlying issues affecting our pilots,” said Victor Rodriguez, cognitive performance specialist for the 101st CAB’s Holistic Health and Fitness program. “The performance results could help us recognize when to discuss stress, oversaturation, or emotional regulation with them to help them improve.”
The press release said that similar headset tests are taking place at Navy Fighter Weapons School, Air Force Special Operations Command, and the 75th Ranger Regiment.

dbd4958f3611.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press By — Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-justice-department-pushes-a-spate-of-politically-sensitive-cases-as-midterm-elections-near Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump's Justice Department pushes a spate of politically sensitive cases as midterm elections near Politics Oct 29, 2026 2:03 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — A crucial and contentious midterm election arrives next week, and President Donald Trump's Justice Department has been scrambling with a blitz of headline-making actions and cases that defense lawyers, Democrats and other critics say is no coincidence and reeks of politics — in both the timing and the targets. READ MORE: Trump administration charges former FBI Director James Comey for the third time This month alone, the Justice Department escalated an investigation into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar with a search of her home; brought criminal charges against two former FBI officials accused of falsely downplaying their knowledge of investigations involving Hunter Biden; revealed a fresh attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey; and made an unsuccessful attempt to indict a former White House aide who delivered dramatic but disputed testimony about Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election. That's on top of lawsuits in Alaska and California related to next week's voting. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
