d20c526d9b5e.text: By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/doordash-offers-17-billion-for-instacart-in-what-would-be-big-grocery-delivery-consolidation Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter DoorDash offers $17 billion for Instacart in what would be big grocery delivery consolidation Economy Oct 29, 2026 6:41 PM EDT DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart in a deal that could consolidate the grocery delivery business in the U.S. and abroad. The companies say the tie-up would combine DoorDash's global reach and expertise in logistics with Instacart's purpose-built technology and long relationships with grocers. It could also help the companies better compete with rivals like Amazon. READ MORE: Instacart ends program where users see different prices for the same item at same store But it could also lead to less competition in the delivery space, which could raise prices for consumers and give grocers fewer partners to negotiate with. "They were competing for a share of consumers' wallet," said Randall Sargent, a partner specializing in grocery and retail at the consulting firm Oliver Wyman. "As a general economic principle, less competition and more consolidation tends to be worse for consumers." The deal is expected to be finalized by the end of 2027 or in early 2028 if it's approved by Instacart shareholders and government regulators. Instacart's name and app will remain Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app would remain, and Instacart's 600,000 shoppers — who are independent contractors — would be able to continue fulfilling orders as before. Consumers who are currently paying $9.99 per month for separate DashPass and Instacart+ memberships, which give them free delivery on most orders and other perks, would be able to pay one fee instead of two, DoorDash said. Instacart customers would also have access to 50,000 additional stores that are on DoorDash's platform. Grocers would also be able to choose either delivery platform. Tony Xu, DoorDash's co-founder and CEO, said the deal could help local grocers compete with larger players. Walmart is the largest U.S. grocer, with 21% share of spending, followed by Costco and Amazon, which each have 8% share, according to Numerator, a market research company. "Over the past decade or even two decades, what you see is the largest companies are only eating more and more of the pie. Why is that? It's because they've invested aggressively into capabilities like a modern technology stack, like fast delivery, like new fulfillment models," Xu said Thursday during a conference call with investors. "That's what this combination is really about, where DoorDash and Instacart can give every retailer a fighting chance at competing in the modern-day era." The deal would also help DoorDash and Instacart fend off rivals like Walmart, which has been moving into restaurant delivery. Walmart partnered with Subway, its largest in-store restaurant tenant, this past summer and has since expanded to select locations at Dunkin' and Papa Johns. The company said it now has 2,400 restaurant locations on its restaurant delivery platform. DoorDash has been growing its grocery business DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food, electronics and many other products. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. That dwarfs Instacart, which fulfilled 338 million orders last year. DoorDash has a market value of $73 billion. DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores. The partnership expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco. DoorDash's move into grocery has hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash's share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats' share held steady at just under 20%. Combined company could attract more ads, but also scrutiny Sargent said a combined DoorDash and Instacart could potentially attract more ad revenue from food companies. Right now, Instacart can only share what consumers put in their baskets, for example, but a combined company could also show them what customers ordered for takeout lunch. "Food companies want to spread their ad dollars around and reach customers efficiently," Sargent said. "The more you can hand them an audience that you know all about, the more formidable a challenger this new company is." But the tie-up will also be subject to scrutiny from antitrust regulators in the U.S. and elsewhere, particularly at a time when consumers are agitated about food price inflation. Ethan Litwin, an antitrust attorney and partner with New York-based Shinder Cantor Lerner, said it could be problematic if DoorDash controls Instacart's technology, since many grocers use that technology to power their online storefronts. "DoorDash could therefore cut rivals off, outmatch them on targeting and logistics, or monitor competitors' pricing and discounting in real time, which could facilitate coordination on pricing," Litwin said. "I expect that the parties will call these efficiencies, but an advantage big enough to build a monopoly will not stay consumer-friendly for long." Acquisition was discussed for a while Apoorva Mehta

81a0adef426b.text: As candidates make a final push to win over voters ahead of Election Day, Lisa Desjardins takes a deep dive into the battle for the House of Representatives. Geoff Bennett: And Lisa Desjardins joins us now at the super screen for a deeper dive into the battle for the House of Representatives. So, Lisa, this is an expensive contest for the House. Where does it all stand? Lisa Desjardins: Expensive and expansive. Look at this map of all the races. These are the 81 somewhat to very competitive races that we are tracking. Now, The Cook Political Report lists a lot of competitive races. It's important to also know this number, three. This is the magic number. Democrats need to flip three seats on net in order to take over the House. So I don't want to just look at this large map, but let's look at the most competitive seats that are toss-ups or leans. These 50 dots represent those 50 seats that may determine the fate of the House of Representatives. What's important here is who occupies them now. Look at this. It's mostly Republicans, 39 of these seats occupied by Republicans. They are on defense. Remember that magic number three? So, essentially Democrats need to pick up three seats right here -- this is the line -- in order to flip the House. Now, The Cook Political Report already forecasts that Democrats are likely to flip some seats. How many? Ten. So, if you remember this line that determines control of the House, Democrats have already put themselves in position to pass that. And, right now, Republicans need to push back. But they are in a good position at this moment, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: And on the substance of all these races, the economy is the top issue, per usual. But how and where is that playing out? Lisa Desjardins: Right. I love looking at this the substance. Let's talk first of all, about housing, that issue that we found in Northeastern Pennsylvania. These are the places where housing is particularly an issue in the campaign. You see it in Florida, in Nevada, in Southern California. But let's talk about the issue that a lot of Americans also feel, gas and fuel prices. It is everywhere, but I want to point out these races where they are particularly facing record high fuel prices, or like in Maine or Alaska, where they are more dependent on diesel or heating oil. And let's focus on one race in particular where this is a factor. Let's go to Colorado's Eighth District. This is a situation where the gas prices have still been rising this month. The Democrat, Manny Rutinel, says that the issue is Iran and tariffs. He says he had pushed back against President Trump. But the Republican, Gabe Evans, says, no, it's the problem of regulation, and he has supported President Trump. So this is a factor in this race. Geoff Bennett: And what about the other issues driving these midterm races? Lisa Desjardins: There's one more I want to talk about because a lot of the country is, and that is data centers. Here's an example of four of the races where that has become a campaign issue this year. And I want to focus on one. This is Central Michigan, Michigan's Seventh District. The Democrat, Will Lawrence, won his primary in part because he campaigned so hard on a ban, at least temporarily, on data centers. This is a district where we just saw a $10 billion data center put on hold because of protests from locals. Now, Tom Barrett, the Republican incumbent, he has a different tact. He instead says each locality should be able to decide whether they want the data center or not. This race is a good test of how far voters want to go when it comes to data centers. And all of these issues, of course, around the country do have ties to the economy. And it's important to see how that layers in. Geoff Bennett: Lisa Desjardins, our thanks to you, as always. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

cfbfc7ba37d7.text: Israel is facing political uncertainty after an election that produced no clear governing majority. But what do the results reveal about how Israelis want leaders to confront the country's challenges? Nick Schifrin discussed that with Tamir Hayman, former chief of Israeli military intelligence and current executive director of the Institute for National Security Studies. Geoff Bennett: Israel is once again facing political uncertainty after an election that has produced no clear governing majority amid competing allegations of voting fraud and irregularities. But beyond the political maneuvering, what do the results reveal about how Israelis want their leaders to confront the country's mounting challenges? For that, our Nick Schifrin spoke with retired Major General Tamir Hayman, former chief of Israeli military intelligence and current executive director of the Institute for National Security Studies. That's a leading Israeli think tank. Nick Schifrin: Tamir Hayman, thank you very much. Welcome to the "News Hour." Regardless of whether Benjamin Netanyahu stays prime minister or Gadi Eisenkot becomes prime minister, is there an overall agreement on how Israel should approach its national security since October the 7th? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): It seems like Israelis are still in the trauma after post-October 7, and they are reluctant on going to any kinds of concessions in the Palestinian-Israeli conflict. Most parties argue for a very hawkish, proactive approach in terms of the next state needed in confronting Hamas and Iran, et cetera, et cetera. So it seems like, in that aspect there's a proactive, hawkish military, security approach that is accepted, and we are not entering a zone of agreements or a peace-aspiring environment. Nick Schifrin: You write that pursuing peace is considered a danger, and -- quote -- "War is necessary and preventive war is preferable." Does that mean Israel is set to be in a perpetual state of war? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): Let me just emphasize that, in this article, I wanted to provoke a discussion, so I exaggerated a little bit in order to be able to observe trends. But it seems to be describing trends that are in the consensus. Nick Schifrin: And where Israel is going? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): And where Israel going, if not diverted. We are headed right now, brings us into very dangerous place. Nick Schifrin: Does Israeli leadership believe that a perpetual state of war is better? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): They do not believe that peace is a viable or tangible solution right now. Most Israelis will consider any form of a peace as weakness, naive approach, trusting the Arabs, trusting the enemies. The general sentiment is, we trusted the Arabs, and they betrayed us. So what left is an ongoing state of confrontation. Nick Schifrin: You describe, even if it's exaggerated, this severing with the United States. And, again, I will I will read it, knowing that you say it's exaggerated, but it's very provocative. "The United States is a declining power, and, given its ongoing social and political shifts, will soon abandon Israel. In any event, excessive dependence on the U.S. exposes Israel to the influence of a progressive American value system incompatible with Israel's Jewish character." I mean, it's an understatement to call that controversial among American Jews, but is that where we're headed? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): It seems like we are losing our position as a consensus among Americans, and we are losing the bipartisan approach. We have already lost the bipartisan position, and we are going to be maybe homeless in the political spectrum of United States. Secondly, the fact that we are dependent on our national security on capabilities and backing from United States create vulnerabilities. So, what is the rational outcome? We must rely on ourselves. Nick Schifrin: Netanyahu has referred to Israel as super Sparta, basically being self-reliant on weapons, as you have been describing. He's even suggested that Israel might have to rely on Bitcoin because of future sanctions. How isolated, in your opinion, is Israel? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The idea that if Israel will be ever isolated, it is an existential threat to the existence of Israel, OK? The economy is based on high-tech and an advanced science. That cannot be established in an isolation mode based on crypto. Second, there's a true threat of isolation and sanctions. But the way to handle it is to approach the causes of that. Nick Schifrin: But given the results of this election, even if we don't know exactly the numbers, in which Netanyahu and his bloc maintained the lead over the opposition bloc, doesn't that suggest that these trends are accelerating, that many Israelis have embraced these ideas that you're critiquing? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The political spectrum map is moving right. The problem is that there is radicalization in the right-wing establishment after October 7. Nick Schifrin: And back to the concept that you write about. And again, acknowledging that you say that you're exaggerating, there's one fundamental conclusion that you have, and that it's that the consensus is to -- quote -- "guarantee Israel's continued existence as a Jewish state, even at the cost of eroding its democratic values." Explain that in simple terms. Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The whole article asks critical question, whether it's good for Israel to move in that path. Of course, it is wrong. And that's what -- that's the whole purpose of this idea. Why do I emphasize the tension between democratic and Jewish values? Because if we're not going to do anything in the Palestinian arena, and we will annex the Palestinian territories, we will annex the West Bank into Israel, we will not have a Jewish majority. And the only way to maintain a Jewish statehood is by eroding democracy. This is an, again, existential threat to the identity of Israel as a Jewish democratic state

In less than two weeks, U.S. Senate leaders plan to take an initial vote on the divisive permitting reform bill aimed at easing regulatory barriers that can delay energy projects. As the date nears, some of the country’s leading environmental groups are ramping up their opposition, arguing that the measure would do more harm than good.
A new report from Resources for the Future, a research nonprofit, projects that the bill’s power-sector provisions would cut carbon emissions by 1.8 gigatons by 2041 and reduce annual electricity-system costs by an average of 3.5 percent to 7 percent compared to a scenario without the bill.
But the projected benefits are unlikely to convince the bill’s critics, partly because the analysis doesn’t address the provisions that have drawn the most opposition, including changes to the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
The debate over the bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, has divided environmental and clean energy advocates and threatens to unravel a compromise between the bill’s Democratic and Republican co-sponsors.
On one side, clean energy business groups and advocacy organizations praise the bill’s approach to accelerating timelines for building transmission lines and renewable energy projects. On the other side, key environmental advocacy groups say the proposal would speed up fossil fuel infrastructure buildout and remove current tools to oppose projects.
“Over the next two years, BAAJA would create more legal runway for this president to make corrupt deals and greenlight harmful projects of all kinds, and it would constrain any future president from repairing the damage,” said Abigail Dillen, president of Earthjustice, an environmental law nonprofit, in a commentary posted on Tuesday.
The same day, four Senate Democrats sent a letter to the bill’s co-sponsors saying they have concerns that President Donald Trump’s administration cannot be trusted to follow through on promises that were made during negotiations.
“Beyond consideration of the actual text, the promise of BAAJA will only succeed if President Trump takes care that it is faithfully executed,” reads the letter from Democratic Sens. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden, both of Oregon. “The Trump administration’s record gives us no basis to assume that he will.”
The senators cite the Trump administration’s cancellation of already-approved clean energy grants and loans and evidence that decisions were made with intent to harm states that voted for Democrats. They said the administration should reinstate all canceled awards and commit in writing to no longer basing grant decisions on the political affiliation of a state’s elected officials.
If the administration doesn’t comply, the senators have threatened to oppose a motion to proceed to debate on the bill at a vote scheduled for Nov. 9. Losing the support of four senators who have been vocal advocates for environmental protection could make it harder to secure the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster.
In a statement, a Trump administration spokesperson said the White House supports the bill because it will deliver jobs and investment.
“The text of the legislation has been published, and all that is left to do is vote,” the spokesperson said. “We are in direct conversations with the lead negotiators in the Senate and are looking forward to action on this historic legislation to unleash more energy in the United States.”
A co-sponsor of the bill, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, has also expressed concerns that the Trump administration will go to extraordinary lengths to oppose renewable energy even if the bill becomes law.
“We await real signs of regulatory good faith,” he said in a post on X, along with a link to a Bloomberg article about the administration’s recent contradictory actions on wind power.
Meanwhile, a coalition of conservative groups, many funded by the petrochemical billionaire Koch family’s network, urged the Senate this week to pass the bill to “protect property rights, promote energy abundance, and restore America’s ability to build.”
Emissions Cuts, But an Incomplete Picture
The new analysis by Resources for the Future follows several by other organizations that also show substantial cuts in emissions resulting from the power-sector provisions of the bill.
Resources for the Future is a leader using economic models to estimate the effects of complex legislation. Among the findings:
- The bill would increase the country’s transmission line capacity by 30 percent by 2041, meaning more power can be transported on interstate power lines. A lack of transmission capacity is one of the main factors impeding construction of new wind, solar and battery projects and more lines would allow more of those systems to be built.
- Building new, cleaner power sources would help displace some of the older, more polluting sources on the grid, adding 60 gigawatts of clean power capacity compared with a baseline scenario without the bill. The analysis also found that removing existing constraints would lead to a small increase in combined-cycle natural gas plants, though that effect would diminish over time.
- Power-sector carbon dioxide emissions would be lower under the bill than without the bill, although both scenarios show emissions growth over the study period. Adopting the bill would reduce cumulative carbon emissions by 1.83 gigatons through 2041. In the final year, emissions would be 6 percent less than the baseline level.

c50d26d44b33.text: Journalist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa chronicled her fight against the Duterte regime in the Philippines in her 2022 book, “How to Stand Up to a Dictator.” She detailed attacks on her reporting and her newsroom's struggle to defend press freedom and democracy. In a new book, Ressa warns of other threats to those same freedoms. Amna Nawaz spoke with Ressa about “The Fight Back." Geoff Bennett: Journalist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa chronicled her fight against the Duterte regime in the Philippines in her 2022 book, ""How to Stand Up to a Dictator." She detailed years of attacks in her reporting and her newsroom's struggle to defend press freedom and democracy. Now, in a new book, Ressa warns of different threats to those same freedoms. Amna Nawaz spoke with her earlier today. Amna Nawaz: According to Maria Ressa, there's a dual threat now by autocratic leaders and big tech companies weaponizing information and algorithms to create new crises for democracy and humanity. That's all in her new book called "The Fight Back: A Citizen's Guide to Standing Up to Dictators." And Maria Ressa joins me now. Welcome back. It's good to see you. Maria Ressa: Good to see you. Thanks for having me, Amna. Amna Nawaz: You talk in the book about what you call an unholy alliance between state power and platform power. What do you mean by that? Maria Ressa: A decade of harms from artificial intelligence, right? We're only talking about the tail end of it. But we have talked a lot about my two dictators in the Philippines. It was Rodrigo Duterte, who won as president in 2016 with the help of Facebook. And my second dictator, who I would argue is more powerful is Mark Zuckerberg, because, at that point, 93 percent of Filipinos on the Internet were on Facebook. Facebook is our Internet. And here's the part. They both act with impunity, but Rodrigo Duterte is now waiting at The Hague for his trial to begin, his charges of crimes against humanity, while, from 2016 to today, Mark Zuckerberg is still acting with impunity. He's not been elected for anything. And the three phases of harms that we have had from the attention economy, the tech that hacks our biology, right, when lies become facts, so the attention economy in social media, chatbots, and the harm, the intimacy that is taken from us, and the last one is agency itself with the agentic and multi-agentic world. Amna Nawaz: We have seen that battle for facts, battle for the truth play out here in the United States. As we talk here, we're days away from another critical midterm election. You break it down in the book to talk about the convergence of three crises, truth, order, and accountability. Maria Ressa: Yes. Amna Nawaz: How similar is all of this to what you saw under Duterte in the Philippines? And be specific to what we're seeing here in the U.S. now. Maria Ressa: What we lived through in the Philippines is that we found out we needed to leave the virtual world to come to the real world, right, and because I was getting an average of 98 messages per hour. When we came into the real world, that was how we had a whole-of-society approach that ultimately led to the arrest of Rodrigo Duterte. And then we had just recently Brazil. Brazil, if you remember, right, they have the same two dictators we had in the Philippines in 2016. President Trump, similar, right?The state and Meta, Mark Zuckerberg under a different name now. And what the -- after the first run-off elections, when it looked like President Lula was going to lose, I'd never sensed such a desperation in Brazilians. And they used WhatsApp to mobilize in the real world. And they mobilized the largest ever out, same thing that happened in Serbia. This time, the students, they moved from the virtual world to the real world. I don't see that same kind of desperation yet in America. But I do see an awareness that AI and, more importantly, data centers are something Americans don't want. And that seems to be bipartisan. But, having said that, this is the moment, right? The world is looking at America. What choices are you going to make? Amna Nawaz: You offer very specific, tangible steps at the end of each of your 10 chapters that you want people to try to follow just to be aware of the role that they play in the spread of misinformation... Maria Ressa: Yes. Amna Nawaz: ... in the maybe falling apart of accountability in many ways too. The very first chapter, step one, you say track your screen time for seven days. Maria Ressa: Yes, absolutely. Amna Nawaz: Why is that important for Americans to do? Maria Ressa: Because think about it. The more time you spend on here, the less time you spend in person with someone else. And this is not meant to educate you or to build real intimacy, real connections. This is done for power and profit. It's meant to keep you scrolling, right? And so that first step, how much of your life have you given to screens, to technology that is both extractive and predatory? And then the second step after that in chapter one is delete the app, one app on your phone, and hopefully it's the one that makes you angriest, because what the technology has done is to take the worst of us as people. And when you're angry, you stay scrolling the longest. So that gives more power and money to the tech company, but takes away from you, right? So that's -- these are the steps, 10 chapters, 10 steps at the end of every chapter. And at the end of it, I put 10 strategic goals to defend our rights, to protect our rights. But I had a debate with my publisher on this because they wanted me to put it in -- at the back cover of the book. I didn't want to do that because then you would look there first and you will look at it and you will say, oh, my God, that's like climbing Mount Everest. It isn't hard. And every step, one step at a time, I learned this in the Philippines. I think the other part is this. When you are the target, and each of us on these platforms are the t

HUNTSVILLE, Ala.—Candidates for Alabama’s second-highest office took the stage Wednesday for what was the first major-party debate for a statewide office since 2010, the year Republicans took the reins of government from Democrats for the first time in the modern era.
In a debate hosted by WHNT, a Huntsville-based television station, state Rep. Phillip Ensler, a Democrat, and former Republican Party Chairman John Wahl answered questions from moderators and engaged in significant back-and-forth for about an hour, including on a couple of environmental and energy issues.
One major sticking point in the debate was the impact of data centers on Alabamians, their communities and their energy bills.
Asked whether he believes data centers are good for Alabama, Wahl said he thinks the facilities are inevitable but that he shares the concerns of some residents about their impacts.
“Data centers are a necessary evil,” Wahl said. “We already have them. We all like our YouTube, our cloud, our streaming services. But the question is when these are moving into communities, we have to make sure that those communities are protected.”
The demand for data centers in Alabama and across the country has been driven largely by the spread of artificial intelligence tools like large language models, not by the use of services like YouTube or Netflix, according to experts. If built to full capacity, data center campuses proposed in Alabama would consume more energy than all of the homes in the state combined, an Inside Climate News analysis found.
“We want the capital investment,” Wahl said. “We need data centers, but we need to do it the right way.”
Ensler, the first statewide candidate to propose a moratorium on new data center construction, said he’s met with residents across the state who have made their views about the facilities clear.
“There are residents all over that are very concerned about the lack of transparency. They’re concerned about data centers being forced on their communities,” he said. “They’re concerned that Alabama Power is [jacking] up their prices.”
An Inside Climate News investigation found that Alabamians paid the highest average residential electricity bills in the nation in 2024, the latest year with complete data at the time.
Ensler has made data centers and concerns around Alabama Power, the state’s powerful electric utility, a focal point of his campaign. Ensler, from Montgomery, has visited Lowndes County, whose residents are fighting a proposed hyperscale data center, five times.
Hours before the debate, and in the days leading up to it, Ensler stood in solidarity with Fenn Church at his home in Shelby County. Church has been in a months-long legal dispute with Alabama Power over its use of eminent domain to lay transmission lines across his property.
“Alabama Power thinks they can just walk over anyone and everyone,” Ensler has said of the situation. “They’re just trying to flex their muscles and intimidate people, and if they can do that to him and do it here, they can do it anywhere.”
In a statement, a representative of Alabama Power said that the utility understands “that property is personal, and we remain committed to treating property owners fairly and respectfully.
“The Alabama Supreme Court’s decision allows work on this section of the transmission line to move forward, supporting a project that is an important investment in the security and reliability of the electric grid for the customers and communities we serve,” the emailed statement said.
Church had won a temporary victory against the utility in lower court earlier this year, receiving a preliminary injunction from a Circuit Court judge that prevented Alabama Power from accessing the property while the lawsuit moved forward.
Last Wednesday, the Alabama Supreme Court granted a motion from the utility to stay that decision. Since then, Fenn and the utility have been at a stalemate.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Church has said he’s attempted to have U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, the Republican candidate for governor, act as a mediator between himself and Alabama Power. But Ensler, Church said, is the only candidate who has come to his property to stand toe to toe with the utility.
“And I so appreciate him for it,” Church said. “It’s not about Republican or Democrat. It’s about what’s right.”
The topic of the Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator, arose at the debate when Wahl accused Ensler of supporting an effort to take away Alabamians’ right to vote for lieutenant governor by having the governor and lieutenant governor run as a ticket.
Alabama lieutenant governor is primarily charged with presiding over the state Senate. If the office of governor becomes vacant, the lieutenant governor assumes the state’s highest office.
Ensler and Doug Jones, the Democratic candidate for governor, have said they would support a state constitutional amendment that would have voters elect their governor and lieutenant governor on the same ticket, the method used by most states with both roles and similar to the way federal elections for president and vice president work.
“I think that’s a bad move,” Wahl said. “I don’t like it.”
Ensler responded that any changes like that would have to be approved by Alabama voters through a constitutional amendment. Ensler then brought up the Public Service Commission overhaul.
“Who has taken away the right to vote from people is Republicans who pushed a bill to change the Public Service Commission and take away people’s voices for a very important body at a time in which utility rates are going up,” Ensler said. “So if we’re concerned about taking away the voice of the people, that was done by Republicans when it comes to the Public Service Commission.”

b7e57a6b26be.text: Much of the debate over higher education today centers on cost, career prospects and whether a college degree can prepare students for a rapidly changing job market. But in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, one of the oldest skills taught on college campuses may be more valuable than ever. Paul Solman reports for our higher education series, Rethinking College. Geoff Bennett: Much of the debate over higher education today centers on cost, career prospects, and whether a college degree can prepare students for a rapidly changing job market. But in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, one of the oldest skills taught on college campuses may be more valuable than ever. Paul Solman reports for the next installment in our higher education series, Rethinking College. Paul Solman: Isolated by COVID, bombarded by social media, screen-swamped in general, and headed for an all-bets-are-off job market, no wonder today's students feel, to use a lament from my college days, as if they're up a tree, that is, precariously perched. Well, most of us remember from college learning to fend for ourselves by making friends outside the safe bubble of home and high school. But nowadays, with all the job pressure today's students face, is learning to socialize still as crucial? Jill Barry: I think, for me, it is one of the most important aspects, because when you're in college, you're meeting all these people of different backgrounds and you want to be able to use that knowledge once you graduate into a job. Paul Solman: Is it the single most important aspect of college, learning to live on your own, be with other people? Kosi Chugbo-Junius: Yes, I think it is like the single most important. 618a213a121d.text: Tap the kegs and break out the bratwurst, the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions! Milwaukee is the smallest market in the major leagues. But this year, the Brewers dominated the regular season, and then rolled through the playoffs with ruthless efficiency. To break it all down, Stephanie Sy spoke with Jason Gay, a sports columnist at The Wall Street Journal. Announcer: Two-one pitch, Palacios grounds one softly. Unshakable, unstoppable, and champions at last, the Milwaukee Brewers! (CHEERING) Geoff Bennett: Well, tap the kegs and break out the bratwurst. The Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions. The win is the first in the franchise's 58-year history. And, as Stephanie Sy tells us, it capped a campaign that was as improbable as it was inevitable -- Stephanie. Stephanie Sy: Yes, you can't forget the cheese curds, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: True. Stephanie Sy: The Brewers are the smallest market team in the Major Leagues, but this year they dominated the regular season and then rolled through the playoffs with ruthless efficiency, including an emphatic sweep of the defending champion Dodgers, a team with a payroll more than twice their size. To break it all down, we're joined now by Jason Gay, sports columnist at The Wall Street Journal. What a night for Milwaukee, right, Jason? I mean, you have called this World Series a triumph. And it has, of course, the irresistible makings of an underdog story with the Brewers outspent, but never outplayed this whole season. How did they do it? Jason Gay, The Wall Street Journal: They did it by reverting to some old-school baseball. They started playing what people know as small ball. They were running. They were hitting to opposite fields. They were even bunting. Bunting's really frowned upon in 2026. They could generate runs and they were relentless. You saw in this World Series, you saw against the Dodgers Milwaukee was never down and out. They were always coming back. This was a team really without a weakness. Their pitching was fantastic, and they were clutch all the way through. Stephanie Sy: And the series itself challenged the assumption that the highest paid players were necessarily going to always win, not only with the Dodgers being bested, but Tampa Bay beating the Yankees on their way through the World Series. What does that say to you? Jason Gay: It says that the high school Bullies were vanquished in the corridor before this World Series. I mean, you had two powerhouse franchises with massive payrolls knocked out embarrassingly by, again, these sort of plucky, well-managed, smart, strategic teams. And what was fun about this World Series, we didn't get the seven-game trauma, which is always great. But you had in the Rays and in the Brewers, of course, the opportunity to see a team that had never won this win this. And that's what we saw on Wednesday night. Stephanie Sy: For all the celebrations, no doubt happening in Milwaukee right now, there's a storm brewing over the MLB, as you know. The players and owners are headed toward a potential lockout with owners wanting these player salary caps. How does this World Series outcome weigh in on either side of this debate over salary caps? Jason Gay: Well, in a funny way, it's kind of a nightmare for baseball ownership, which very much wants a salary cap. They want the ceiling, they want a floor, maybe, but they definitely want a ceiling in the same way you have in basketball, football, other sports. When a team like the Rays comes forward, when a team like the Brewers comes forward and does it on a shoestring budget, it gives ammunition to the players to say, hey, look we don't need a cap. You guys just need to be better managed. You just have to be smarter with your money. What do we need a cap for? I still think that the ownership is going to be very, very adamant about getting that cap. And we could see a lockout situation, which really would be a terrible setup for the league. Stephanie Sy: Well, I know this is a story you're going to be following in coming weeks. Jason Gay with The Wall Street Journal, thank you. Jason Gay: Thank you.

e6cbde931621.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/senate-is-skeptical-about-making-daylight-saving-time-permanent-despite-trumps-pressure Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump's pressure Politics Oct 29, 2026 6:19 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, defying President Donald Trump and dashing the hopes of Americans who don't like having to change their clocks twice a year. As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice. Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn't see the sun until after 9 a.m. READ MORE: Daylight saving time is coming to an end again. Here's how the time change may impact you "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump's ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to "GET IT DONE!" But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard. READ MORE: America already tried permanent daylight saving time. Could it work now? Several other Republicans, particularly those from some Northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it. "You'd be sending kids to school in the dark," said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. Trump's pressure campaign hasn't worked Trump has aggressively pushed the change, putting pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the House bill and send it to his desk. In the posts targeting Cotton earlier this month, Trump wrote that sunshine is better in the afternoon than the morning and "CRIMINALS DON'T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT." He renewed his call in a social media post this week, writing on Truth Social that "United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it." An avid golfer, Trump has made clear that adding daylight hours would mean more time to hit the links. He has argued that changing the time can be dangerous, especially when "you have high and dangerous steeples to reach, like on churches and municipal buildings." WATCH: Ditch the switch? Senators debate future of daylight saving time Even as many Americans now rely on digital clocks that change on their own, Trump said that "nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year." The president's arguments don't appear to have changed many votes in the Senate, however. Cotton has doubled down in response to Trump's pressure, and several Republicans predicted in recent weeks that the bill won't come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election. Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said that it's his understanding that the House bill is a "non-starter" for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon. "No way," Moreno said. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn't weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past. Previous laws have been repealed In the winter of 1973, amid an energy crisis, Congress passed a law instituting permanent daylight saving time for what was supposed to be a trial period. But it was repealed by that October as public support had sharply dropped, partly because of concern for children who were walking to school in the dark. Now more than 50 years later, fewer Americans recall that experiment. Like Trump, many want to ditch the twice-yearly time change and add more daylight hours later in the day. An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of the current system, while almost half opposed it. Proponents of a single time include the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine. Florida Sen. Rick Scott signed legislation when he was governor in 2018 that would allow the state to remain on daylight saving time year round, pending federal approval. Now in the Senate, the Republican has led efforts to make that happen. "I hear from Americans constantly that they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year — it's an unnecessary, decades-old practice that's more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them," Scott said. Several Democrats are on board, as well. "The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness," said Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, when Scott introduced his own bill last year. "Let's say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets." Associated Press writer Darlene Superville contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press

Google parent Alphabet lost just over $500bn (Â£374bn) in value on Thursday after it rattled Wall Street with its last update of the year on its business operations.
Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its artificial intelligence (AI) summaries on search were affecting ad revenue.
Microsoft and Amazon also updated investors this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending astronomical sums of cash in an ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
Google AI is eating its core business - search
At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.
Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.
However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And for the second time in its history as a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.
Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.
By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter.
The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.
Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."
Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.
Investors not buying Amazon's trillion-dollar business hopes
Amazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.
Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.
"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Microsoft begs the question of AI's real value
Wall Street reacted less enthusiastically to Microsoft's update, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.
The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.
"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

bf484f4d8dcd.text: The Pentagon's top military planner admitted to leaking classified information about Ukraine and Iran to two reporters from separate outlets over a one-year period, according to an internal report of the investigation shared with Axios. Why it matters: Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was fired this week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for the alleged misconduct, which the career soldier acknowledged on video after he failed four polygraph tests, a U.S. official said. "He had trouble passing multiple polygraph interviews," the report said. The report accused the general of making "unauthorized disclosures to the media," and said he "was cooperative with answering questions about interactions with the media to resolve this, and provided his personal phone for a forensics examination." Zoom in: The report and U.S. officials said that Sylvia's leaking began as early as June 2025 — before mainstream media outlets were removed from the Pentagon — and continued afterward via secure Signal app and once at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Va. "The meeting at the diner occurred because [redacted's] access to the Pentagon was revoked between meetings," the report says. "During the meeting at the diner, [Sylvia] relied on notes he took while reviewing a classified secret report to orally give redacted on U.S. assistance to Ukraine, the report says. The report says the reporter in question was writing a book and met twice with Sylvia. It also emphasized that the general "did not coordinate these meetings with [the Pentagon's Public Affairs Office], or seek to have the information reviewed before providing it to the reporter." The intrigue: U.S. officials suspect that Sylvia intentionally deleted any trace of contact on Signal between him and one of the reporters, but pretended it was an accident. "Sometime between June or July, Sylvia received Signal messages from [redacted]. Sylvia is unable to recall exactly what was in that message," the report said. "But he believes it had something to do with Iran." "He stated that he did not respond to the message and instead deleted it. While deleting it, he believes he deleted the entire message thread with [redacted]," the report said. "This erased Signal messages and Signal phone calls that would have been recorded in Signal on his personal phone." For another story, the report said, Sylvia "admitted to being one of the 20 officials" cited in a story criticizing Pentagon leadership. Another U.S. official told Axios that Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and his office lobbied the Joint Staff to put out a statement supporting Sylvia "to minimize the damage about any future claims of him leaking classified information." After someone within the Defense Department revealed to the Joint Staff why Sylvia was fired, the Joint Staff retracted its statement. Sylvia's dismissal marks the latest crackdown on leakers and the press from Hegseth's Pentagon. In July, the Defense Department announced a joint task force with the Justice Department that aimed to identify Pentagon leakers. It also called on the Pentagon's Office of General Counsel to prioritize prosecutions of those who make unauthorized disclosures to the media. Last year, in response to restrictive rules imposed by the Pentagon, several defense reporters and media outlets turned in their media passes. What they're saying: Sylvia did not immediately respond to a phone call, voicemail and text message left at the phone number listed for him in public records.

eb69976f8f92.text: By — Liz Landers Liz Landers By — Dan Cooney Dan Cooney By — Joshua Barajas Joshua Barajas By — Steff Staples Steff Staples By — Kelsey Paul Kelsey Paul Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/5-expert-takeaways-on-2026-midterm-election-security Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security Politics Oct 29, 2026 5:35 PM EDT With Election Day around the corner, states have been working hard to prepare, with some adopting new congressional maps and voting rules on top of normal election security measures. While President Donald Trump persists in making unfounded claims about the security and integrity of the nation's elections, the Department of Justice is planning to send 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states, more than double the number dispatched during the 2022 midterms. READ MORE: How some states are responding to DOJ's plan to send 1,000 monitors on Election Day As part of our coverage of the midterm groundwork happening across the country, PBS News' Liz Landers and Votebeat editorial director Jessica Huseman hosted a Reddit "Ask Me Anything" Q&A on Wednesday to address people's questions on election security. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Several questions touched on people's concerns about their vote being tampered with or not being counted, alongside broader concerns about possible meddling from the federal government. The Trump administration is attempting measures that haven't been tried before, Huseman said. Those actions include attempts to change election rules through executive orders, repeated demands for voter data and efforts to expand the government's role – specifically the executive branch – in elections. All of this amounts to an "unprecedented environment now," she said. And yet, "elections officials are confident the system will hold," she added. Here are five major takeaways from the Reddit AMA. Evidence shows that illegal voting is extremely rare Ballots for the upcoming midterm elections are stacked inside a locked, secured and monitored cage at the Durham County Board of Elections, as election officials boost security to fortify the building and protect staff in preparation for the upcoming midterm elections, in Durham, North Carolina, on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Jonathan Drake/ Reuters Trump has routinely cast doubt on the security of the vote, making false claims of "rampant" voter fraud even a week ahead of Nov. 3. The president, who has continued to falsely claim that the 2020 presidential election was "rigged," has fixated on rooting out what he claims is election fraud this election cycle. The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas to more than a dozen states requesting voter roll data, expanding its efforts to tamp down alleged noncitizen voting. But illegal voting by noncitizens voting is vanishingly rare. READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say Votebeat spent more than a year investigating claims from a group called the Election Truth Alliance that promoted a statistical analysis suggesting votes in the 2024 election had been manipulated in Pennsylvania, she said. The nonprofit newsroom consulted nearly a dozen experts and put the Election Truth Alliance's claims through peer review. "What we actually found was that the model would identify fraud even on datasets intentionally built not to contain any fraud," Huseman said. "Despite much of their analysis not standing up to scrutiny, it still managed to raise more than $400,000 in a single year." WATCH: Inside Georgia's push to rebuild trust in elections after Trump's false claims Huseman said it's worth remembering that "elections are not black boxes." "In the places where the Election Truth Alliance alleged truly incredible problems, there were audits, observers, paper ballots and an entire staff of people whose jobs are ensuring the accuracy of these numbers," she said. "We can scrutinize the evidence as it's presented, but when we have it, we have to look it squarely in the face and call it what it is." Trump can't declare a national emergency to interfere with elections Nowhere in the U.S. Constitution does the president of the United States have express authority over how elections are run. As laid out in the country's founding document, states determine the time, place and manner of elections. And Congress has a role in passing legislation over federal elections, though they have not passed major laws like this in a while, Landers said. READ MORE: Immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship targeted in Trump administration's illegal voting crackdown To put a finer point on it: The president cannot declare some kind of national emergency and expect all 50 states to stop their elections. "I know from speaking with election officials across the country that they will not stop their election administration just because the president declared something over a process he does not have any legal authority," Landers said. She also asked Trump in February if he would declare a national emergency — as some of his allies have urged. He said no at the time, adding he'd never heard about that. Federal election monitors are there to observe The Justice Department is planning to dispatch more than 1,000 federal election monitors to observe proceedings on Election Day. What they can do at polling places is fairly limited. WATCH: DOJ monitoring plans and DHS voter checks raise concerns of election interference To be clear: Federal election monitors are a normal part of both midterm and presidential elections, and the Biden administration deployed them in the 2024 presidential election cycle. Six military freezers went bad in August. Was it a cyber attack?
After food spoiled at commissaries, Pentagon investigators are looking at similar incidents in France.
The Pentagon is investigating a suspected cyberattack behind freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the United States in August, according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter.
The outages affected some six commissaries — the on-base grocery stores serving military personnel — per the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the situation. At Fort Huachuca in Arizona, officials reported that a freezer had entered defrost mode and heated its contents, leaving food spoiled.
Reuters first reported Thursday that investigators were treating the incidents as a possible hack. It’s unclear who might be responsible or whether investigators have conclusively determined what caused the failures.
Cyber Command and various Defense Department law-enforcement units are probing the incident. French authorities are also working with officials examining the matter. Earlier this month, hackers overrode temperature controls on commercial refrigeration equipment at more than 350 French establishments, forcing supermarkets to discard spoiled food.
The investigation draws attention to the computers that control everyday equipment used to store and handle food, an often overlooked area of cybersecurity where a hack can spoil supplies or interrupt distribution of goods.
The unusual U.S. outages and the possibility of hacking were initially flagged in August by the Signal and Silence blog. Stars and Stripes subsequently reported the involvement of military investigators, and The Telegraph also reported officials’ contact with French authorities.
A 2021 DHS assessment of threats to food and agriculture specifically identified refrigeration failures and shipping delays as cybersecurity risks that could cause spoilage and shortages.
The Food and Agriculture Information Sharing and Analysis Center, an industry group that shares cyber threat intelligence on the nation's food supply, has warned that attackers are targeting internet-accessible industrial controls that may not have optimal cyberdefenses in place.
The agri-food sector’s sensitivity to downtime often gives ransomware groups leverage to demand payment, the organization said in a separate report.
Lawmakers have sought to improve federal protections. A bipartisan group reintroduced the Farm and Food Cybersecurity Act in 2025, following an earlier proposal introduced in 2024.

The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

f0d8e1dc1d05.text: Reddit on Thursday said it's moving to become a primarily logged-in experience, marking one of the most significant shifts in its 21-year history. Why it matters: Reddit has long championed the open web. Now, it's pushing to build a more direct relationship with users while also protecting its data from increased scraping in the AI era. Driving the news: In an interview Thursday, Reddit co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman said the company is making the change to improve its user experience, bolster its ads business and prevent bots from scraping its proprietary data. Chief operating officer Jen Wong told Axios the move doesn't represent a change in strategy as the company has always focused on building a direct destination. "It's just that in the last 10 years, because our [data] corpus was open, we got a lot of search traffic, so that became part of the equation" but didn't change the company's mission. Zoom in: Huffman expressed confidence that the change would ultimately improve engagement and monetization, even as changes to traditional search continue to impact user growth in the U.S. "When users log in, they spend more time on Reddit, and we can we better know their interests, so we can target ads better," he said. He also noted that the short-term risk is limited because "the vast majority of engagement and over 80% of our monetization comes from our app and logged-in users." In a shareholder letter, Reddit acknowledged that search referral traffic was "down meaningfully in Q3" and said daily users could decline by a "low-double-digit percentage" in Q4 if search referral trends persist. How it works: Reddit will begin testing the fully logged-in experience this quarter outside the U.S. and collect data on the best approach before it rolls out broader changes gradually. Logged-in users can get tailored content, feeds and recommended communities based on their activity and interests, although they can opt out of personalization. The company is still working through what content will be available to users who do not login. Participation features, such as commenting and content ranking, will continue to be accessible only to logged-in users. Its homepage will still be accessible to logged-out visitors. People accessing the platform via search engines or shared links will still be able to see that linked content. Huffman said the company will monitor the conversion rate to logged-in users as one metric of success. Between the lines: Reddit has long prioritized user privacy and has supported user anonymity as a way to encourage authentic expression. Logged-in users will not be required to reveal their real name or real-world identity, the company said. The company is relaunching its incognito browsing mode within its app, which lets users browse and search without affecting their logged-in accounts. But the platform will be read-only in incognito mode, meaning users can't comment or engage. Follow the money: The changes will make user personalization more central to the Reddit experience, which Wong said will bolster the company's ads business. Logged-in user engagement is about five times that of logged-out users, Wong said. "They see more impressions, and therefore, yield more business outcomes for advertisers," she noted. Performance advertising, which now amounts to more than 60% of Reddit's ad revenue, is the fastest-growing part of the company's business. Reality check: Most other major consumer internet platforms have already made this shift. Huffman said he personally resisted the changes because of his belief in the open internet. He ultimately came around because Reddit's scale made personalization more important for users today and because protecting the platform's content from unauthorized scraping has become more urgent. The company said most of its unauthorized scrapes are of content that lives outside of the logged-in experience on the open web. The big picture: The change was announced alongside Reddit's Q3 earnings results, which saw the ads business grow a whopping 54% year over year. The company beat Wall Street estimates on revenue and earnings growth, but missed expectations on U.S. user growth amid weakened search traffic. Since going public in March 2024, Reddit's ads business has nearly tripled. The company earned $222.7 million in ad revenue in Q1 2024, compared with $847 million in Q3 this year. The vast majority of Reddit's revenue (94.7%) comes from ads. Zoom out: Reddit believes its content will become more valuable in the AI era, as people look for authentic human recommendations and content to validate information from chatbots. "We are a collection of human experiences and preferences that is extremely vast and fresh, and I don't think there's anything comparable to it," Wong said. As of Q3, Reddit has more than 27 billion posts and comments, an unprecedented trove of human data. Reddit will still license its content to third parties and rely on those agreements to set equitable terms for scraping and content usage. In its earnings release, the company said revenue outside of advertising, which includes data licensing, totaled $48 million in third quarter, up 35% year over year. What to watch: The shift to logged-in users will help Reddit be more intentional about third-party access to its data. Huffman explained the way that data is used and displayed on other platforms can impact the core experience of Reddit. Reddit announced an expanded partnership with Google in 2024, reportedly with $60 million annually. It announced a similar deal with OpenAI later that year. The company sued Anthropic and Perplexity in 2025 for unauthorized scraping. The bottom line: Huffman said the shift is not a response to Google Search changes, but rather "about making the best version of Reddit." 051d757f798c.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/judge-blocks-trump-administrations-medicaid-work-requirement-rule-forcing-proof-of-medical-frailty Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge blocks Trump administration's Medicaid work requirement rule forcing proof of medical frailty Health Oct 29, 2026 3:53 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Chronically ill people on Medicaid won't be bound by new work requirement rules that the latest Trump administration guidance requires in order to qualify for "medically frail" exemptions, a federal judge ruled Thursday. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston gave a partial victory to a coalition of 25 states and the District of Columbia, which sued the Trump administration in June over the new Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services guidance linked to the 2025 law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill." READ MORE: As states face stricter Medicaid work requirements, Nebraska is an early test The law says the definition of medically frail must include people who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders, have certain disabilities that significantly impair daily activities, or have serious or complex medical conditions. But the CMS rule went further, requiring people in those categories to show that their conditions also "significantly impair" their ability to comply with the law's work requirements. The plaintiffs argued that the stricter rule would prevent eligible Americans from accessing the care they need — and oversteps the text of the law itself as well. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The states have met their burden of showing irreparable harm for which monetary damages would provide inadequate compensation — they face the burden of costly and intensive alterations to their eligibility verification systems," Stearns said in his 16-page ruling. Notably, while the ruling will make it easier for some Medicaid recipients with qualifying medical conditions to obtain an exemption from the new work requirements, Stearns' decision does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful. Additionally, Stearns upheld two other federal restrictions on how states can verify medical frailty: including the requirement that states reject proof of patients' medical frailty if the diagnosis is more than a year old. He also upheld a policy allowing states to accept only one self-attestation per continuous period of enrollment. Explaining why he upheld the portions in favor of the government, Stearns said "the government provided a non-frivolous rationale for adopting each provision and explained why it did not find the States' concerns of disenrollment compelling." Representatives from the Department of Health and Human Services and CMS did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment. The new Medicaid restrictions are part of Trump's big tax and policy law in 2025. The change affects those covered through an expansion in most states that gave more lower-income people access to the government's safety net healthcare program. Starting Jan. 1, expansion enrollees aged 19 to 64 must show that they work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or are in school at least half the time. There are exceptions for those considered medically frail or in addiction treatment programs, among others. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Thick fog has formed on Friday morning across parts of the United Kingdom which could lead to hazardous driving conditions.
The Met Office has issued a yellow severe weather warning for fog from Lincolnshire, the East Midlands, the Home Counties into parts of Greater London.
Fog will be dense in places with visibility below 100 metres at times and it will be most extensive and disruptive during the morning rush hour.
It will slowly begin to thin, lift and clear later this morning but in some rural spots in eastern England it may not clear until this afternoon.
The weekend forecast
Early morning mist and fog patches on Saturday may lift into low cloud, which could hang around all day.
Some areas will fare better with some spells of sunshine with many areas staying dry.
The exception to this theme will be north-west Scotland, where a weak weather front will bring thicker cloud and rain for a time.
Temperatures will be close to average and will be overall, similar to recent days.
By Sunday this dying weather front will bring some thicker cloud to Wales and central England threatening a few patches of light rain or drizzle, but not much.
The rest of the UK will have a dry day on Sunday with variable cloud and some spells of sunshine at times.
When will we see Storm Chloe?
High pressure has been building and is set to dominate across the UK in the coming days.
This is in stark contrast to last week which saw areas buffeted by a cluster of storms developed by a powerful Atlantic jet stream.
The jet stream, still running close to the UK, with the building area of high pressure bringing us much quieter weather.
Whilst Storms Austen and Boelo provided some short-term hydrological benefit, 82% of England remains in drought status according to the Environment Agency.
The area of high pressure will stay over or close to the UK for at least ten days as a result of a 'diffluent blocking pattern' forming in the Atlantic jet stream across the UK and western Europe, which will prevent weather systems reaching our shores.
It means we are heading into a long stretch of mostly dry weather. There could still be some patches of low cloud and drizzle associated with early morning mist and fog, however, rainfall amounts will be negligible.
With no storms on the horizon any time soon, it is likely to be a while before we see the arrival of Chloe, the next name on this year's storm list.
In the short-term this lack of rainfall will raise concerns about the drought and low water levels in England's reservoirs.
Following the latest meeting of the National Drought Group, water companies are being urged to speed up the fixing of leaks and members of the public to take shorter showers and turn off the tap when brushing their teeth.
The Environment Agency (EA) says that 20% more rain than average is needed over the next six months, external for the drought to end.
Philip Duffy, Chief Executive of the Environment Agency, said: "The recent rain is welcome, but the drought isn't over. A few wet days cannot reverse months of hot, dry weather.
"Our rivers, reservoirs and groundwater need sustained rainfall to recover, and the effects on nature can last much longer."
El NiÃ±o has been linked to wetter and stormier weather in late autumn and early winter. The current three month outlook from the Met Office forecasts that there is double the chance of it being wetter than normal.
