PHOENIX— Koral Casillas’ American Dream was simple: Leave her corporate job to start a local business serving her community.
Five years ago, she did just that. She’s now the co-owner of two local Phoenix businesses—Monsoon Market, a purveyor of local goods, and Strip Mall, a coffee and wine shop. But this summer, Casillas said, she was rudely awakened from her dream when her August utility bill came in at $1,500—far higher than any bill she had received before; the next month, it rose again, to $1,700.
Casillas’ story quickly made the rounds on social media, and she’s using the recent attention to highlight a little-known elected office in Arizona tasked with regulating the state’s utilities, the Arizona Corporation Commission. The ACC is currently considering approving another 14 percent rate increase from Arizona Power Service—its third price hike from the utility in four years.
“It’s already pretty hard to operate a small business here in Arizona, and the risk of utility bills continuing to rise [is] probably [the] greatest one facing us today,” Casillas said at a press conference at Strip Mall featuring Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill, Democratic candidates for the ACC. They are running against Republicans Kevin Thompson, a current commissioner, and Ralph Heap, a state lawmaker facing a campaign finance investigation, neither of whom responded to requests for comment.
“While I can shop around for cheaper costs for coffee beans and paper goods, I am sadly stuck with my utility provider, APS,” Casillas said. “This story isn’t unique, and I know that I’m not alone here. Our members on the ACC are supposed to negotiate and regulate companies like APS to ensure that they are providing safe and reliable power to all of us Arizona residents and small business owners. They have failed us.”
Created in 1912 under the state’s constitution, the ACC regulates the state’s water and power utilities, determining how much customers can be charged, how much profit utilities can make and how Arizona’s power grid is built and operated, among other responsibilities. The state is one of 10 where the commissioners are elected and are separate from the state’s other branches of government, meaning only elections and lawsuits can hold them accountable.
In the 2024 election, Republicans took control of all five seats on the commission. In the two years since, the commission has repealed the state’s energy efficiency standards and renewable energy standards. It also approved the first formula rate plans, which allow utilities to adjust their rates annually based on a pre-established formula, rather than go through a rate hearing process that involves more oversight and transparency about the need for the increase.
“Each of these decisions dealt a blow to consumers. Combined, it’s like a knockout punch,” said Diane Brown, executive director of the nonprofit Arizona Public Interest Research Group Education Fund. “In the upcoming year, the next commission will have major consequential decisions to make related to rate cases, data centers and energy resources, and the decisions of the next commission are extremely likely to impact ratepayer bills for years to come.”
Recent polling from The Nature Conservancy in Arizona and the Arizona PIRG Education Fund found about 80 percent of Arizonans said their electricity bills rose in the last two years. Over 60 percent said their summer bills are difficult to afford, and another roughly 60 percent said they keep their thermostat set above comfortable temperatures to save money in the hot summer months.
“The polling signifies a disconnect between what Arizonans want when it comes to energy efficiency programs provided by their utility, and what the Arizona Corporation Commission has done by repealing Arizona’s very successful energy efficiency standard,” which saved Arizonans over $1.7 billion dollars and over 2,000 megawatts in cumulative peak demand energy savings, Brown said.
Pratte and Hill have campaigned on bringing transparency and accountability to the commission, limiting excessive rate increases for ratepayers, requiring large energy users to pay their fair share and developing more renewable energy in the state.
“Arizonans are sick and tired of commissioners who will not fight for them,” said Pratte at the press conference. Pratte is a member of the Navajo Nation and co-founded Navajo Power, which partners with tribal communities to build renewable energy projects.
Pratte and Hill cite a recent analysis that shows between 2023 and 2025, homeowners and businesses paid $587 million for costs associated with the “large load” sector, such as data centers. In a statement, APS said the analysis “reaches false conclusions” and “oversimplifies a complex issue.”
But Pratte and Hill are calling on the ACC to require APS to open its books and launch an investigation into the claims. “Arizona ratepayers deserve an answer to this very important question” of whether ratepayers are helping pay for the surge of electricity costs driven by data centers in the state, Hill said.
“If small businesses, families, seniors are paying for billions of dollars of data center costs, we will demand an immediate reimbursement for those customers,” Hill said. “Arizonans are paying attention to these issues like they never have before, because it’s affecting them so much. Arizonans are realizing that something needs to change, because they’re seeing their utility bills every month, and the problem is only getting worse.”

A stalemate in the conflict between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo is raising fresh doubts about the Trump administrationâs ability to influence it.
The US imposed sanctions on Rwandaâs Ministry of Defense and a bank serving its security services earlier this week, accusing Kigali of backing and fighting alongside M23 rebels in eastern Congo nearly a year after US President Donald Trump declared the war over.
âIt will continue raising questions about US leadership within these matters, because the US is the guarantor of this particular agreement,â said Mvemba Phezo Dizolele, a senior fellow at Johns Hopkins Universityâs Foreign Policy Institute, of the stalemate.
Trump hosted Rwandan President Paul Kagame and Congo President FÃ©lix Tshisekedi in Washington last December to sign accords to end the war. But fighting never abated.
The State Department now says âthousandsâ of Rwanda Defense Force troops are fighting in Congo and that some âhave also brought in surface-to-air missiles and jamming equipment that endanger civilian aviation.â
In announcing the sanctions, the Treasury Department accused Zigama Credit and Savings Society of helping finance the Rwandan militaryâs support for Congolese rebels, including moving gold out of M23-held territory. The action follows sanctions on Rwandaâs army and four senior commanders in March and on a Kigali gold refinery in June.
The sanctions, however, are unlikely to have a major impact on Rwanda, argued Dizolele, though Kigali will be cognizant of the impact on its image in the eyes of the West. âThey will shrug it off, they will adjust, but it stings,â he said.
Trumpâs foreign policy moves have often generated controversy and backlash, particularly among Democrats, but in this case he has bipartisan support. Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., who pressed the NBA this week over its Rwanda partnership alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said he supported the new sanctions.
âRwanda remains ready to fully implement the Washington Accords, concurrently with the willingness of the DRC to fulfill those commitments, and with the mediator holding all parties accountable,â Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo said, accusing Congo of failing to meet its own requirements under the deal.

The CEO Signal
Any interference in next weekâs US midterm elections should be a âred lineâ that prompts business leaders to rally behind American democratic norms, Ken Chenault is warning his peers. But the influential chairman of venture capital firm General Catalyst worries that some leaders have lost sight of where to draw such lines, as theyâve retreated from a social responsibility agenda they espoused just a few years ago.
Chenault, who was one of the first Black CEOs to lead a Fortune 500 company and ran American Express for 17 years, says people concerned about meddling in Tuesdayâs election or damaging disputes over the results have been calling him to ask: âWill business stand up?â
In 2021, Chenault helped rally hundreds of executives in other companies to oppose restrictive voting bills. But he thinks it would be âvery challengingâ to muster the same response from executives now. Back then, businesses issued statements in favor of a peaceful transfer of power around the 2020 election and subsequent attack on the US Capitol.
But theyâve since âbacked down,â he notes. âThey said, âHereâs what weâre not going to do.â And then, in fact, they changed. And then the hammer came down.â
CEOs have pulled back from public comment on issues they fear will attract a costly backlash, having watched President Donald Trump go after law firms, universities, and corporations in his second term.
Some US officials have raised concerns about possible threats to the integrity of the midterms and campaigners have called on CEOs to express support for free and fair elections. Robert Rubin, the former Treasury Secretary, wrote recently that any manipulation of the process would have lasting economic effects. But very few active CEOs of large US companies have echoed such concerns publicly, and investors have been calm.
âPeople feel threatened by consequences,â Chenault says. Some executives see voting rights as too political a topic to touch, but âitâs not political; weâre talking about a fundamental right here. Weâre not saying Republican [or] Democrat.â
In Equal to the Task, a memoir that will be published next week, Chenault argues a point many CEOs wonât: that it is âvitally importantâ for business to protect the democratic process.
âAs the integrity of elections becomes compromised, segments of the population become alienated, communities become less stable and less prosperous, and individual businesses suffer,â he writes.
Chenaultâs stance seems an increasingly lonely one in corporate America. He does not believe that every CEO should have to take a public position on every social or political controversy, he stresses, âbut we need a few people.â
A call to get business off the sidelines
Warren Buffett, who appointed Chenault to the board of Berkshire Hathaway, has called him âthe gold standard for corporate leaders and the benchmark that I measure others against.â The onetime lawyer earned widespread respect in the upper reaches of US business for the way he led Amex through struggles including the September 11 attacks, the 2008 financial crisis, and a US antitrust probe.
âI think I confronted more major challenges than frankly, some of the CEOs of today,â he says. But he does not belittle the complexity of the environment facing this generation of executives, saying that âthe transforming impact of AI, the geopolitical environment, [and] the increasing movement to authoritarianism [are] existential challenges.â
Chenaultâs book is both a personal account of his âuniquely American storyâ and an attempt to guide his successors through those challenges. And it ends with a call for a broader ârebalancingâ of the relationship between business and society, which he implies will require a bolder stance from business leaders on issues from democracy to diversity.
âI canât recall a moment that has called for greater courage than today,â he writes, adding in an interview: âBusiness canât afford to just be on the sidelines.â
Chenault, who has mentored founders including Airbnbâs Brian Chesky in his role at General Catalyst, says he often asks CEOs what their core beliefs are beyond their strategy and which âred linesâ they would never cross in business. He has grown concerned that âpeople are increasingly uncomfortable with that question,â he says, adding that executives should see any election interference as one of those boundaries.
Organizations that know what behavior they would find beyond the pale have the advantage of being able to prepare for how to respond if they encounter it, Chenault says. The Harvard Corporation, the university governing body on which he served until earlier this year, discussed its red lines âbefore things happened,â he says, referring to the Trump administrationâs multi-front campaign against the institution.
Some people told him privately that they agreed with how Harvard responded, but said, âI could never do that; Iâve got to be silent,â Chenault says. âIâve said to people, you canât be silent about principles.â
A âproud capitalistâ makes the case for social responsibility
Chenault calls himself a âproud capitalist,â but he has long rejected Milton Friedmanâs argument that the only social responsibility a business has is to use its resources to increase its profits âwithin the rules of the game.â
âI believe that business exists because society allows it to exist. And, to me, that confers a level of responsibility,â Chenault says.
As an example of what needs to change, he adapts a line popularized by the founder of Meta, whose board Chenault briefly served on and now says was ânot a fitâ for him. âThe era of âmove fast and break thingsâ is over,â he says. âObviously that line is attributed to Mark Zuckerberg, but I think there are a range of people in business generally and technology specifically that have lost sight of what their responsibilities are.â

In what might have been his last hearing as chair of Pennsylvania’s House Environmental and Natural Resource Protection committee, long-time Democratic state Rep. Greg Vitali seemed to have little interest in soaking it all in.
During the October hearing, Vitali instead furrowed his brow as he watched a parade of witnesses discussing “roadspreading,” a practice in which some oil and gas companies dump waste brine from drilling on rural roadways, ostensibly to help control dust.
The regulations governing roadspreading are riddled with complex loopholes, and Vitali called the hearing after state officials issued a roadspreading permit he took issue with. That move proved the most recent example of a recalcitrance that may have contributed to ending Vitali’s decades-long career in Pennsylvania’s legislature earlier this year.
But if his loss in a competitive primary in his suburban Philadelphia district was humbling, Vitali seems determined to keep advocating for the climate and environmental issues he has always cared about. For the past 34 years, no one in the state legislature has spoken out more consistently or forcefully for fossil fuel regulation or clean energy alternatives in Pennsylvania, even as political polarization and the rise of the gas industry made those positions increasingly embattled. Vitali was the first Pennsylvania lawmaker to introduce climate change legislation and a chief advocate pushing for a “severance” tax on gas drilling in the state during the fracking boom.
David Hess, a former secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, said what really sets Vitali apart is his willingness to act as a thorn in the side of even his own party’s leadership.
“I think, in some ways, he became sort of the conscience of the Democratic caucus on a lot of environmental issues,” Hess said. “Some people admired him for that. Some people didn’t admire him for that because he was very plain-spoken.”
Now Pennsylvania will find out what it’s like not to hear his voice in Harrisburg at all. Some of Vitali’s critics welcome his impending exit at the end of November, contending that his principled stands made it more difficult to forge the kind of compromises that are necessary to pass laws in a divided government. His allies think the state will be worse off without his dedication to the environment and sense of moral clarity.
With the House’s current term winding down, Democratic state Rep. Danielle Friel Otten said Vitali’s calling of the October hearing was like a teacher assigning homework on the penultimate day of school: Otten was one of just six lawmakers present from the 27-member committee. Even after Republican Minority Chair Rep. Jack Rader Jr. closed the hearing by thanking Vitali for his time in office, which began in 1992, Vitali signaled he still has miles to go.
“Oh, we’ve got almost two months left,” Vitali said with a wry smile. “You’re not done.”
Filling a Leadership Vacuum
Vitali’s career in politics began with a recycling regulation. In 1988, Pennsylvania passed Act 101, requiring large municipalities to provide curbside recycling for the first time. In Vitali’s view, his local Haverford Township was only doing the “bare minimum” the law required. He said he had an interest in environmental topics dating to when they rose to the top of the priority list for Democratic activists following the Vietnam War. Then a young lawyer, Act 101 became his personal call to action.
“I actually set up my mother’s card table by a recycling center and got signatures on a petition for the township to do more recycling, and took those to a township meeting,” Vitali said, adding the effort was ultimately successful. “It struck me that people wanted to make a contribution, but not be the prime mover or leader. And I felt I was filling a leadership vacuum.”
That solo effort grew into a drive to push surrounding Delaware County to establish a household hazardous waste collection program, which in turn provided the political base on which Vitali launched his first campaign for the State House in 1992. That year, he won the open seat for Pennsylvania’s 166th House District, previously held by a Republican. When the next session began, Vitali made the environment committee his first choice and got the assignment.
The first half of his career in Harrisburg was relatively fruitful. In 2004, he was among the Pennsylvania House members who voted for the Pennsylvania Alternative Energy Portfolio Standards, among the first regulations in the country to require electric utilities to purchase power from renewable sources like wind and solar. That same year, he introduced the legislature’s first-ever climate specific bill to require the state DEP to develop an inventory of greenhouse gas emissions, and in 2008 co-sponsored a similar bill that passed both chambers and became law.
That same year also saw the passage of Act 129, a so-called “smart metering” bill that supported statewide energy efficiency measures for utilities. John Hanger, then secretary of the DEP, said Vitali played a “significant role in its passage.”
Then came seismic shifts: Pennsylvania’s Marcellus Shale natural gas boom took off, enabled by advances in hydraulic fracturing, just as national political discourse began to polarize in the wake of the Obama presidency. Since then, even Vitali acknowledges his legislative track record has been more limited.
“It’s very difficult doing climate policy in Pennsylvania. Obviously, it has a lot of coal and oil and natural gas. So when you choose climate policy as the most important thing to work on, your life is not going to be filled with victories,” Vitali said. “It’s been frustrating. I like to give myself credit for being at the plate swinging.”

88855c740bf5.text: The people at the frontlines of the ongoing barrage of AI-enabled cyberattacks are being pummeled with attacks, vulnerabilities and false alarms. Why it matters: Humans are still at the frontlines of a fight enabled largely by AI — and they're struggling to wade through mountains of threat data to determine who's been hit and which attacks pose a real danger to companies. What they're saying: "The last month has been the longest year of my life," Justin Timothy, threat intelligence consultant at GuidePoint Security, told Axios. Even before "Black October," Timothy was already swamped and dealing with hacker gangs that returned from a seasonal summer lull. These groups specialize in ransomware, essentially attacking the networks of an institution and holding it hostage. While AI is playing a role in many new cyberattacks, the ransomware scourge has already been shutting down pipeline systems, hospitals, education software and other essential services for years. It's only expected to get worse this year as powerful new AI systems are amplifying the capabilities of attackers faster than defenders can insulate vast corners of the unprotected internet. The big picture: The people companies call when they're hacked are being swamped, piling onto the persistent burnout that has plagued the industry. Troy Bettencourt, who leads Palo Alto Networks' global digital forensics and incident response practice, told Axios that demand for his team's services has climbed by double digits over the last six weeks. Unlike past surges tied to historically harmful attacks like SolarWinds , this year's workload has been relentless. "It's just a continuous grind that increases," Bettencourt said. The same heavy workload is happening across the industry, and even Palo Alto Networks' incident response subcontractors are at max capacity, he said. Investigations that could once be handled by a single consultant now require teams of five to 20 people, he said. The company is also pulling employees off other projects and shifting staff into incident response as it braces for more attacks exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities disclosed last week. Zoom in: Samantha Lewis, head of threat intelligence at Armadin, said her team has been inundated with requests from customers scrambling to determine whether their systems are exposed to AI-discovered flaws in foundational internet code. "This week has been pure chaos," she said. "The burden of that has been tremendous." Her team spent days sorting through hundreds of purported exploits, many of which didn't work , to determine which posed real threats to customers. Between the lines: AI's ability to uncover more software flaws threatens to bury defenders in even more work. The mounting workload is pushing security firms to use AI and automation to identify weaknesses and accelerate investigations. "The number of people you would need to actually defend against this starts to become entirely untenable," Lewis said. Yet the shift comes with another headache: Palo Alto's Bettencourt said he's juggling workers who are both exhausted by the caseload and worried that the AI tools being developed to ease their workloads could replace them. "They're burning out, and they're hearing everything in the media that AI is going to take everyone's job," Bettencourt said. "It's a tough balance." The intrigue: Even companies that largely escaped the latest security scares haven't been spared. Jack Nelson, Ivanti's chief information security officer and deputy general counsel, said he got "less sleep than normal this past week," despite the company's limited exposure to the PHP vulnerabilities. "It's been busy, there's no doubt about it," Nelson said. What to watch: Cyber defenders can't keep working at this pace indefinitely, but many are hopeful AI will offer them more ammunition in a battle some expect to go on for 12 to 18 months.

In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (Â£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

A Pakistani anti-terrorism court has sentenced human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to 10 years in prison, over an alleged security breach during a cricket tour in 2024.
The couple were accused of removing road barriers and obstructing police officers in Islamabad - charges that both have denied.
Mazari and Chattha were previously sentenced to up to 17 years in prison for social media posts criticising the military.
Pakistan's Supreme Court had suspended those sentences in August, but police re-arrested the couple before they could be released. They have been imprisoned in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail for the past several months.
This latest case concerns an incident on 25 October 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.
Prosecutors accused Mazari and Chattha of removing barriers from a road designated for the team's security convoy and obstructing police officers at Zero Point, a major cloverleaf road junction in Islamabad.
They were each sentenced to 10 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Act, as well as additional one-year and two-year terms for obstructing and using force against public servants. All sentences will run concurrently.
The court also fined each of them 200,000 Pakistani Rupees (Â£541:$723).
In statements recorded during the trial, the couple described themselves as "prisoners of conscience" who had faced state persecution.
"I am being punished for not only supporting my wife's work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together," Chatta said in his statement to Dawn News.
The couple had earlier said that they were "being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression, and injustice".
Amnesty International has criticised the proceedings, saying the couple were denied an open and fair trial.
"These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan's justice system." said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact.
"Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."
The organisation also raised concerns that the trial had been moved inside the prison, where Mazari and Chattha were kept behind a cage-like structure during hearings.
The couple have faced several criminal cases in recent months.
They have been in custody since 23 January, when they were arrested in a separate case involving an alleged altercation outside the Islamabad High Court. A day later, they were sentenced to up to 17 years in prison under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act over social media posts critical of the military.
Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended those sentences and granted them bail on 17 September - but they were arrested again the same day in connection with a separate case over a protest in March 2025, in which they were accused of chanting "anti-government slogans" and "blocking roads".
Mazari and Chattha are prominent human rights lawyers who have represented activists, journalists and marginalised communities subjected to enforced disappearances.
Mazari's mother, Shireen Mazari, is a former human rights minister who served in the government of former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan.
The couple's convictions have long drawn criticism from international human rights organisations, which have raised concerns about the treatment of lawyers and activists in Pakistan.

'I made the wrong decision,' Hyrox athlete who soiled herself in race tells BBC
Australian Hyrox athlete Joanna Wietrzyk says she made the wrong decision when she continued to race after soiling herself during a competition in Beijing.
Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she suggested her determination to win the race in September had clouded her judgement.
Roughly halfway through her event last month, Wietrzyk suffered a bout of diarrhoea and images of faecal matter on parts of her body were widely shared online.
"I didn't really think about those around meâ¦ the decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect," the athlete told the BBC.
She also talked about the effect of the social media reaction after the incident, saying she should not have received "such backlash", and that she is "only human".

f142ae8dbbf7.text:
When BaRupOn LLC, a California-based developer, bought land in East Texas for a 700-acre industrial campus in 2023, the company received a warm welcome from the state. The developer set out to build numerous data centers and rare-earth manufacturing facilities at the site, as well as its own power plants.
At first, Gov. Greg Abbott’s office worked closely with BaRupOn, said Balaji Tammabattula, the chief operating officer.
The governor’s office staff would recommend site locations for future projects and which county officials they should get in touch with, Tammabattula said. Developers were encouraged to seek out incentives and tax breaks. The governor’s office, which was just a phone call away, even gave the planned industrial campus, in Liberty, Texas, the codename of “Project Tough,” Tammabattula said.
“Texas used to be the best place,” he said. “Fast forward to 2026, it’s impossible to have [the governor’s office] respond to our emails.”
The climate around data centers has soured so severely that new developments in Texas are essentially on pause until after November’s elections. The land, energy and water usage of the large warehouses filled with server racks have elicited strong protest across the country—even becoming a bipartisan issue among midterm election candidates, including in Texas.
Abbott has gone against his typical business-first approach and led some companies to rethink their major data center investments in Texas, analysts and developers said. Those seeking to keep their spot in the lengthy line for grid power are laboring to not only secure state permits but social permission from communities across the state.
The data center industry flocked to invest billions of dollars in the state to quickly construct the physical infrastructure required for tech companies to develop the most mature artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies. The developers, many of whom were new to the industry, saw a state not only open to doing business but a grid committed to connecting projects to power faster than anywhere else. Texas became the epicenter of A.I. development as Abbott willed last year. But that tune changed fast.
The state has long been seen as the best place for business development in the country, with its previously unfussy regulatory environment. It’s a reputation that’s carried throughout Abbott’s 11 years in office. Yet that’s changed amid the staunch opposition data centers have ignited and a race which could result in a Democrat representing Texas in the U.S. Senate for the first time in more than 30 years. And there’s another unanticipated outcome for Abbott: his own unusually tight race for reelection against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa from Austin.
Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, said Abbott has taken decisive action to set clear guardrails to protect Texans against intrusive data center development.
In August, he ordered the state’s utilities regulator, the Public Utility Commission, and its grid operator, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, to audit how much power and water every data center project being developed would consume. In September, he ordered the Texas Water Development Board to enforce water-use reporting requirements on data center projects.
“Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits,” Mahaleris said in a statement to Inside Climate News. “Until they do, no state agency will issue related permits, and any project that fails those standards will be denied.”
Abbott’s audit and directive to pause all environmental permits is on top of new regulations and planning processes implemented after the last legislative session, which seek to verify the validity of the massive amounts of data center projects trying to connect to the grid.
Six months ago, the industry in Texas was most concerned about how fast their projects could get interconnected to the grid, said Olivier Beaufils, a head researcher at Aurora Energy Research. Now, the industry is nervous, Beaufils said, because there’s more political uncertainty than there was earlier this year, when developers were solely dealing with the wave of new rules.
“Political backlash and political risk was sort of a remote risk that people weren’t considering as their core problem they had to deal with,” Beaufils said. “That has shifted very rapidly.”
There’s anguish within the industry over whether the political issues they’re facing today will subside after the midterms are over, or whether they will multiply during the legislative session in January, Beaufils said.
“I think there’s a recognition that this is not a risk that is going to disappear in November,” Beaufils said. “This is something they’re going to have to engage with over the next six months until there’s a bit more clarity.”
After Diode Ventures, a data center developer, withdrew its plans for a data center near a residential community in Henderson County as a result of Abbott’s directives and community pushback about its water usage, Abbott celebrated the company’s decision.
“Data centers that want to do business in Texas must meet a clear standard. This project did not,” Abbott said in a July statement. “Diode did the right thing by withdrawing their project. If other data center developments refuse to meet these standards, I expect them to do the same.”

Beaufils said he expects to see more projects withdrawn as there’s more community opposition.
Abbott stated that he plans to seek legislation to require large data centers to annually report electricity and water usage data to the PUC and repeal any sales tax exemptions or other outdated or unnecessary incentives for the facilities.

841509f9c60a.text: A federal judge announced Friday she plans to appoint a special master to investigate whether Justice and Interior Department officials misled the court about the Trump administration's plans to renovate a D.C. golf course, according to news reports . Why it matters: The investigation could lead to professional sanctions, contempt proceedings or criminal referrals against administration officials over allegations government lawyers misled the judge. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes opened a hearing Friday by reading ethics rules requiring attorneys to be truthful with courts, then questioned Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. about the administration's conflicting accounts, according to news reports. Trump announced Oct. 18 the golf course would close Nov. 15 for roughly 15 months of renovations. Woodward told the court the next day there was "no plan to close the course." On Oct. 28, the Justice Department acknowledged Trump had directed the closure. Catch up quick: A preservation group and two golfers are suing the administration over what they say is President Trump's illegal plan to convert the historic, public East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level golf course. After government crews cut down more than 400 trees, Reyes barred further tree removal without court approval and required 10 business days' notice before closing the park or making irreversible changes. The administration has appealed. What's next: Reyes said she intends to appoint a special master who could review documents, question witnesses under oath and hold hearings. The government would have five business days to object after a special master is selected, the Washington Post reported . This is a breaking news story and will be updated. Go deeper: Exclusive: Congress presses Trump on D.C. golf course plans

3d6f71384535.text: Pope Leo XIV voted in the 2026 Illinois midterm elections using a mail-in ballot, the Vatican confirmed Friday, becoming the first sitting pope known to vote in an American election. Why it matters: The pontiff, an American citizen, may be the first to vote in any secular democratic election. Joliet radio station WJOL first reported Oct. 23 that Leo had requested a mail-in ballot. What they're saying: The pope believes "in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Holy See Press Office said in a statement . The Vatican said Leo "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so" and that "in keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago." Pope Leo also voted whenever eligible during his years living in Peru, the Vatican's statement said. Zoom in: The pope's ballot includes Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker 's reelection bid, the race to succeed Sen. Dick Durbin and a House contest between Democratic Rep. Jonathan Jackson and Republican Christian Maxwell. Jackson, the son of the late Rev. Jesse Jackson, won his district handily in 2024. The pontiff's ballot will have to travel from Vatican city to Joliet, Illinois. Worth noting : Leo has voted in both Democratic and Republican primaries in the last two decades. Leo requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010 when he lived in heavily blue Cook County, per the AP. He then started voting in GOP primaries in subsequent elections when he moved to the more conservative Will County, where he is currently registered to vote. He's also voted as an undeclared voter off and on in recent elections, according to the Will County clerk's office. His party affiliation is currently undeclared. Zoom out: The pope, who has been recovering from lung cancer surgery , met with Chicago-area advocates Wednesday who are supporting immigrants at an ICE facility in Broadview , Illinois. He's also clashed with President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who is Catholic, over the war in Iran and the treatment of immigrants in America. Go deeper: Pope Leo XIV discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery Axios Chicago's Carrie Shepherd contributed.

9f96bcb90801.text: The U.S. naval blockade, sweeping economic sanctions and obstruction of overland export routes have crippled Iran's economy and intensified pressure on the regime, according to a new Treasury Department report obtained by Axios. Why it matters: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is leading an economic pressure campaign dubbed "Operation Economic Outcast," is one of Trump's closest aides urging him to let the initiative play out rather than rush back into combat. Though the report doesn't argue that the Iranian regime is close to collapsing, it does lay out the Treasury Department's view that its efforts have crippled Iran's economy and limited its ability to generate revenue. Driving the news: As he did before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump is pursuing dual tracks — trying to reach a deal to restart peace talks while also preparing to possibly resume major combat operations after the midterms. The Treasury campaign, which launched in late August, is a third track. But U.S. officials say it needs more time to destabilize the regime and potentially convince the Iranian leadership to make concessions at the negotiations table. On Thursday, Trump met with his top national security and foreign policy aides to discuss the war. U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper, who commands forces in the Middle East, briefed Trump on the ongoing naval blockade . Bessent discussed the economic pressure campaign. "Bessent is telling the President the economic pressure campaign is working and that things are getting worse in Iran and that this could further destabilize the regime and push the Supreme Leader to agree to a deal," a U.S. official said. Zoom in: The Treasury report highlights several indicators of Iran's economic crisis: Currency collapse: The Iranian rial has lost roughly a quarter of its value since the operation began in August. In October, the unofficial exchange rate reached a record low of 2.687 million rials to the dollar. "The currency's decline reflects mounting pressure on Iran's economy and financial system, eroding purchasing power and making it increasingly costly for the regime to access goods and services abroad," the report argues. Soaring inflation: Iran's annual inflation rate reached 90% in September, compared to roughly 35% in early 2025. Oil exports: Iran has not loaded any oil onto tankers since Aug. 25 because of the blockade and sanctions, the report says. Tehran has also sold off its remaining oil stranded at sea, according to Kpler, which tracks maritime trade. Between the lines: The report details how the U.S. is seeking to cut Iran off not only from oil revenue but also from international trade routes, commercial aviation, banking networks and even digital currency alternatives. It states that Iran's effort to reroute trade overland around the U.S. naval blockade is facing major bottlenecks at borders with Pakistan, Turkey, Afghanistan, and Turkmenistan. Thousands of trucks are reportedly stranded at the Turkish border, facing delays of up to 20 days, while hundreds more are waiting at the Pakistani border, the report says. The UAE, Oman, Iraq, Georgia and Azerbaijan have barred Iranian airlines and canceled flights to Iran. Turkey has suspended all Mahan Air flights. Iranian banks have faced additional restrictions in Turkey, Lebanon and the UAE, while Treasury is targeting cryptocurrency exchanges used to evade sanctions.

845be682b087.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/2-trump-attempts-to-change-the-d-c-landscape-play-out-in-the-courts-as-midterms-near Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 2 Trump attempts to change the D.C. landscape play out in the courts as midterms near Politics Oct 30, 2026 2:34 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Hearings in lawsuits against two separate administration-backed projects were unfolding in a single federal court building Friday, revealing the breadth of President Donald Trump's attempts to mold parts of the District of Columbia as he wishes — and the underlying executive authority claims that lie beneath them. The cases involved are an impending shutdown and reconfiguration of a historic public golf course and the construction of the monumental arch that, at 250 feet (75 meters), would be 100 feet taller than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch. The two projects are barely three miles or five kilometers apart. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The hearing on the proposed golf course change began as other recent ones have: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes grilled Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. over how Trump's desires to turn the golf course, near the National Mall, into a world-class facility have become urgent plans that match his public pronouncements. At one point, Reyes read the code of conduct to government attorneys on presenting erroneous or false information during a hearing. Reyes ordered Friday's hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated that there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed 15 months while work goes on. A flurry of Trump posts sets off chaos The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when officials from the Interior Department, Justice and National Park Service could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Wednesday night that the plans were real. "On Friday, October 30, 2026, the National Park Service will submit to the National Capital Planning Commission for review a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events," the notice said. Reyes locked in on the filing and Trump's multiple Truth Social announcements as she questioned Woodward. READ MORE: Trump says he will close historic D.C. golf course for 15 months of renovations At one point, as they talked about plans that Woodward said only came about this week, he slipped and included tree cutting as part of the preparation for the closure. Reyes responded immediately: "News flash." She allowed him to correct himself that the tree cutting, which occurred earlier this month, was not part of the plan to close the East Potomac Golf Links. She said she intended to appoint a special master to investigate the administration's statements to the court. Another case is also a referendum on executive authority The golf course lawsuit was one of two cases in court Friday dealing with the Trump administration's push to expand its executive authority as the president remakes the federal areas of the capital near the National Mall and along the Potomac River. Three courtrooms away, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan was to hold a hearing on a motion asking that she call a temporary halt to plans to begin construction as early as Nov. 5 on the memorial arch. The arch is opposed by a small group of veterans and an architectural historian who sued in federal court in Washington, saying Congress must endorse the project. READ MORE: Trump's memorial arch faces a new lawsuit from Arlington County, Virginia "The public interest leans heavily against allowing defendants to blaze ahead," the plaintiffs said in seeking the injunction. "This court should enter a preliminary injunction blocking defendants from beginning construction on Memorial Circle in the hope that they can render the arch a fait accompli before this Court has made a final determination." Legal experts who have been watching the numerous cases underway say that what might appear at first glance to be vanity projects are in truth cases that test the limits of presidential power. Past administrations pursued legal theories that were sometimes legally sound, sometimes not, said David Super, law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center. "But there was always the assumption that you would try to do things that were legal," he said. "What we're seeing here now is that if you think the federal courts can't stop you, you can do things there indisputably illegal. He said that's "going to do long-term damage to the country." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press

e6b7370770fe.text: A Texas grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales with a charge of second-degree aggravated assault Friday after prosecutors said he deliberately drove his SUV into a fleeing immigrant in early October. Why it matters: This may be the first time an ICE agent has ever been indicted in Texas, making it a rare case of a federal immigration officer facing state charges. What they're saying: Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare announced the grand jury's charge of second-degree aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, namely a motor vehicle. Morales faces two to 20 years if convicted, Teare said. "Just because you have an ICE badge or any badge, if you are in Harris County and you are violating our community members' constitutional rights, there will be repercussions," he said. Catch up quick: Morales struck Miguel Parra Hernandez on Oct. 10 as Parra Hernandez fled on foot. Parra Hernandez, a Mexican national who has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years, had no criminal record and no pending immigration proceedings against him before the incident, Teare said. ICE has said Morales and other agents were looking for a different man identified as a deportation target, but that man's relatives say he died nearly a decade ago. Teare said Parra Hernandez is still rehabilitating from his injuries but is in ICE custody. The other side: An ICE spokesperson called the indictment "nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians" in a statement to Axios. "Federal officers acting in the course of their duties can only be investigated by other Federal agencies. Local governments do not have the authority to run such an investigation." "Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct." Zoom out: Teare said Morales was among the "surge hires" as part of efforts to speed up President Trump's mass deportation agenda. The DA declined to go into detail about the agent's prior work history, but said he could "unequivocally tell you that I've reviewed 1000s of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around the state, and I'm not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person based on his past." He also said he had "concerns about a number of the individuals that were hired during that surge" based on the investigation, and "concerns about the length of time that they're trained, and about what that training entails." What we're watching: Morales could attempt to move the case to federal court and argue federal law shields him from state prosecution. Teare said he was prepared to litigate such a move. Go deeper: Questions about Lorenzo Salgado Araujo's killing by ICE remain - Axios Houston

807d81990916.text: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is endorsing a trio of insurgent Democratic candidates who are challenging his fellow California House Democrats, Axios has learned. Why it matters: This is an aggressive move by a potential 2028 presidential contender who styles himself as one of the few Democrats willing to get into direct confrontations with the party establishment. He has backed members of the progressive "Bloc" who have refused to commit to voting for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as speaker. This is territory where even other high-profile House progressives — including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), another potential 2028er — have largely refused to tread. Driving the news: "Today I'm endorsing three new generation leaders Angela Gonzales-Torres, Eric Jones, and Mai Vang," Khanna said in a statement first shared with Axios. Gonzales-Torres, a former local elected official challenging Rep. Jimmy Gomez, "will join us in our fight against corruption, to stand up for survivors, and to lead with a moral vision," Khanna said. Khanna said he has known Jones — a venture capitalist running against Rep. Mike Thompson — "for many years," calling him "a change agent who understands the working class and building a better life for those left out." Vang, a Sacramento City Council member running against Rep. Doris Matsui, "will call out the genocide in Gaza, be for taxing billionaires, and stand for Medicare for All and the working class," Khanna said. Between the lines: Khanna said he has a "tremendous respect and admiration," for Thompson, 75, who has been in office since 1999. "But voters are crying out for change." Khanna said of Matsui, 82, who has held her seat since 2005: "I respect Doris Matsui's incredible service to our state and nation. This is the time to pass the baton." Jones is 35. Vang is 41. Khanna did not reference Gomez, who is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee over allegations of sexual misconduct. Gomez has admitted to "personal mistakes outside my marriage," but said his actions were "consensual" and denied breaking House rules. Asked about potential backlash from his colleagues for endorsing against fellow Democratic incumbents, Khanna said in a brief interview with Axios, "I think we need a new politics in this country, and we need a new party." "I've always been a reformer and independent-minded, that's what I believe," he added. The other side: A spokesperson for Gomez's campaign told Axios, "Instead of some Silicon Valley politician, the people of Los Angeles care a lot more about what Planned Parenthood thinks, what local teachers, nurses, and unions think – and they all support Jimmy Gomez." Said Thomas Dowling, a spokesperson for Thompson: "San Francisco venture capitalist Eric Jones and his Silicon Valley supporters are trying to buy our congressional seat, but it's not for sale. Mike's support comes from the people who actually live here." Matsui's campaign manager Bill Wong told Axios: "Voters in our district care about real results. Doris Matsui delivers. That's why the local teachers, firefighters, nurses, and women's and environmental organizations who see those results up close are standing with her." The intrigue: Khanna previously endorsed Thompson this cycle, which the latter congressman touted on social media as recently as May. The Thompson campaign even sent out a text to supporters, the content of which was shared with Axios, that reads: "This is Ro Khanna. I endorsed Mike Thompson for CA-4." Asked about the apparent discrepancy, Khanna told Axios: "I wanted to endorse [Gonzales]-Torres and then Mai Vang ... and I just thought, 'it's time for new blood,' and wanted to endorse Eric Jones." "I think very highly of Mike. I had, with the delegation, endorsed him earlier, so it's nothing against him. I just think it's a new generation and we're seeing bolder progressives win across the country," he added. Catch up quick: Matsui, Thompson and Gomez are each locked in Democrat vs. Democrat general elections with their rivals. All candidates ran in a single jungle primary in June, with the top two finishers — regardless of party — moving to the Nov. 3 general election. That means, unlike the rest of their colleagues who faced primary challenges, the trio will have to wait a little longer to find out if they will be returning to Capitol Hill next January. State of play: Jones and Gonzales-Torres both finished second in their respective primaries, while Vang narrowly came out ahead of Matsui. Polls have shown Jones leading Thompson and Gonzales-Torres essentially tied with Gomez. A senior House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid thoughts on Matsui's reelection, said party leaders "think she is gone" next Congress.

eaeaf25f6a65.text: By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-rubio-welcomes-g20-foreign-ministers-to-atlanta-at-critical-moment Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Rubio welcomes G20 foreign ministers to Atlanta at 'critical moment' Politics Oct 30, 2026 2:10 PM EDT ATLANTA (AP) — The top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies opened two days of meetings in Atlanta on Friday after European objections to Russia's participation forced the U.S. to cancel a photo of the foreign ministers, underscoring deep rifts among the group over global crises. Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug on the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that usually helps kick off such diplomatic gatherings. But he still opened the talks, which otherwise went ahead as planned, with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "We are in a critical moment — I would call it a moment of choosing, and I would say not just for my country, the United States of America, but frankly, for the world," Rubio told his colleagues. "We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he added, pointing to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation. Many are posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order." Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they face. Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, U.S. tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade. Russia's presence at G20 gathering roils European allies Concerns about any prospects for the talks escalated when the Europeans balked at being photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Rubio decided to scrap the picture because he thought the controversy would be a distraction, according to two U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter. Some G20 countries had already expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance. The British foreign office said in a statement that the United Kingdom "has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that." Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said the cancellation of the group photo was "the right decision" by the U.S., telling media in Atlanta that "I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov." READ MORE: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes after call with Rubio German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said "there is no normality with Russia" but "we must exchange the controversies at the table here," the German news agency dpa reported. He added that "we also must not send falsely optimistic signals." Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. His presence in Atlanta could cause domestic political problems for Trump just days before the U.S. congressional midterm elections as well as roil the G20, according to Ian Kelly, a U.S. ambassador to Georgia during Trump's first term. "It seems politically boneheaded to invite him," said Kelly, who now teaches international relations and diplomacy at Northwestern University outside Chicago. The meeting in Atlanta is meant to set the stage for a G20 leaders' summit hosted by President Donald Trump at his Miami golf club in December. It is unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump's invitation to that gathering. G20 member South Africa was not invited Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as U.S. officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group. But missing from the invite list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top U.S. officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted. READ MORE: Rubio says U.S. pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile' "We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola. Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate "on an equal footing with other members" when Britain takes over the presidency next year. The Iran war hangs over the G20 event The U.S. has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea. The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors. But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. The Associated Pr

136f386e40d0.text: By — Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America By — Lekan Oyekanmi, Associated Press Lekan Oyekanmi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/an-ice-officer-has-been-charged-after-striking-a-man-with-a-car-in-houston Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter An ICE officer is charged with assault for striking a man with a car in Houston Nation Updated on Oct 30, 2026 2:41 PM EDT — Published on Oct 30, 2026 1:53 PM EDT HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was indicted by a grand jury Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said. The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, the Harris County District Attorney's Office said. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, District Attorney Sean Teare said. READ MORE: ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas prosecutor says ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Teare said is contradicted by video. "The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated," Teare said. Morales, 33, of Brownsville, Texas, is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, although other encounters have come under investigation, including a fatal shooting by an ICE officer this summer in Houston. Morales' attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client didn't commit a crime and he accused Teare of indicting Morales "for political gain." Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. "Mr. Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, that has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement," Lindenmuth told The Associated Press. "To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident — the DA's office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air." WATCH: ICE shooting of man in New York with child in his car sparks outrage Teare hinted at concerns over Morales' background but would not provide details. Morales, who is charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare. ICE asserted that local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties. "Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the agency said in a statement. The district attorney played Morales' body camera footage Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales' body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone. The video shows Morales making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes. Morales stops the vehicle, then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away. The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain. Morales is heard saying, "He got hit with a car, bro." It is not clear to whom he is talking. "I was coming in and I hit him with the car," Morales says. Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Teare. Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question. READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day. ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. Teare's office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement. ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years. Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation Teare has said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence "either intentionally or through gross negligence." He has said Morales left the scene before the vehicle could be impounded. In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had "weaponized his vehicle" before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account. Wilder reported from Austin, Texas. Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. This story was originally published by Civil Beat.
The Maui Department of the Prosecuting Attorney is expected to soon have an investigator working full-time on contractor fraud cases targeting survivors of the deadly 2023 Lahaina wildfire, county officials say.
Mayor Richard Bissen asked Maui County Council Chair Alice Lee to introduce legislation to authorize the new hire after the department experienced a rise in the number of reports related to post-disaster contractor fraud. Last week, the council unanimously voted to advance the bill, with final passage expected on Nov. 13.
“This was an underreported crime at one time, where people may have felt embarrassed or didn’t know who to go to, or didn’t want to say what happened to them,” Bissen told Civil Beat Wednesday. “But I think since more people have come forward, others feel comfortable coming forward, especially if it’s the same individual whose name is brought up.”
The mayor’s request came in the weeks after Civil Beat and Inside Climate News co-published a joint investigation revealing that even though dozens of wildfire survivors have reported serious problems with the contractors they hired to rebuild their homes, government officials had not announced any actions against contractors for post-wildfire misconduct.
Contractors stopped showing up, were unable to account for large sums of money paid to them or performed work so poorly it had to be redone. Civil Beat and Inside Climate News reviewed hundreds of pages of public and private records, including police reports, court filings, contracts and text messages exchanged between contractors and property owners. Many community members said they believe contractor fraud and misconduct in the Lahaina burn zone is a far bigger problem than documented in official reports.
Maui prosecutor Andrew Martin told Civil Beat that he believed the story was among the factors that helped people feel more comfortable speaking to officials about their negative experiences with contractors.
“I think it’s all helpful,” he said, adding that the increase in reports also followed a Lahaina community meeting during which he and other county officials gave a presentation on post-disaster contractor fraud. “There is this segment of the population that, for a variety of different reasons, are not comfortable coming forward, and the more we get it out there, I think it puts people in a position to say, ‘OK, someone out there is going to listen.’”
The investigative services division of the prosecutor’s office currently employs six investigators. The legislation would amend the Fiscal Year 2027 budget to let the department hire a seventh. This would allow Martin to assign one of his office’s investigators to work full-time on active contractor fraud investigations, he told council members last week.
“These cases — because of the need to be able to distinguish between whether or not this is a civil complaint or a criminal complaint — are complex and involved,” Martin said at the meeting Friday. “I need to be able to assign an investigator to this full time.”
Martin has said his office had a deputy prosecutor and an investigator dedicating most of their time to reports of contractor fraud targeting wildfire survivors. He said this week that a recently hired deputy prosecutor — a former assistant U.S. attorney with complex white-collar experience — will also be assigned to the project full-time when they begin work on Nov. 6.
“When I talked to my team about what their needs are right now, they indicated they needed another investigator,” Martin told Civil Beat Wednesday. “That’s just where we’re at in terms of the current workload.”
There would be no immediate cost associated with adding the additional salaried staff position, according to an Oct. 15 letter to the council from Maui Budget Director Lesley Milner. Martin said during Friday’s council meeting that the new investigator would be funded through cost savings.
The need for another investigator “arises from the unforeseen scope and complexity of investigating potential contractor fraud related to the 2023 Maui wildfires,” Milner said in the letter. “As the investigations progressed, the department identified significant workload demands involving the review of financial records and contractual documentation, interviews with witnesses and victims, and preparation of cases for potential prosecution.”
The prosecutor’s office began referring tips related to contractor fraud to the Maui Police Department in May 2025, and the prosecutor’s office eventually opened its own investigation in an effort to more quickly move cases forward, according to Martin.
“We’re now moving on to a second one,” he told council members last week. “These investigations are incredibly time-consuming. The number of financial records that we are gathering through search warrants and subpoenas … are voluminous.”
Martin added that the new hire would also be in support of his efforts to improve his office’s ability to investigate other white-collar crimes, including elder abuse — “one of the fastest-growing areas of fraud-related, financial-related crimes in the country,” he said. “We’re going to need to be able to address that in a meaningful way and do it quickly.”
Bissen was glad to see council members unanimously support adding another investigator to Martin’s staff, he said.
“I really do think it’s prioritizing the needs of the folks who are already struggling and going through a difficult time,” Bissen said. “The question for us is: How do we help recoup people’s money? How do we hold people accountable? How do we stop them from doing this to others? Those are all the goals behind this bill, and I’m grateful that the council took it up.”
Council member Tamara Paltin, who represents Lahaina, said she personally knew fire survivors who had lost hundreds of thousands of dollars to the contractors they hired to rebuild their homes after the fire.
